Sports.title: Former Premier League star and son of Chelsea legend looks unrecognisable with dramatic new muscular look
Sports.content:
THE son of a former Premier League cult hero has undergone a dramatic body transformation since hanging up his boots.

Players are no strangers to drastic new looks after calling it a day, with many piling on the beef due to a lack of exercise.



Some, however, opt to go down the health and fitness route.

Former Arsenal and Chelsea stars Mesut Ozil and Fernando Torres are part of that group having put on several pounds of muscle since their respective retirements.



And the same has been done by Diego Poyet, the son of former Chelsea and Tottenham ace Gus.

Former Charlton and West Ham ace Diego retired from professional football in 2020, two years after his departure from Pafos.



Diego has clearly hit the gym hard over the last six years, as he’s no longer the lean and mean running machine he was once.

He’s now a hulking ball of muscle with biceps a prime Arnold Schwarzenegger would be proud of.

Diego’s passion for bodybuilding is apparent from his Instagram page, which is full of videos of himself performing some incredible lifts in gruelling workouts.

His incredible body transformation is clearly the result of hundreds of hours of grafting in the gym and adhering to a strict diet.



And according to his old man, it’s also the result of him forgoing several of life’s pleasures.

The Uruguayan said of his son’s transformation into a bodybuilder: “From what I understand, because I’m not a specialist, is he’s 100 per cent in everything that he does – to the top.

“For example, we went to dinner one day and people will have a beer or a glass of wine – no chance.



“He doesn’t touch alcohol. Never.

“We finished dinner and we put three or four desserts in the middle; proper, proper desserts.

“I love them, but he doesn’t touch them.



“So his way of behaving, what his aim is, he’s 100 per cent, he’s not 99 per cent.

“His way of training, knowing when he needs to grow, when he needs to slim down, when he needs to do a kind of diet, it’s all proper.”

Sports.title: Micky van de Ven signs new deal in huge Tottenham boost with defensive partner Cristian Romero OPEN to Arsenal transfer
Sports.content:
MICKY VAN DE VEN has handed Tottenham a huge boost by signing a new contract with the club.

The Dutch defender has committed his future to Spurs after developing into one of the Premier League’s top centre-backs since arriving from Wolfsburg in 2023.



Micky van de Ven, 25, told the club’s website:: “It’s a special moment to sign a new deal and a proud moment for me and my family.

“I’ve always loved Spurs, from the first day I stepped in here. I love the Club, I love the fans and I’ve developed really well here.



“It’s clear the direction the Club wants to go in and I want to be a part of it. I’m excited about what’s to come.”

His commitment is particularly significant with defensive partner Cristian Romero expected to leave North London this summer.



SunSport revealed World Cup winner Romero, 28, is OPEN to joining Tottenham’s bitter rivals Arsenal.

The Gunners are understood to be interested in the Argentine, while Atletico Madrid and Inter Milan are also admirers.

But Spurs have NO intention of selling Romero to Arsenal and a high-level club source has told SunSport they would not entertain doing business with their fiercest rivals.

Romero still has three years remaining on his contract, leaving Tottenham in a strong negotiating position over his future.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Sol Campbell was the last player to move directly from Spurs to Arsenal when he made his infamous free transfer in 2001.

Nobody has crossed the North London divide in either direction since William Gallas joined Tottenham after leaving Arsenal in 2010.

While uncertainty surrounds Romero, Spurs have now ensured Van de Ven will remain a key part of Roberto De Zerbi’s plans.

The Netherlands international captained Tottenham for the final six matches of last season and is closing in on 100 appearances for the club.



He has played 96 times and scored ten goals, having featured 45 times in all competitions last term.

Boss De Zerbi said: “Micky is one of the best centre-backs in Europe and an important player for us.

“He has the qualities, mentality and ambition that we want at Tottenham Hotspur, and I am very happy that he has decided to continue his journey with the Club.

“We are building something strong here, and players like Micky are an important part of that future.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Spurs will feel the re-signing of Van de Ven is another booster to an already strengthened squad – alongside marquee arrivals like Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, and fellow Dutchman Jan Paul van Hecke.



The squad has also been heavily reinforced with the experienced depth of Andy Robertson, Marcos Senesi, and Martin Dubravka.

Sports.title: Jeff Bezos set to hand Liverpool £1.5BILLION kitty boost as Bradley Barcola and Alex Scott targeted after Ronald Araujo
Sports.content:
AMAZON magnate Jeff Bezos is on course to deliver Liverpool a major boost by completing a £1.5BILLION investment.

Bezos’ consortium is close to finalising a deal to buy around a third of the Anfield club from Reds owners Fenway Sports Group.



And his business expertise should see Liverpool’s revenues increase further — meaning even bigger transfer sprees down the line.

Virgil van Dijk yesterday admitted his side need to sign more quality as Barcelona captain Ronald Araujo arrived on loan to bolster new boss Andoni Iraola’s defence.



The Reds have so far spent just £34.5million on Spanish winger Victor Munoz from Osasuna, with defender Jeremy Jacquet arriving from Rennes in a £60m deal that was struck in January.

It has been a conservative summer in comparison to the previous one where the club lavished an incredible £452.5m on new players — including £130m on a British transfer record deal for Alexander Isak.



Hinting that Liverpool’s squad needs upgrading, skipper Van Dijk, 35, said: “Any quality we can add to the team will definitely be welcome.”

Bezos has an estimated net worth of around £192BN after founding e-commerce giant Amazon.

He is part of a consortium led by British-Indian businessman Amit Bhatia, which includes Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.

If the consortium can help drive up revenues — from a club-record £703m — then it will allow the Reds to splash even more cash under Uefa and the Premier League Squad Cost Ratio rules.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Premier League clubs can spend 85 per cent of their revenue on football- related salaries, though that is restricted to 70 per cent for clubs in Europe.

Liverpool CEO Billy Hogan has already confirmed that the club are considering a partial sell-up.

FSG — principally owned by John Henry — paid £300m to buy the Reds in 2010 and have only sold off around four per cent of the club, to global sports investment firm Dynasty Equity in 2023.



A deal to sell around one-third of the club for £1.5bn would value Liverpool at a staggering £4.5bn.

Hogan said: “John Henry has been very up front about the fact that if there ever was an opportunity for investment that would help the club, then they would seriously consider it.

“In this case, a consortium led, managed and represented by Amit Bhatia has come forward to make a minority investment in the club.”

FSG declined to comment on whether a deal is close to completion but, with progress understood to have been made, the news will excite Spanish boss Iraola.

One priority has been to replace Mo Salah, who left this summer and joined Trabzonspor on a free transfer.



Liverpool want to sign more superstars — although talks have stalled over a bid for Paris Saint-Germain’s Bradley Barcola, with the Reds well short of the Champions League holders’ £128m valuation of the French winger, 23.

Bournemouth midfielder Adam Scott is another target.

But FSG have baulked at the £80m asking fee set by Iraola’s former club.



Iraola has also complained that he is desperately short of experienced defenders — and Barcelona’s Araujo, 27, last night completed a season-long loan which Liverpool have an option to make permanent for £47.1m.

Uruguayan Araujo, who will wear the No 33 shirt, said: “Without a shadow of a doubt, the aim is to win trophies.

“We need to be battling it out on all fronts. You aim high at a club like this — that’s what we’ll all be doing.

“It was the ideal move for me at this stage in my career, a move that was necessary for me to take.



“My attributes will suit this league down to the ground.

“The style of play in the English league should be perfect for my qualities as a player.

“We all know what a great player Virgil is.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“He’s a real reference point for the team and he’s a kind of role model and reference for me personally as well.

“I am excited to have that opportunity and will enjoy learning from him and playing alongside him.”

Sports.title: Tom Cleverley backs Man Utd pal Michael Carrick to lead new generation of English managers to conquer the Premier League
Sports.content:
CLEVER BOY Tom Cleverley backs Man Utd pal Michael Carrick to lead new generation of English managers to conquer the Premier League

TOM CLEVERLEY wants a new generation of home-grown managers to follow Michael Carrick and reclaim their place at the top of world football.

The Plymouth boss believes the success of Spanish titans like Pep Guardiola, Mikel Arteta, Unai Emery and Andoni Iraola should spur on English coaches.



And he points straight to his former Manchester United team-mate Carrick as the man leading the charge.

Cleverley, 36, said: “We must acknowledge the dominance of Spanish coaches in this era at international, Champions League and Premier League level.



“They’re a football superpower at the minute. That motivates English coaches like myself, Jack Wilshere at Luton and Richie Wellens at Orient in League One or Gary O’Neil who has gone in at Ipswich in the Prem.

“Eddie Howe has been up there for a while before he stepped down at Newcastle — but a big motivation of mine as a coach is can we put English coaches on the map again?

“Michael Carrick, we hope, can really stamp his authority at United and put English coaches on the radar of the top four.

“That would do tonnes for the young or middle-aged English coach.

“Frank Lampard getting back into the Premier League on the back of winning promotion with Coventry, we’re all rooting for him to take it on to the next level.”



Tactically, Cleverley refuses to be boxed in by modern stereotypes or rigid identity — taking inspiration from those top bosses while relying on an Old Trafford legend’s advice.

SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

The former England player said: “I couldn’t speak highly enough of guys like Emery, Guardiola and Arteta.

“The reason they’ve had so much success is how much they’ve adapted to English football. They embraced the high intensity, valuing the basics and the dark arts.

“To match that level, you have to embrace the modern game too. I am very aware of the data. Shots on target and xG are big for me, as is high-speed running.

“I’m a bit of a hybrid. My philosophy is always, one, how do I get the best out of my players? Two, how do I create the best environment for success?



“And three, do you attack their box more than they attack yours?

“I want my team to be entertaining. Sir Alex installed that in all of us: ultimately, if we’re not getting bums off seats, we’re not doing our job.”

The former England, United, Everton and Watford midfielder is carving out his own path in Devon.

After 14 months in charge of the Hornets, he has been at Plymouth since last June — missing out on the League One play-offs by just two points.

Argyle face some of the most gruelling away trips in English football.



But Cleverley has turned their extreme geographical isolation into a real weapon.

He said: “I don’t want to use the phrase siege mentality but because we’re so far from everywhere, there’s a real togetherness and passion.

“Down here in the south-west, it’s Argyle from Penzance all the way to Exeter or Bristol.

“So it’s really got that togetherness and real passion, which I think is healthy for a club. We embrace that as players and staff.

“Because we’re fairly isolated, the city completely revolves around the military and football club. We enjoy that responsibility.



“Our players are probably with each other more than any other club in the country. We use it to our advantage.

“The flip side of that is, can we make our home ground really uncomfortable for teams to come to, because they have to do the reverse?”

To cope with the brutal EFL travel schedule, Cleverley admits he regularly calls on his old friends at top-flight clubs to keep his squad fresh for matchdays.



He said: “We travel at 9am — that’s when the traffic’s the best.

“We try and get the best venue we can close to where we’re playing the next day, which is calling on a lot of favours from United and Everton.

“Recovery is of course important. If we played at Bradford on a Tuesday night and we’re not back until 4am, we do simple things like train late on Thursday — give them a lie-in to make sure they catch up on that missed sleep.

“Just small adaptations to make sure that we give them the best chance to deal with a challenge. We’ve dealt with the travelling really well.”

Transitioning into the dugout also meant learning how to command the dressing room — including managing players who were recently his team-mates or peers.



Cleverley explained: “I found it very easy sort of creating that distance. I don’t want to say barrier because I like to communicate, connect with the players, but I’m not going out for a drink with them anymore.

“I’m not sitting at their table for dinner because ultimately you’re the one who tells them they’re not playing.

“I’m that one that’s got to have some real honest conversations with them. So it’s a distance that I’ve been able to create as well as feeling really connected to them.

“I’m just myself, just trying to be myself. I think they can feel the honesty that I bring to the table and they respect that.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

TOM CLEVERLEY was speaking to SunSport ahead of the new season after Plymouth Argyle received a £65,000 grant from the Sky Bet EFL Building Foundations Fund to launch a new programme supporting women through perimenopause and menopause

Sports.title: Jose Mourinho’s Netflix revelation reopens old wounds for Sir Alex Ferguson over botched Man Utd succession
Sports.content:
JOSE MOURINHO’S tears over the Manchester United job first emerged shortly after David Moyes was appointed.

In Spanish journalist Diego Torres’ 2013 biography of Mourinho that charted his fraught three years at Real Madrid, chapter 1 is entitled “Crying”.



Staff at Jorge Mendes’s Gestifute agency “had heard him sobbing loudly and down the line” on the date Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement was announced, with it already established that David Moyes would replace him.

According to Torres, Mourinho had asked Mendes to “get in touch with United urgently”.



Some tidbits even made their way into the much-missed but defunct United fanzine Red Issue before Torres’s book hit shelves.

If Mourinho’s tears in his new Netflix documentary are nothing new, the revelation that he signed a contract with United before reneging is.



The water works are presented in a different context. Mourinho insists his “love” for Chelsea caused him to reject United.

The timelines stack up. Moyes was summoned to Ferguson’s home in Wilmslow on May 1. Days later, Sun Sport revealed that Mourinho had agreed to rejoin Chelsea.

Ferguson can be so economical with the truth he once imagined a fight between Juan Sebastian Veron and Gabriel Heinze at Portsmouth. Veron left United in 2003. Heinze signed in 2004.

When Moyes was announced on May 10 2013, the first bullet point on the club website read, “Manchester United Board unanimously approves the recommendation of Sir Alex Ferguson”.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

It also featured a rare quote from United co-owner Avram Glazer: “The search for a new manager has been very short. Alex was very clear with his recommendation and we are delighted that David has agreed to accept the job.”

Ferguson added: “When we discussed the candidates that we felt had the right attributes we unanimously agreed on David Moyes.”

The fallow period post-Ferguson has not reflected well on United’s greatest manager. In his 2013 autobiography, there was no mention of his approach to Mourinho.

In the updated version a year later, he attempted to suggest there was a “methodical procedure” to choose Moyes, as if the input of Avram, Joel and Bryan Glazer and Ed Woodward was required.

Ferguson released another book in September 2015 called Leading. Moyes was sacked in April 2014 and Ferguson’s latest tome clarified the “Chosen One” was actually the sixth-choice one



“I asked Pep to phone me before he accepted an offer from another club but he didn’t and wound up joining Bayern Munich in July 2013,” Ferguson wrote.

“When we started the process of looking for my replacement, we established that several very desirable candidates were unavailable.

“It became apparent that Jose Mourinho had given his word to Roman Abramovich that he would return to Chelsea and that Carlo Ancelotti would succeed him at Real Madrid.



“We also knew that Jurgen Klopp was happy at Borussia Dortmund and would be signing a new contract.

“Meantime, Louis van Gaal had undertaken to lead the Dutch attempt to win the 2014 World Cup.”

The mention of Van Gaal, the United manager at the time the book was released, was suspicious. Van Gaal was absolutely never in the running to replace Ferguson in the 2010s, so why mention him?

That Mourinho “had given his word to Roman Abramovich that he would return to Chelsea” tallies with the latest version of events.

In the Netflix documentary, Ferguson says: “One night, he phoned me and he was crying and he says: ‘Alex, I can’t take it. I’ve given my word to Chelsea and I’m not going to break my word.’”



To coincide with the 2015 book, Ferguson also appeared in the BBC documentary Sir Alex Ferguson: Secrets of Success. Mourinho was a contributor.

“He told me a huge secret,” Mourinho said of Ferguson’s retirement. “Not many people knew, like one month or two months before the decision to stop.

“I know that he trusts me because if he doesn’t he doesn’t tell me, but I was scared. I was scared.

“So when finally he informed the media about his decision it was a sense of relief.

“Every manager in the world looks at Manchester United as a huge club but I wanted to come to Chelsea and we didn’t bring that to the table.



“Because we were so open and he knew so much about myself that he knew for almost a season I wanted to leave Real Madrid and go to Chelsea.”

Given the documentary was aired two years after Ferguson had headed upstairs, perhaps the dust had not settled for him and Mourinho to disclose the contract signing. Hodder & Stoughton and Hachette Books missed out with Ferguson’s two tomes.

Ferguson said after his final match in charge at Old Trafford that he had not told his brother, Martin, until the evening of May 8 when the news leaked.

When United confirmed the appointment of Moyes, they attached a quote from Sir Bobby Charlton: “I have always said that we wanted the next manager to be a genuine Manchester United man.

“In David Moyes, we have someone who understands the things that make this such a special club. We have secured a man who is committed to the long-term and will build teams for the future as well as now.



“Stability breeds success. David has tremendous strength of character and recognises the importance of bringing young players through and developing them alongside world class talent.”

Charlton’s quotes were widely considered to be barbs aimed at Mourinho.

Only five months earlier, Charlton, a close confidant of Ferguson’s during his 26-and-a-half year epoch, said in an interview: “Mourinho is a really good coach but that’s as far as I would go really.



“He (Ferguson) doesn’t like him too much, though.”

However it all played out, United missed out. With Mourinho, they would have conceivably defended their title in 2013-14.

Mourinho would have commanded the respect of the dressing room. Moyes never lost the dressing room as he never won it over.

United had targeted Cesc Fabregas and Gareth Bale that summer. Bale had long had his heart set on a move to Real Madrid but Fabregas would have been more gettable. He ended up joining Mourinho’s Chelsea in 2014.

The Premier League landscape was ripe to be ridden roughshod over. Arsenal were also-rans under Arsene Wenger, Brendan Rodgers had failed to take Liverpool into Europe, Andre Villas-Boas soon spiralled at Tottenham and Chelsea would have been without their greatest manager.



Only Manchester City under new manager Manuel Pellegrini would have been credible competitors. City regained the title in 2014 and won six more under Guardiola, Ferguson’s first choice.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

United, meanwhile, are still stuck on 20 titles and their drought is ticking towards the 14-year mark.

That’s enough for some supporters to shed tears.

Sports.title: Nottingham Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis suing Crystal Palace over offensive banner that resulted in £50k fine
Sports.content:
NOTTINGHAM Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis is suing Crystal Palace over a banner displayed at Selhurst Park last season.

The controversial City Ground chief has taken to Palace to court after he was depicted holding a gun to Morgan Gibbs-White’s head.

That followed the breakdown of Gibbs-White’s planned move to Tottenham a year ago – with the Forest skipper signing a new deal instead.



Marinakis’ lawyers lodged a defamation claim in the High Court today, with CPFC Limited listed as a defendant – as the year-long feud between the clubs rumbled on.



The banner was unfurled during the sides’ August meeting in South London.

It also read: “Mr Marinakis is not involved in blackmail, match-fixing, drug trafficking or corruption.”

Marinakis has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to such allegations.



The FA charged Palace over the incident in November before handing them a £50,000 fine.

But two clubs have clashed off the field over the past 12 months – after Forest had challenged Palace’s place in the Europa League due to UEFA’s multi-club ownership rules.

As a result, Forest took Palace’s place in the Europa League, with the Eagles dropping to the Conference League which they won.

In another twist, Palace boss Oliver Glasner left the club and joined Forest this summer after being persuaded by Marinakis.



Daniel P. Astaire, Managing Partner of leading London law firm Grosvenor Law said: “Mr Marinakis will need to demonstrate not only that there is a defamatory meaning – which appears at first glance straightforward given the image – but that the ‘publication’ caused him serious harm.

“He will also need to show that Crystal Palace was liable for the publication.

“These points will both be challenging to prove.”

Sports.title: Liverpool sign Araujo from Barcelona
Sports.content:
Liverpool have confirmed the signing of defender Ronald Araujo from Barcelona.

The deal is an initial loan for the 27-year-old, who signed a new contract with Barca until 2031 last year, and also includes an option to buy for around £47.14m (€55m).

⁠Liverpool are not paying Barcelona a loan fee and will cover the entirety of Araujo's salary for the duration of the season-long loan. It is understood Araujo has taken a pay cut to facilitate the move.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Liverpool sign Barcelona defender Ronald Araujo on loan with an option to buy.

Araujo, who will wear the No 33 shirt, told Liverpoolfc.com: "I can't wait to get started. I'm very, very happy.

"I'm excited to be here at this massive club with lots of history. I'm excited to meet my team-mates, excited to get started playing, and I'm very motivated and really up for getting going.

"I think it was the ideal move for me at this stage in my career. I think it was a move that was necessary for me to take. As soon as I heard that interest from Liverpool, everything went into action really, really quickly.

"As I say, I'm super-happy to be here and excited to get started. I'm glad about the interest and it was the right move at the right time."

The Uruguay international, who did not play at the World Cup due to injury, is expected to train with his new team-mates this week.

Araujo will add to Andoni Iraola's options at the heart of his defence following the departure of Ibrahima Konate to Real Madrid and fitness concerns over inexperienced 21-year-old Jeremy Jacquet.

Jacquet, a summer signing from Rennes, has made fewer than 100 senior career appearances and has not featured in pre-season yet after missing the second half of last season following shoulder surgery.

Joe Gomez suffered a muscle injury in Liverpool's opening pre-season game, while teenage centre-back Giovanni Leoni is still recovering from an ACL injury, leaving captain Virgil van Dijk as Liverpool's only fully-fit senior centre-back.

Image: Liverpool have signed Barcelona defender Ronald Araujo on a season-long loan

Araujo, who can play at right-back and centre-back, moved from his native Uruguay in 2018 and made his Barcelona debut the following October, going on to play more than 200 games for the LaLiga side.

He was named as one of the club captains following the departure of Marc-Andre ter Stegen in January, but started only 11 LaLiga matches for the Catalan giants last season after an extended break from football in November 2025 to recover from what he later revealed was depression.

Why the Araujo deal works for Liverpool...

Liverpool had not been actively seeking out defensive reinforcements, their priority firmly on adding a wide forward, but this was a market opportunity that made sense for a number of reasons.

Ronald Araujo can play at centre-back or right-back, and, crucially, he was available on loan. This offered an appropriate solution to injury concerns that are deemed to be more short-term.

Liverpool have already committed £60m to signing Jeremy Jacquet from Rennes, with a view to him partnering Virgil van Dijk at centre-back.

However, it remains to be seen if he will be fit for the start of the season, as Liverpool take caution with his re-integration to competitive action following a shoulder injury that has kept him out since February.

A muscle problem for Joe Gomez, which will keep him out for the Premier League opener against Newcastle, has worsened the problem for new head coach Andoni Iraola, who by his own admission is slim on options at the back.

Araujo arriving on a temporary move alleviates that injury headache and adds a layer of experience to Liverpool's backline that is sorely missing. He has played more than 200 games for Barcelona after all.

There are understandable concerns around whether Araujo can turn around his struggles with form and fitness. Liverpool are not short on defenders with patchy injury records.

Liverpool are taking on a deal with an element of risk in that regard. But there is also a potentially big reward if Araujo does rediscover his best form thanks to the option to buy inserted in the deal worth around £47m.

At the peak of his powers, Araujo was being valued at around double that figure. Liverpool will hope to see his best in the Premier League, a division which is seemingly suited to his strengths.

How Liverpool were able to get Araujo

This is a deal that suits all parties. Liverpool require defensive cover amid injury worries around a number of players, while Araujo is not part of Hansi Flick's plans at Barcelona and is in need of a fresh start.

Araujo signed a new contract with Barcelona last year in January that reportedly put him among the club's highest earners. Six months earlier, he had been named Barcelona's vice-captain.

However, the Uruguay defender has since been unable to reach the heights that earned him such high status at Barcelona amid struggles with injury and his mental health.

Araujo wore the captain's armband as Barcelona celebrated becoming champions of Spain in May, but he had only played 24 times throughout the season.

Flick admitted when confirming the deal that Araujo was not suited to the way he wants to play and said the defender was excited about having the chance to move to a new environment.

Barcelona can now bring in a defender that Flick wants to work with, and Araujo has the opportunity to rebuild his career in the Premier League. If he performs, they will either earn a decent fee from Liverpool or his value will increase.

Sports.title: Sciver-Brunt helps Trent Rockets Women into Hundred final
Sports.content:
England all-rounder Nat Sciver-Brunt timed her introduction to perfection as 32 off 19 balls batting down the order secured Trent Rockets' progress to the final of The Hundred with a seventh successive victory.

Chasing 118 to win, the league leaders slipped to 10-3 against Southern Brave, the lowest powerplay score in the history of the competition, and even though passing 27 guaranteed their place in the final, the result remained in doubt.

Sciver-Brunt came in at number seven with the score on 66-5 and with 31 deliveries remaining - Ash Gardner having top-scored with 37 - and her experience avoided further drama.

She was run out going for a second which would have clinched victory, but Rockets still won with two balls to spare.

Southern Brave's 117-5 was built around their top order with Maia Bouchier scoring 38, Lizelle Lee 31 and Laura Woolvaardt adding 24.

They will get a second chance as they had already secured a place in the eliminator on Friday at The Kia Oval. Brave will discover their opponents on Tuesday, who will either be third-placed SunRisers Leeds or fourth-placed Manchester Super Giants who play each other at Emirates Old Trafford in their final group match.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Georgia Adams was run out in unfortunate fashion after Sarah Glenn fumbled a drive from Nat Sciver-Brunt and deflected the ball on to the stumps

Sciver-Brunt said: "I'm happy to be on the winning side. The wicket was a bit slow, and they bowled pretty well in the first half."

On batting down the order, she said: "It was a bit tactical and a bit injury management. We have got a lot of people in form and high on confidence. We have balanced our side nicely and building up to Sunday we sort of know what we need to do."

Sports.title: Rangers meeting Q&A: McInnes-Klopp compared, club failure admission & new signings update
Sports.content:
Rangers chairman Andrew Cavanagh believes the Ibrox side have become used to finishing second or worse over the last 15 years, and admits that failure had begun to "seep through" every corner of the club.

He was speaking at the club's shareholders' meeting, where it was also revealed they expect to add three to five more players this window, while Derek McInnes' appointment was compared to that of former Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp.

It was also confirmed that Rangers have asked for an explanation over Hibernian's penalty in Sunday's 2-1 defeat as refereeing concerns were raised.

Image: Jim Gillespie was appointed Rangers chief executive in January

Chairman Andrew Cavenagh, Paraag Marathe of the San Francisco 49ers [who are part of the US consortium who took over the club], executive director Fraser Thornton and chief executive officer Jim Gillespie addressed a number of club issues and answered questions from the floor.

Here are some of the key takeaways...

On Derek McInnes

Image: Derek McInnes left Hearts to take charge of Rangers this summer

During the meeting, one shareholder asked why Derek McInnes, the man they wanted to ask questions to after a winless start to the season, was absent. Andrew Cavenagh explained that the panel had been arranged months ago and that McInnes' focus was at the training ground to help prepare the team.

When asked later about the process behind hiring McInnes, Jim Gillespie said you can either hire a 'Klopp' or a 'Guardiola' type. He said McInnes fitted the 'Klopp' type of being a manager who wants his teams to be agressive, on the front foot and attack the opposition.

During the summer when McInnes was appointed, Sky Sports News revealed he was the only candidate who was spoken to, and Gillespie defended that by adding he was the only option Ibrox chiefs felt "ticked all the boxes".

Cavenagh reminded shareholders that "culture eats strategy for breakfast", and when speaking about standards, revealed people had been late to training and not eating well. He went on to say he believed McInnes was the right man to address this.

On Recruitment

Image: Daisuke Yokota is one of nine summer signings at Rangers so far

Multiple shareholders raised concerns about player recruitment. However, Cavenagh defended the work in that department, adding he believes the squad is better than it was 12 months ago.

He admitted the team still requires between three and five more players before the end of the transfer window.

The meeting was called following a £16m share issue. Cavenagh confirmed that was needed to get the club through this "significant" summer transfer window. He added the club "will need more capital going forward".

Marathe insisted that they were "building something special" and referenced Youssef Chermiti's performances in the second half of last season, after initially struggling with the pressure of his price tag and playing for Rangers.

Image: Youssef Chermiti was injured in Sunday's defeat to Hibs, hours after it was revealed a bid had been rejected for the striker

On Chermiti, the club hierarchy were asked why he was selected for Sunday's match against Hibernian despite being the subject of a bid from Galatasaray. The striker was subsequently stretched off injured in the first half of that defeat.

It was explained that to accept a bid, Rangers need their value of the player to be met, and for sufficient time to reinvest those funds in the squad to make it equal or better. They reiterated there is no pressure to sell.

On Refereeing standards

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Hibernian were awarded a first-half penalty in their 2-1 win at Rangers

Gillespie said that Rangers should be a leading club and want to have a constructive relationship with the Scottish FA and SPFL, while also holding both to account.

He was interrupted by a shareholder who said: "It's not working. It's been going on for years, nothing happens."

Marathe replied: "You're not wrong" but backed up Gillespie by saying, "we can't make it worse, we can't be in any more of what feels like a disadvantage".

Marathe added "he couldn't believe" the decision to award Hibernian a penalty in the first half of Sunday's match at Ibrox. Gillespie confirmed that Rangers have made contact with the Scottish FA to seek an explanation.

On Ibrox stadium

Image: Ibrox could be redeveloped with several proposals being considered

Marathe - who has overseen stadium expansion at Leeds United and the 49ers - discussed possible changes at Ibrox.

He said there would be news on that soon, while revealing one proposal is to lower the pitch at Ibrox, adding 5,000 to 6,000 seats.

It was also revealed, following fan surveys, a number of other ideas have been through a feasibility group and seen by architects.

Call for unity

Sports.title: Donald Trump says it would be a ‘terrible mistake’ to replace Fifa’s Gianni Infantino
Sports.content:
US president Donald Trump has warned Fifa would be making a “terrible mistake” if they get rid of Gianni Infantino as the head of world football’s governing body.

Infantino has come under pressure following his doomed plan to sell off stakes in the men’s World Cup to private investors.

But in a post on his Truth Social social media site early on Tuesday, Trump said removing the Fifa president would be a costly move.

The US president wrote: “Fifa would be making a terrible mistake if, for any reason, they even considered replacing president Gianni Infantino.

“He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented. If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again!”

Uefa and two other confederations have held initial talks about organising competitions themselves amid the backlash against the embattled Fifa president.

Europe’s governing body, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Concacaf, which oversees football in the ‌Caribbean, North and Central America, have accused Infantino of “deception” and while it is understood they want to give him the chance to resign and leave his position with dignity without seeking re-election in March next year, they want to insulate themselves from the unfolding crisis.

Uefa has previously threatened a boycott of Fifa competitions.

Infantino apologised for his proposal to create Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), a company to run the commercial and operational aspects of Fifa’s tournaments, with an idea to sell off around 20% to private investors.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

But an open letter signed by the heads of Uefa, AFC and Concacaf has urged Fifa to hold an independent review into Infantino’s scheme, while not naming the Swiss directly.

“Leadership in football is not a possession,” the letter said. “It is not about holding – or demanding – power to be held. It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it.

“When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned.”

Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 3: Bournemouth
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 12th (NB: this is not necessarily Ben Fisher’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 6th

Prospects

It was the day after the final game of last season at Bournemouth’s secluded, swish training base and, before clearing his belongings on his last day in the building, the departing head coach, Andoni Iraola, spent a couple of hours in his office chewing the fat with his successor, Marco Rose, talking players, pubs and tactics. The story goes that, with time moving on, Tiago Pinto, the club’s sporting director, knocked on the door to advise them there were other things to tackle.

It was an interesting scenario that speaks volumes of the respect between the pair. Long before joining Bournemouth, Iraola cited Rose’s Borussia Mönchengladbach side as one of his favourite teams to watch, the German’s “vertical football” helping them qualify for the Champions League in Rose’s first season in charge.

Rose accepts that Iraola, in absorbing the sales of key players totalling more than £250m last season and qualifying for Europe for the first time, has set a high bar. Remarkably, Bournemouth did not lose a game after the sale of Antoine Semenyo in the second week of January. Rose put it succinctly during pre-season in Austria. “Andoni didn’t leave a lot of space to improve,” he said. “Pressure’s on.”

In his first session, Rose told the players he loved the way they attacked the Premier League last season. Playing in the Europa League, however, represents uncharted territory for a team in the second tier as recently as four years ago. It is why Bournemouth’s hierarchy contacted peers at Crystal Palace and Nottingham Forest to understand the realities of juggling the Thursday-Sunday rhythm the competition will bring. Rose is close friends with Oliver Glasner, who is now at Forest, but won the Conference League last season with Palace. “We are not going to Europe just to enjoy, we want to be competitive,” Rose said. “We are not there just to watch.”

Unlike last summer, so far they have retained all key players, chiefly Alex Scott, Rayan and Eli Junior Kroupi, the 20-year-old forward who breezed into double figures in his debut Premier League season and the club consider a generational talent. Kroupi attracted serious interest from Paris Saint-Germain, among other European superpowers, but a freak foot injury during a pre-season drill means he is sidelined for at least three months.

At the end of the season, Bournemouth earmarked a centre-back to replace Marcos Senesi and a striker to compete with Evanilson as key priorities and by the start of August the club had recruited Álvaro Rodríguez, whom Rose wanted to sign at Leipzig, and António Silva from Elche and Benfica respectively. Juanlu Sánchez joined from Sevilla to provide competition for Adam Smith, the evergreen 35-year-old into his 14th season at the club, and will also fill the void left by Álex Jiménez, who has joined Fiorentina on loan with an option to sign permanently because he remains suspended in England while under investigation by the Football Association.

Off-field picture

The smallest stadium in the Premier League has been a building site this summer, with the club working to ensure their 11,357-seater ground complies with Uefa regulations. There has been a wider facelift, too, with every seat being replaced, while they are filling in two corners to increase the capacity by 800 this season. Playing in Europe brings the challenge of meeting Uefa’s squad-cost ratio (SCR) rules, which caps on-pitch spending at 70% of a club’s revenue. Bournemouth finished the 2025-26 season at 82% and they continue to work towards meeting the threshold. Last month the academy was awarded category one status, four years after being category three.

Owner-fan relationship

The American billionaire Bill Foley described himself as a dictator upon buying the club approaching four years ago, but supporters are grateful for his naked ambition. Foley, who made his fortune in insurance, is forthright and somewhat prophetic. In 2023, he said the club would play in Europe within five years – and achieved it in three. It was a similar story with Vegas Golden Knights, whom he vowed would win the Stanley Cup within six years of him launching the ice hockey franchise in 2017 – they won it in their sixth season. Foley recently added rugby union’s Exeter Chiefs to his sporting stable, which extends to Lorient, Auckland FC and Moreirense. Not every decision is universally popular but Foley, who turns 82 in December and predominantly splits his time between California and Vegas, puts his money where his mouth is.

The manager

As a defender, Marco Rose was schooled by Jürgen Klopp and Thomas Tuchel at Mainz, and Ralf Rangnick at Hannover, so had quite the education before beginning his coaching career at home town club Lokomotive Leipzig. Klopp told Rose, after promotion to the Bundesliga in 2004, that he would excel in the dugout and he has since managed some of the biggest names: Erling Haaland and Jude Bellingham at Borussia Dortmund, Dominik Szoboszlai and Dani Olmo at RB Leipzig. Rose has been compared to Klopp and, naturally, Iraola, given his appetite for high-energy tactics. Bournemouth routed Genoa 10-1 in pre-season so, could his style be even more aggressive than Iraola’s? “I would say [to be] even more aggressive than Andoni is quite difficult,” came the reply. His grandfather, Walter Rose, represented Germany in 1937.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen António Silva has all the attributes to be a bargain buy for Bournemouth. Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty Images

These days, £50m is about the going rate for an elite defender. Tottenham paid £52m to sign Jan Paul van Hecke. Chelsea paid the same fee to take Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace. Bournemouth pocketed £50m when Dean Huijsen joined Real Madrid last year, though that price was set by a release clause. They are deals that make Bournemouth’s £25.7m purchase of António Silva, a 22-year-old who has been a regular at Benfica since breaking into the team and has experience in the Champions League, Europa League and 20 caps for Portugal, appear a snip. Silva, who is right-footed but prefers to play as a left-centre back, is a direct replacement for Senesi.

Stat attack

Bournemouth scored nine goals from Opta-defined counterattacks last season, the joint most in the Premier League. But their threat was varied; in only two of their preceding eight top-flight campaigns did they score more set-piece goals than the 14 they managed in 2025-26. It is very rare for a team to be so productive on both fronts.

Set for a breakthrough

It was a November night of ecstasy when Scotland qualified for the World Cup for the first time in 28 years, but for Ben Gannon-Doak it was a bittersweet evening and one that curtailed his club season. The 20-year-old was forced off after 21 minutes, replaced by Kenny McLean who capped the scoring in style. A £25m arrival from Liverpool last August, Gannon-Doak featured in all three of Scotland’s World Cup matches, starting the first and last, and has impressed in pre-season. After being limited to 113 minutes in eight league appearances as a substitute last campaign, there is optimism Gannon-Doak will make his mark.

World Cup impact

Rayan became the first Brazilian teenager to start a World Cup match since Marco Antônio in 1970 when he was named in Carlo Ancelotti’s starting XI for their Group C game against Scotland. The then 19-year-old, signed from Vasco de Gama in January, set up Vinícius Júnior for Brazil’s opener in the 3-0 win and afterwards swapped shirts with Gannon-Doak. Tyler Adams enhanced his reputation, impressing for the USA en route to the last 16. Two new members of Bournemouth’s coaching staff, the set-piece coach, Nicolas Gagnon, and goalkeeping coach, Frederic de Boever, worked with Canada and Belgium respectively. Alex Scott’s inclusion in Tuchel’s pre-World Cup training camp in Florida spoke volumes of the Guernsey-born midfielder’s wider standing.

Sports.title: Liverpool owners close to £1.35bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff Bezos
Sports.content:
A consortium including the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, is close to completing a deal for a 30% stake in Liverpool after months of talks with Fenway Sports Group. The investors are led by Amit Bhatia, the son-in-law of the Indian billionaire Lakshmi Mittal and who previously was a shareholder and director at Queens Park Rangers.

The Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is another member of the group who will pay in the region of £1.35bn. The deal is effectively agreed, but may take up to a month to complete.

Bezos has a personal fortune of around $257bn (£190bn), according to Forbes, making him the fourth-richest person in the world, while Saverin is reportedly worth $32bn. This will be Bezos’s first investment in football, but he has previously looked into bidding for NFL franchises. The 62-year-old will receive equity as part of the deal, which Deloitte has advised on.

Bezos is the executive chair of Amazon having relinquished day-to-day control when he stepped down as chief executive five years ago. Under his leadership, the online retailer has diversified into being an entertainment provider and has bought numerous sports rights for its streaming service.

Amazon had live UK rights for 20 Premier League games each season for six seasons until the end of last year and broadcasts the Champions League in several European countries, as well as some NFL games in the US.

FSG bought Liverpool in 2010 and have overseen two Premier League titles. FSG sold 3% of the club to the US private equity firm Dynasty Equity in 2023.

It has been a summer of change at Anfield, with Andoni Iraola replacing Arne Slot as head coach, Mohamed Salah left on a free transfer and has joined Trabzonspor and Michael Edwards departed his role as chief executive officer at FSG.

Sports.title: Nottingham Forest owner Marinakis sues Crystal Palace over fan banner
Sports.content:
The Nottingham Forest owner, Evangelos Marinakis, is suing Crystal Palace for defamation after supporters of the south London club displayed a banner depicting him holding a gun to the head of the England midfielder Morgan Gibbs-White.

Almost 12 months since the banner appeared midway through the first half of Palace’s 1-1 draw with Forest at Selhurst Park, lawyers for Marinakis lodged the claim for defamation against CPFC Ltd and “persons unknown” at the high court on Monday.

The banner showed the Greek shipping magnate pointing the gun at Gibbs-White, who had been set to join Tottenham last summer before Forest pulled out of the deal, and also featured the message: “Mr Marinakis is not involved in blackmail, match‑fixing, drug trafficking or corruption.” Marinakis has previously rejected all those allegations. Lawyers for Marinakis were approached for comment. A spokesperson for Palace did not comment.

Palace were fined £50,000 by the Football Association in February after being found guilty of failing “to ensure its spectators and/or supporters (and anyone purporting to be supporters or followers) didn’t behave in an improper, offensive, abusive, insulting and/or provocative way at this match”. The FA added in its statement: “The fact that Crystal Palace had a policy to prevent banners being smuggled into the stadium demonstrates that it was aware of the risk.”

Last summer, Palace and Forest were at loggerheads after Forest wrote to Uefa to voice their concerns that Palace could be in breach of multiclub ownership rules. The FA Cup winners ended up being demoted to the Conference League, with Forest – who had finished seventh in the Premier League and originally qualified for the Conference League – promoted in their place. Palace went on to win that competition under Oliver Glasner, while Forest reached the Europa League semi-finals.

Glasner has since joined Forest after leaving Palace at the end of his contract in a move that has surprised both sets of supporters. The Austrian said this week that Marinakis had persuaded him to change his mind over dinner in Athens after previously rejecting Forest because they were not in Europe next season.

“Then I had a more detailed look and there are two reasons why I changed my mind and I told him,” Glasner said. “No 1 is I think there is more potential in the squad than they have shown. And No 2 is you, it’s your ambition, because I am very ambitious.”

Sports.title: Are Manchester United returning to relevance under Michael Carrick? | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Manchester United finally seem to have something that resembles stability in the dressing room under Michael Carrick. I feel with quality signings in defence and midfield, they could mount a decent challenge for the Premier League next season. How do you feel they will fare? – Sterling.

There’s an odd sense that Michael Carrick’s level of achievement last season was at precisely the most awkward level for the board. United didn’t produce indisputably brilliant football under him but equally 12 wins and three draws in 17 games was good enough that they pretty much had to give him the job. But it’s one thing to turn out those kinds of results when the pressure’s off, you’re already out of both cup competitions and you don’t have any European football; it’s quite another to do it in the heat of a full season. United don’t have to have an especially amazing season to play 15 more games this season than they did in 2025-26.

That’s not to say that Carrick won’t be successful. There was much that he did last season that was very impressive. Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans bolster an area of the squad that desperately needed to improve. A left-back seems almost certain to arrive before the end of the month and there’s probably the need for one more high-class experienced central defender. It’s not clear what Marcus Rashford’s future is after his return from loan at Barcelona, but he has two years left on his contract and could add dynamism and finishing to the left side of the attack. It’s probably not a title-winning squad, but it’s certainly one that should qualify for the Champions League.

Two questions remain that will only be answered as the season goes on. First, Carrick himself: can he cope with the churn of two games a week, and operating with a squad that is at least as fatigued as their opponents? And second, where is the club psychologically? Part of the problem for United, a familiar trait of big clubs who have fallen from grace, is that they have got into a routine of failure, that no success can ever quite be trusted, and every setback is seen as a further example of the terminal decline (although just as damaging would be suddenly believing everything is fine if United were to win, say, their first three games of the season). Retaining clarity of thought and making realistic assessments are perhaps the greatest challenges for a club that has known greatness but is struggling to return to those heights.

What do you see the broader impact of the VAR changes that Fifa made this year being? Do you think that other soccer leagues will see the increasingly automated, faster but less human approach taken by Fifa this summer and choose to adopt it? (I am aware that the Premier League has already chosen to reject much of it) – Dennis.

The most notable changes implemented before the World Cup allowed VAR to review and overturn incorrectly awarded corner kicks, certain attacking fouls and clear mistakes relating to red cards given from a second yellow. The only one of these adopted by the Premier League is to allow VAR to overturn a second yellow leading to a red (VAR cannot recommend that a referee should award a second yellow that would lead to a red). If we have to have VAR, that seems reasonable enough; nobody wants to see a team incorrectly reduced to 10 men.

At the World Cup, the corner issue only rarely came up, but it always seemed slightly odd that incorrectly awarded goal kicks could not be turned into corners. Personally, I would scrap VAR, or at least this form of it, but if incorrect decisions can be corrected quickly and unobtrusively then they probably should be. I understand, though, why the Premier League, aiming for a “light touch” – good luck with that – would be resistant.

Greater use of VAR, though, seemed to be the direction of travel. I suspect relatively soon offsides will be almost fully automated, which probably makes sense so long as it’s almost instantaneous. Whatever doubts there may be about margins of error and frame rates, it’s still going to be more accurate than a 40-year-old running the line 30 yards away, peering through a thicket of players.

More significant is probably the Premier League’s adoption of regulations against timewasting: speeded-up substitutions, players who receive treatment having to remain off the field for 60 rather than 30 seconds, an outfield player having to be withdrawn for 60 seconds after a goalkeeper receives treatment, and a five-second clock on throw-ins and goal kicks. All should speed up the game and improve the spectacle. It’ll be interesting as well to see the level of tolerance for grappling in the box, particularly by attacking players, which was an area in which the Premier League seemed out of step with the rest of Europe last season.

Which of the Premier League’s promoted sides have the best chance of staying up, and why? – Nicholas.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The achievements of Sunderland and Leeds last season, finishing seventh and 14th, will have heartened the promoted sides, but the truth is it will be extremely difficult for all three. Both those sides invested heavily in a way that is impossible for Coventry, Ipswich or Hull. It’s very hard to see how Hull, who were promoted unexpectedly, can survive. Coventry, perhaps, with the euphoria of their Premier League return and the Frank Lampard factor can give it a go, but their summer spending has been modest. Ipswich, with recent Premier League experience, have a chance and have made some intriguing signings in Daizen Maeda, Abdul Fatawu, Issa Diop and Chuba Akpom, but they’ve lost the manager who got them up, with Kieran McKenna opting for a break rather than another Premier League campaign. Gary O’Neil perhaps feels he has unfinished business, but if any of the promoted sides are to survive, they need another club to have a dreadful campaign.

Sports.title: Carabao Cup second-round draw: Chelsea host Luton, Forest at home to Leeds
Sports.content:
Five-time winners Chelsea have been handed a home draw against League One Luton in the second round of the Carabao Cup. Chelsea’s new manager, Xabi Alonso, will begin the club’s attempt to win the competition for the first time since 2015 later this month.

Fellow Premier League side Tottenham have also benefited from a home draw, against Championship opponents Charlton. The 11 top-tier sides not involved in European competition enter the draw in the second round, with the remaining nine following in round three.

Fulham host League One AFC Wimbledon, Brentford have a potentially tricky away day at second-tier Birmingham while Ipswich host Leicester. Also in the southern section West Ham, who beat Portsmouth in Saturday’s first round, travel to Championship side Southampton.
