World.title: At least 132 dead in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia
World.content:
At least 132 dead in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 08:51 UTC Full article

Pereira and its metropolitan area account for most of the dead

At least 132 people were killed and 570 injured by the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western and central Colombia on Monday, according to the latest report submitted by the Colombian Association of Capital Cities at 7:00 p.m. local time. Authorities warned the figure is preliminary and that rescue work is continuing.

The quake struck at 07:34, with its epicenter near the municipality of San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, at a depth of more than 80 kilometers, according to the Colombian Geological Service. It is the strongest recorded in the country in the past decade.

Pereira and its metropolitan area account for most of the dead. Departmental tolls released by governors and mayors correspond to different cutoff times and do not match one another: Chocó governor Nubia Carolina Córdoba-Curi reported 12 dead and 84 injured in that department, while the mayor of Manizales confirmed two deaths. Fatalities were also reported in Valle del Cauca and Antioquia.

| URGENTE: Momento del derrumbe de un edificio de 3 pisos tras el terremoto de magnitud 7,4 en Pereira, Colombia. pic.twitter.com/r3v2lW5pU3 — Alerta News 24 (@AlertaNews24) August 10, 2026

The government put the number of damaged homes at more than 1,500, with 37 destroyed and 61 buildings completely collapsed, along with damage to 18 health centers, 52 schools, 17 community centers and 18 roads. The civil aviation authority suspended operations at seven air terminals: Cali, Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura.

Damage to the hospital network is among the most critical. In Cali, the Hospital Universitario del Valle partially collapsed and seven large health care institutions were closed and evacuated because of structural damage. Valle del Cauca governor Dilian Francisca Toro said at least five intensive care patients were trapped under rubble. Cali mayor Alejandro Eder reported at least twenty collapsed structures with people trapped inside and requested rescue teams from Bogotá and Medellín. The capital's mayor, Carlos Fernando Galán, dispatched a hundred rescue workers.

De la Espriella agreed to declare a national disaster situation and is leading a unified command post at the National Disaster Risk Management Unit, with additional posts in Armenia and Quibdó. The foreign ministry is coordinating international cooperation. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc was ready to provide assistance.

The Colombian Geological Service reported two aftershocks, of magnitude 2.8 and 4.8. The agency also recorded an emission of ash and gases from the Puracé volcano, in Cauca department, on orange alert since July, coinciding in time with the earthquake.

World.title: Kast descarta impulsar el proyecto que condiciona el aborto a escuchar el latido fetal
World.content:
Kast descarta impulsar el proyecto que condiciona el aborto a escuchar el latido fetal

10th Monday, August 2026 - 19:40 UTC Full article

“It is legitimate for lawmakers to introduce their bills and for a debate to be generated around that, but we are not going to move forward on this matter,” the president said

Chilean President José Antonio Kast said on Monday that his government would not push forward a bill introduced by lawmakers from his own coalition that would condition access to legal abortion on a woman agreeing to hear the fetus's cardiac activity.

“It is legitimate for lawmakers to introduce their bills and for a debate to be generated around that, but we are not going to move forward on this matter,” the president said in an interview with T13 Radio. He recalled that his campaign centered on an emergency government focused on the economy, security and social issues, and that he would not promote measures that generate tension.

Kast also drew a distinction about the text itself. “In other countries, the heartbeat is voluntary. The difference with the parliamentary bill in Chile is that it was made compulsory,” he said.

The initiative, named “Escucha su corazón,” was introduced in July by lawmaker Cristóbal Urruticoechea of the Partido Nacional Libertario, with signatures from members of that party and of the Partido Republicano, founded by Kast. It would amend the Health Code so that when a woman requests an abortion, the physician informs her whether cardiac activity is detectable and offers her the chance to hear it. If she declines the offer, the practitioner would have to refrain from carrying out the procedure.

Abortion has been legal in Chile since 2017 on three grounds: risk to the woman's life, fetal unviability and rape. The law was passed during Michelle Bachelet's second term, and the bill would not repeal it.

Objections also came from within the governing coalition. The president of the Unión Demócrata Independiente, Guillermo Ramírez, called the proposal ineffective and difficult to enforce. Health Minister May Chomali said last week there is no scientific basis for expecting a woman to change her decision. The World Health Organization recommends that ultrasounds not be a mandatory requirement for accessing an abortion and that information provided be objective and not aimed at influencing the decision. In late July, hundreds of women demonstrated in Santiago and about 30 other cities under the slogans “Hear my heart” and “Hear my decision.”

Kast's position drew discontent among the bill's sponsors. “We will not give up, we will keep up the fight, the battle, until we rebuild everything that former president Gabriel Boric's government tore down,” Urruticoechea said. His fellow party member Paulina Muñoz said: “The defense of innocent life has no timetable. I expected more from the president.” The head of the Partido Republicano, Arturo Squella, agreed with Kast that the debate should remain in Congress without executive involvement.

Similar measures have been in force in Hungary since 2022 and in Spain's Castilla y León region.

World.title: De la Espriella gives the first earthquake toll and entrusts Colombia to Jesus Christ
World.content:
De la Espriella gives the first earthquake toll and entrusts Colombia to Jesus Christ

10th Monday, August 2026 - 19:16 UTC Full article

The toll, as of 12:30 local time, is preliminary

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella reported 111 dead and 87 injured on Monday from the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck the west and center of the country, in an address containing extensive religious references. “I entrust our country to the Lord Jesus Christ,” he said after chairing a meeting of the unified command post set up at the National Disaster Risk Management Unit.

The toll, as of 12:30 local time, is preliminary. The president listed 1,575 homes damaged and 37 destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, 18 health centers, 52 schools and 17 community centers damaged, 18 roads affected and six airports out of service. The priority, he said, is rescuing people trapped under rubble. The government agreed to declare a national disaster situation, to be signed during the day.

De la Espriella announced he would personally lead the response and issue updates every two or three hours. He will travel to Quibdó, capital of Chocó, with the health and defense ministers, while Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara Restrepo heads to the coffee-growing region and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera to Valle del Cauca. Command posts have been set up in Bogotá, Armenia and Quibdó. The foreign ministry will coordinate international cooperation, and the president said the country's allies had offered assistance.

“Today all Colombians, without ideological distinctions, have to unite behind a single cause: the victims of this natural disaster,” he said. He argued that those affected would recover “with the help of God,” of the government and of the international community, and asked God to “protect Colombia.” Unlike his earlier appearances, he did not close with his customary slogan, “Firm for the Homeland.”

Religious language has been a constant feature since before he took office. The president was sworn in on Friday using the constitutional formula “I swear to God,” closed a speech to troops in Cali with “Long live Christ the King,” and included an interfaith segment in the ceremony. Days earlier he had gathered his incoming cabinet at a spiritual retreat, after which he said that “God must be placed at the center of every decision.”

Those statements have opened a debate over the scope of state secularism. The 1991 constitution established a non-confessional state, and in 1994 the Constitutional Court struck down a provision requiring the president to renew annually the country's official consecration to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. Senator Jennifer Pedraza walked out of the inauguration session, saying the ceremony threatened the secular character of the state. Constitutional lawyer Juan Manuel Charry has argued, by contrast, that a public official retains personal convictions while exercising office.

World.title: Colombia records its strongest earthquake in a decade, geological service says
World.content:
Colombia records its strongest earthquake in a decade, geological service says

10th Monday, August 2026 - 14:29 UTC Full article

The quake struck at 07:34 local time (12:34 GMT), with its epicenter about five kilometers east of the municipality of San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, some 240 kilometers west of Bogotá

A magnitude 7.4 earthquake shook western and central Colombia on Monday, causing damage in several cities and affecting six airports. It is the strongest earthquake recorded in the country in the past decade, according to the Colombian Geological Service (SGC). No official casualty figures have been released so far.

The quake struck at 07:34 local time (12:34 GMT), with its epicenter about five kilometers east of the municipality of San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, some 240 kilometers west of Bogotá. The SGC initially reported magnitudes of 6.6 and 6.7 before raising the figure to 7.4 in a later bulletin. The focus was located at more than 80 kilometers depth, an intermediate range that explains why the tremor was felt across such a wide area. The agency has recorded two aftershocks, of magnitude 2.8 and 4.8, the second widely felt.

The earthquake was felt in Bogotá, Cali, Medellín, Popayán, Manizales, Armenia and Pereira, as well as in Panama, Ecuador and Venezuela. Buildings and hospitals were evacuated in the Panamanian capital. The National Disaster Risk Management Unit ruled out a tsunami threat along the Pacific coast.

In Manizales, one of the cathedral towers was severely damaged and left leaning against the main body of the church. At Pereira's Matecaña international airport, part of the roof came down in a passenger transit area. The civil aviation authority reported damage at the Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura terminals and suspended air operations at all of them pending structural assessment.

In Cali, the country's third city, facades came away, buildings collapsed and power, gas and water services were cut. Firefighters and rescue teams deployed to inspect structures while the municipal risk management council carries out its damage assessment. Injuries have been reported in Quibdó and at Pereira airport, without confirmed figures.

President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on Friday, ordered the establishment of a unified command post to coordinate the response and announced he would travel to Pereira. “You are not alone. The state is present and acting,” he wrote on his X account. He also requested a detailed report from the head of the national disaster risk management unit.

Colombia is one of the few countries in the world where three tectonic plates converge, and it records an average of 50,000 earthquakes a month, most of them imperceptible. The deadliest events in its recent history were the 1999 Armenia quake, magnitude 6.2 with close to 1,000 dead; the 1994 Páez quake, with about 800; and the 1983 Popayán quake, with 287.

World.title: Reform UK in talks with El Salvador over sending foreign prisoners to Bukele's jails
World.content:
Reform UK in talks with El Salvador over sending foreign prisoners to Bukele's jails

10th Monday, August 2026 - 09:23 UTC Full article

The precedent invoked by Reform UK is the arrangement reached by Donald Trump's administration with El Salvador

Britain's Reform UK party, led by Nigel Farage, has opened contacts with the government of El Salvador to transfer foreign prisoners to jails in that country should it win the next United Kingdom general election, which must be held by 2029 at the latest. The report was published on Monday by the newspaper The Sun and has not been confirmed by San Salvador.

The party's home affairs spokesman, Zia Yusuf, set out its prisons policy on Sunday night. “We will deport all foreign nationals from our jails. If their home countries won't take them back we will send them to serve their sentences in countries like El Salvador and Kosovo,” he said. Yusuf put the number of foreign nationals in British prisons at more than 10,000 and argued that the space freed up would keep dangerous offenders behind bars.

According to The Sun, a delegation headed by party chairman Lee Anderson will travel to Central America in the coming months to assess the feasibility of the scheme, which would involve renting prison places funded by the United Kingdom. The announcement also includes creating 12,000 places through temporary prisons and ending early release for those convicted of serious offenses.

The proposal emerges as Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces criticism over his early release program, which takes effect in October and would affect some 5,000 inmates. Burnham took office in July following the resignation of Keir Starmer, without a general election.

The precedent invoked by Reform UK is the arrangement reached by Donald Trump's administration with El Salvador. In March 2025, the United States deported 238 Venezuelans to the Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), opened in 2023 in Tecoluca with a stated official capacity of 40,000 inmates. As MercoPress reported in April 2025, President Nayib Bukele then announced plans to double the capacity of the facility, which held more than 15,000 prisoners.

CECOT is the emblem of Bukele's security policy and also its most contested element. Cells have no windows and family visits are not permitted, and human rights organizations have documented arbitrary detentions and deaths in custody under the state of exception in force since March 2022, which has produced more than 91,000 detentions without judicial order. In April 2026, 413 of the 486 defendants in the largest trial in Salvadoran history against the Mara Salvatrucha leadership appeared by video link from the prison, as MercoPress reported.

Farage is seeking on Thursday to regain the Clacton seat he vacated in July to trigger a by-election. His resignation came amid an investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner into an alleged undeclared gift of five million pounds, on which no findings have been reached.

World.title: De la Espriella sets ten armed group leaders as his target for his first 90 days
World.content:
De la Espriella sets ten armed group leaders as his target for his first 90 days

10th Monday, August 2026 - 08:32 UTC Full article

The first results came over the weekend

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has pledged to capture or kill ten leaders of illegal armed groups during the first 90 days of his term, which began on Friday in Cali. The commitment, made during his campaign, is the centerpiece of the “shock plan” with which the new president seeks to reverse the negotiation policy of his predecessor, Gustavo Petro.

De la Espriella inherits a country with nearly 29,000 members of organized armed groups and at least 14 zones of active dispute between illegal actors, according to security force estimates compiled by the Fundación Ideas para la Paz. The most critical areas are Catatumbo and Arauca, on the Venezuelan border; Cauca and Nariño, on the Pacific coast; Putumayo, bordering Ecuador; and the jungle department of Guaviare.

Those identified include Néstor Gregorio Vera Fernández, known as Iván Mordisco, head of the self-styled Estado Mayor Central, a federation of structures that split from the former FARC. Also Alexander Díaz Mendoza, alias Calarcá Córdoba, who leads the Estado Mayor de los Bloques y Frente, a breakaway from that group and now its rival; Jobanis de Jesús Ávila, alias Chiquito Malo, top leader of the Clan del Golfo, with more than 10,000 members; and the commanders of the 33rd Front and of the National Liberation Army's Northeastern War Front in Catatumbo, to whom the president gave a one-month ultimatum during a visit to Cúcuta. None has been convicted of the acts authorities attribute to them.

The first results came over the weekend. On Sunday, De la Espriella announced the killing of alias Ruso or Alemán, identified by the government as the man sent from Arauca to take command of the 28th Front, along with three other alleged members, in a joint military intelligence and air force operation in the area bordering Meta, Guaviare and Vichada. The same day, at least five alleged members of the Carlos Patiño structure died in an offensive in rural El Tambo, in Cauca, where several families were confined to their homes. On Saturday, a vehicle loaded with explosives had detonated beside a toll plaza under construction near Santander de Quilichao.

The International Crisis Group warned in a briefing published on inauguration day that the severity of the planned offensive carries risks. Decapitating these organizations tends to fragment them and to trigger internal disputes over territorial control, the document states, adding that Colombian forces are already operating at the limit of their capacity.

“The strategy of going after leaders tends to generate more violence, at least in the short and medium term,” said Elizabeth Dickinson, the organization's deputy director for Latin America. The most cited precedent is Dairo Antonio Úsuga, alias Otoniel, captured in 2021 and extradited to the United States: the Clan del Golfo grew stronger afterward.

World.title: Keiko Fujimori starts her term in Peru with 60% approval, Datum poll finds
World.content:
Keiko Fujimori starts her term in Peru with 60% approval, Datum poll finds

9th Sunday, August 2026 - 20:58 UTC Full article

The poll is the first national measurement since Fujimori took office on July 28, after winning the June 7 runoff by one of the narrowest margins in Peruvian electoral history

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori has begun her five-year term with a 60% approval rating, against 24% disapproval and 16% who gave no opinion, according to a Datum Internacional survey published on Sunday by the newspaper El Comercio.

The poll is the first national measurement since Fujimori took office on July 28, after winning the June 7 runoff by one of the narrowest margins in Peruvian electoral history. The Fuerza Popular leader took 50.135% of valid votes, or 9,223,396 ballots, against 49.865% for Roberto Sánchez of Juntos por el Perú, who received 9,173,755. The gap was 49,641 votes.

Despite that result, approval exceeds disapproval in every macro-region. It stands at 66% in the north, 64% in Lima and Callao, 62% in the central region and 54% in the Amazon east. In the south, where she lost the election, approval reaches 44% against 39% disapproval. By age group, the strongest backing comes from those aged 18 to 24, at 71%.

Sixty-two percent of respondents said they feel optimistic about the country's future, while 32% said they were pessimistic. On her first address to the nation, 62% said they had seen, heard or read about it; among those, 84% rated it positively and 13% negatively.

Expectations of the new administration center on the economy. Seventy-one percent expect the government to boost private investment, 66% to create jobs and 65% to improve the economy. Sixty-two percent believe it will bring order to the country, 60% that it will reduce crime and 51% that it will reduce corruption.

Security drew the widest consensus. Eighty-seven percent said they agreed with the armed forces joining National Police duties and with soldiers patrolling the streets, a measure announced by Fujimori. Some 86% support the military leading citizen security in jurisdictions under a state of emergency, and 85% back its taking charge of security in prisons.

On the new bicameral Congress, installed on July 24 after 34 years of a single-chamber system, 47% anticipate a confrontational relationship with the executive and 44% expect dialogue. Fuerza Popular is the largest bloc, with 22 of 60 senators and 41 of 130 deputies, short of an absolute majority. Sixty-seven percent said Congress should grant the legislative powers the executive has announced it will request on El Niño prevention, citizen security, economic affairs and labor.

The survey covered 1,205 people nationwide between August 5 and 7, with a margin of error of 2.8% and a 95% confidence level.

World.title: Bolivia records its first same-sex civil marriage after a court ruling
World.content:
Bolivia records its first same-sex civil marriage after a court ruling

9th Sunday, August 2026 - 20:44 UTC Full article

The couple, Fabiana Banzer and Scarlett Rocha, formally applied for a civil marriage on October 12, 2022

Bolivia has recorded its first civil marriage between two people of the same sex, held on Friday, August 7, in Santa Cruz, the country's most populous city, following a legal process that lasted three years and ten months.

The couple, Fabiana Banzer and Scarlett Rocha, formally applied for a civil marriage on October 12, 2022. The non-governmental organization IGUAL Bolivia, which provided legal support, said the union was completed after a lengthy administrative process and two constitutional injunctions filed by its team, until the couple obtained recognition and legal protection from the Bolivian state.

“Scar and I have been together for more than 4 years. It makes me very happy to announce to our family and friends that after a legal fight of 3 years and 10 months we have finally been able to access civil marriage as two women,” Banzer wrote on social media.

The decision does not alter Bolivia's legal framework. Article 63 of the constitution states that marriage is constituted between a woman and a man through legal bonds, and the Banzer-Rocha union was authorized through the courts in an individual case rather than by legislative reform. Bolivia therefore remains among the South American countries that do not recognize same-sex marriage in law, alongside Peru, Paraguay and Venezuela.

The immediate precedent dates to December 2020, when David Aruquipa and Guido Montaño secured registration of the country's first free union between two people of the same sex, following a ruling by the Second Constitutional Chamber of the La Paz departmental court that was later upheld by the Plurinational Constitutional Court. The Civil Registry Service has since recorded dozens of such unions.

Aruquipa said on Sunday that he and Montaño were marking the Banzer-Rocha marriage as a new and significant milestone in the advance of rights for same-sex couples in Bolivia, and as a development that widens the boundaries of equality. He argued the case should be read as part of a sequence: “Rather than speaking of a beginning, we should speak of a historical continuity: from the first recognized union to the first civil marriage.”

The transfeminist collective La Pesada Subversiva said the process involved a harsh legal battle against Bolivian institutions, marked by what it described as discrimination and mistreatment by authorities and public officials. The group noted that the application drew on advisory opinion 24/17, issued in 2017 by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights on gender identity and equality for same-sex couples.

The collective also argued that the free union, recognized since 2020, does not carry the same social recognition and standing as marriage. Bolivian authorities have not issued public statements on the case.

World.title: US border wall expansion threatens memory of Porvenir massacre
World.content:
A border wall construction project in Big Bend National Park in West Texas began last week, with a separate, nearby access road threatening the archaeological landscape of Porvenir, the site of a 1918 massacre of ethnic Mexican villagers.

Contractors began work Thursday on 17 miles of low, noncontiguous barrier fences and patrol roads, with conservationists reporting bulldozers clearing native vegetation.

One new access road appears to cut directly through Porvenir, which was a small farming community along the Rio Grande over 100 years ago.

On Jan. 28, 1918, Texas Rangers, local ranchers and apparently U.S. Army soldiers removed 15 unarmed ethnic Mexican residents (13 men and two teenage boys) from their homes and executed them, according to a lengthy report in Texas Monthly last week.

The location remains a sacred place for descendants and an archaeological site. A 2015 excavation found military-issued cartridge casings, evidence that challenged the historical narrative that the killings were carried out solely by vigilantes and Texas Rangers. The Texas Historical Commission erected a marker in 2018 after descendants campaigned for recognition.

Archaeologist David Keller told Texas Monthly that a newly built access road about 16 feet wide crosses the eastern third of the archaeological area and has been traversed by heavy machinery.

He said contractors and local officials indicated the route could eventually be widened to 100 or 120 feet.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is managing the project through Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

The CBP said the barriers, though low and not connected, are intended to prevent off-road vehicles from traveling to and from the Rio Grande, adding that the Porvenir access route is not finalized and public feedback will be considered.

DHS awarded a US $1.7 billion contract in May for the work, which has drawn widespread bipartisan opposition.

Even supporters of President Donald Trump have opposed the project for using billions of taxpayer dollars to build low fencing in a rugged, remote part of Texas where few illegal crossings have been recorded.

Podcaster Joe Rogan, who endorsed Trump in 2024, called the plan “B.S.” on his podcast, the San Antonio Current reported.

“This is the most heinous attack on an American national park in generations,” Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate for the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a statement posted to Instagram.

The Current reported that it was the first time in U.S. history that the federal government waived such a broad set of environmental protections for construction inside a national park.

With reports from Texas Monthly, AZFamily, San Antonio Current and Texas Standard

World.title: Mexico sends over 300 firefighters to British Columbia
World.content:
Listen to this article

More than 300 Mexican firefighters and technical personnel specializing in forest fires have travelled to British Columbia (B.C.), Canada, to support emergency efforts during the intense wildfires that have led to the evacuation of more than 20,000 people in the areas of Summerland and Peachland.

The Mexican teams arrived in separate contingents during the first few days of August, with the first group, comprising more than 100 people, arriving in Abbotsford on Aug. 3, and more than 200 crew arriving subsequently. A fourth delegation left on Sunday.

We’re beyond grateful to our friends and partners in Mexico for sending hundreds of firefighters to B.C. They’re joining a team of roughly 2,000 wildfire service personnel who are working tirelessly to get these fires under control. pic.twitter.com/5i8vFQFStr — David Eby (@Dave_Eby) August 6, 2026

Groups are deployed primarily throughout Fraser Canyon and the Thompson/Okanagan region, where they are participating in firefighting and control operations.

The contingent also features an incident management team, marking the first from Mexico to be deployed to B.C. under the mutual aid agreement between the two countries.

The tasks that the Mexican crew carry out include direct fire attack and the extinguishing of hot spots using hand tools and pumps, as well as reconnaissance and monitoring of areas where heat persists. They also participate in felling trees deemed hazardous and installing equipment to ensure a water supply during suppression operations.

B.C. Premier David Eby recognized the crew’s work and gave a welcoming speech as one of the contingents arrived at the airport.

“Mexico heard the call and, as you can see, has stepped up in a significant way,” Eby said.

Okanagan Falls park acting as base camp for over 300 wildfire firefighters from B.C. and Mexico

Watch this video on YouTube

Meanwhile, Minister of Forests Ravi Parmar said that he felt proud of the firefighters’ joint work.

“I’m proud of the wildland firefighters from Canada and Mexico who are not thinking about borders but are answering the call, as we do when our neighbours need us,” Parmar said.

Mexico’s envoys are made up of experienced personnel from the National Forestry Commission (Conafor), the National Commission of Protected Natural Areas (Conanp), state and municipal environmental agencies, Civil Protection, rural fire management brigades and civil society organizations.

The arrival of the firefighting crews comes as B.C. faces more than 100 active wildfires spanning 156 square kilometers. In addition to Mexico, British Columbia has received support from Australia, New Zealand and other Canadian provinces and territories.

With reports from Now Toronto, Publimetro, CBN Noticias and the CBC

World.title: Navy ramps up security presence in Mazatlán after high July homicide count
World.content:
After Mazatlán in July recorded its highest monthly homicide total of the year, the Mexican Navy on Saturday announced the deployment of more than 1,700 of its personnel to the Sinaloa port and resort city.

In a statement, the Navy Ministry (SEMAR) said that the deployment was occurring “within the framework of ‘Operation Sable’ Mazatlán” and was aimed at the “strengthening of security” in the city, the second largest in Sinaloa after state capital Culiacán.

The deployment comes after 36 homicides in Mazatlán in July, the city’s highest monthly total of murders in 2026, according to the newspaper El Sol de Mazatlán. It also follows the arrival of 900 Mexican Army troops in Mazatlán on July 23. The bolstering of the army’s presence in the city was part of a security reinforcement in response to a series of armed attacks.

In its statement, SEMAR said that the navy deployment reflects “the institution’s ongoing commitment to the well-being” of Mazatlán residents and tourists.

The ministry said that “operational actions will be focused on strategic areas … with the priority objective of reestablishing peace and public order and weakening illicit infrastructure that fuels schemes of violence and places the health of the population at risk.”

The term “illicit infrastructure” was a reference to clandestine drug laboratories and the cartel assets that support the distribution of narcotics, such as vehicles.

In its statement, SEMAR also issued what it called a “respectful call” for citizens and tourists to have “full confidence and certainty in the deployed forces.”

The ministry said that the central focus of the Mexican Navy’s operations is to “protect Mexican families while acting at all times with strict adherence to human rights, the proportional use of force and the current legal framework.”

“Its presence in the streets and on the coast has the sole aim of providing a safe and protected environment,” SEMAR said.

Violence in Mazatlán

Of the 36 people murdered in Mazatlán in July, 32 were men and four were women, El Sol de Mazatlán reported on Monday. The newspaper wrote that two cases were investigated as femicides, while two of the victims were minors.

Among the armed attacks in Mazatlán last month was one allegedly perpetrated by the “Los Chapitos” faction of the Sinaloa Cartel against marines, two of whom died from wounds they sustained. Marines returned fire and killed 10 criminals.

Much of the violence in Sinaloa is related to an ongoing battle between Los Chapitos, led by sons of convicted drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, and “Los Mayos,” a Sinaloa Cartel faction formerly led by Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada. The battle intensified in 2024 after Zambada was kidnapped by Joaquín Guzmán López and forced onto a plane that flew him to New Mexico. Both Zambada and Guzmán López, a son of “El Chapo,” were arrested by U.S. authorities at the Doña Ana County International Jetport in the U.S. border state in July 2024.

While the majority of the fighting between Los Chapitos and Los Mayos has occurred in Culiacán and surrounding areas, the battle has spilled into other parts of Sinaloa, including Mazatlán.

As Mexico News Daily reported last month, on July 17 and 18, six armed attacks were reported in Mazatlán in less than 24 hours, leaving four people dead and three others wounded. Between July 22 and 23, five more people were murdered.

El Sol de Mazatlán reported that episodes of violence in Mazatlán in July, including attacks on homes with firearms and explosives, occurred in rural and urban areas of the municipality of Mazatlán, including parts of the city frequented by tourists. Among those areas, the newspaper reported, were San Marcos, Lomas de Monterrey, Santa Fe, Infonavit Alarcón, Hacienda del Seminario, Lomas del Ébano, Zona Dorada and Pradera Dorada.

With reports from Expansión and El Sol de Mazatlán

World.title: Most avocado exports to the US have resumed after last week’s suspension
World.content:
Approximately 75% of avocado packing facilities in Mexico’s Michoacán state have been cleared for export following a pause in the avocado trade with the United States over security concerns, Julio Berdegué, Mexico’s advisor for international agri-food affairs and strategic issues under the USMCA, announced on Saturday.

The re-approved facilities handle roughly 85% of Michoacán’s avocado exports and the rest will be restored soon, according to Berdegué.

Mexico exports over 1 million tonnes of avocados a year, according to data from the Mexican Agriculture Ministry. Meanwhile, Michoacán contributes the highest avocado production of any Mexican state, with an export market valued at US $3.65 billion.

U.S. avocado imports from Michoacán were temporarily suspended on Wednesday after the U.S. Embassy issued an alert regarding a “threat to U.S. interests.” It marked the third time in just over four years that the United States has suspended avocado trade with Mexico for security reasons.

The embassy statement announcing the suspension did not reveal the nature of the threat, but President Sheinbaum has since said that the suspension followed a meeting at the U.S. embassy related to threats against some of the inspectors hired by the United States to monitor sanitary quality.

A meeting scheduled for the following day with an organization of avocado producers revealed that there had been an increase in extortion cases in certain regions of Michoacán.

In response to the news, Mexico worked to “rapidly strengthen” security in the state for the “immediate and gradual” resumption of the export program, said U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson.

Following the suspension, Michoacán Governor Alfredo Ramírez Bedolla deployed an extra 300 security operatives to Michoacán’s avocado-growing region “as a preventive measure.” Then, on Thursday morning, the federal Defense Ministry announced it had sent more than 1,500 soldiers to the state to “protect avocado producers and packing plants in the region.”

Exports resumed from the municipalities of Tancítaro, Tacámbaro and Uruapan, as well as the area between Morelia and Pátzcuaro, on Saturday.

To prevent future security issues, the Mexican government has established a permanent working group to monitor security in the region and prevent extortion of producers.

With reports from ABC Noticias and La Jornada

World.title: Opinion: After growing up in Mexico, was I prepared for US high school?
World.content:
My parents took a big risk when they moved their newborn twins from Manhattan to a small town in central Mexico. Yet, I couldn’t be more grateful that they did.

My family came to San Miguel de Allende when I was six months old, and I lived there until I was 15. And although we love San Miguel, my parents thought it best to send me back to the United States for high school. Having mastered the arts of reading, writing and calculating in Mexican schools, I think it’s safe to say that I learned to be a student there.

I attended SMA-based Academia Internacional from preschool through third grade. Their school emphasizes diversity and individuality, with a multicultural student body comprising both Mexican and American students. At Academia, I met my best friends and made my favorite childhood memories. I began studying French in the third grade, took advanced English classes through the Cambridge program at school, performed dance shows at the local theater and, most importantly, became queen of the monkey bars.

In fourth grade, I transferred to Colegio Newland, another bilingual and diverse school that emphasizes leadership and hands-on learning. The school follows an innovative curriculum that integrates technology into the classroom, with much of our learning centered around a platform called Knotion. At Newland, I was the middle school student body president, competed in spelling bees, traveled to geography competitions in other cities and even created a haircare brand for my entrepreneurship class. I also played tennis and took piano lessons outside of school.

As I reflect on my schooling, I realize many people assume the Mexican education system is mediocre or easy. But in reality, it challenged me while providing a foundation I needed to comfortably transition to a U.S. high school. I recall my middle school teachers constantly assigning pop quizzes, and to make matters worse, they would hand back our tests from lowest grade to highest — yikes. I struggled a lot in the subject of history, and after failing an exam, I spent weeks studying to improve my grade, only to discover that the content was fascinating. Thanks to Newland, I found a passion for it.

My parents loved raising my brother and me in San Miguel and considered it the perfect place for young children. However, they believed it made sense for us to return to the United States for high school. And like many parents, mine worried about the transition and whether I was academically prepared for a more “rigorous” school. Nevertheless, they were confident my brother and I would be okay because of the values we grew up learning. In San Miguel, people respect each other, always offer help and love to joke around. My brother and I were raised with those same values. And because of them, we adapted and made friends quickly.

I started by studying for the SSAT, the entrance exam required by most private high schools in the U.S., and it was rough. In Mexico, standardized tests barely exist, so I was unfamiliar with the idea of them. Additionally, I had never taken an exam in English, making it difficult to understand academic vocabulary. However, being fluent in Spanish often helped me identify the meaning of words with Latin roots. And ironically, my Mexican upbringing was the strongest part of my application as I drew on my childhood experiences in my essays. I wrote about Christmas, listening to mariachis and visiting Oaxaca.

After a long admissions process, I enrolled in a small boarding school in northern California. At first, the Spanish-to-English transition was difficult. My first year, I remember getting a 60% on a physics exam and feeling completely defeated. But seeing my international friends excel after going through the same transition motivated me to keep trying my best.

It’s crazy to think that I moved away from home at just 15. My parents still live in Mexico while I’m at school thousands of miles away. Of course I was scared to be on my own, but growing up between two cultures has made adapting to a new environment much easier, and California has quickly become my second home.

Throughout the two years that I’ve studied in the U.S., I’ve learned so much. My love for history persists and I have even grown to like math! (sort of). I found that attending Spanish-speaking schools didn’t hold me back, but rather, it is one of the most fascinating parts of who I am.

Now, I am going into my senior year, in which I will be editor-in-chief of the school newspaper and a prefect in the dorms. I continue to challenge myself academically with Advanced Placement (AP) and Honors courses, and can’t wait to have as much fun as possible with my friends.

As the college application process begins, I continue to write about my Mexican upbringing in every essay. I couldn’t be more grateful to have grown up and studied in such a beautiful place. I truly believe that I wouldn’t be as outgoing, determined or academically accomplished had my parents chosen to raise me in Manhattan instead.

Zella Golden grew up in San Miguel de Allende and is a senior in high school in Marin, California. Golden is completing an internship with MND.

World.title: Taylor Farms recalls its Mexico-sourced jalapeños, cuts ties with Sinaloa supplier over salmonella scare
World.content:
Just weeks after Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled iceberg lettuce products sourced from central Mexico, the Salinas, California-based company is voluntarily recalling some products that include jalapeño chiles due to concerns about possible salmonella contamination.

The decision by Taylor Fresh Foods — the parent company — is linked to a recall issued by San Diego-based Coast Citrus Distributors, which announced it was voluntarily recalling fresh jalapeños due to food safety concerns.

Taylor Fresh Foods said in a statement that it is not aware of any reported illnesses linked to its products containing jalapeños.

In its own statement, Coast Citrus said it will “no longer” source peppers from a farmer based in the northwestern Mexican state of Sinaloa, while it “seeks alternative suppliers.”

Taylor Fresh Foods also stated that it no longer purchases products from the Sinaloa farmer and “will fulfill orders with alternative suppliers.”

Besides the chiles themselves, guacamole, pico de gallo, taco salsa, burritos and spicy sandwiches are among the jalapeño-containing prepared foods included in the latest Taylor Farms recall.

Several U.S. states have been notified that all such products that feature a “Best If Used By” date up to and including Aug. 16, 2026, have been recalled. The products were sold at stores such as Kroger, Stop & Shop, Target, Whole Foods, Trader Joe’s and Walmart.

The recall comes as a result of a salmonella outbreak in the U.S. linked to jalapeño peppers imported from Mexico that had sickened 345 people in 27 states and led to 36 hospitalizations as of last Wednesday.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued an alert on Aug. 5, while the Food and Drug Administration is “working to determine if recalled jalapeños went to grocery stores,” so additional recalls could be announced.

As a result of the alert, Coast Citrus immediately agreed to recall the affected products and notify its customers. The Chipotle Mexican Grill and Qdoba restaurant chains also stopped serving the jalapeños in question.

Salmonella infections can cause diarrhea, fever and stomach cramps, and can be especially serious in young children, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems. The illness usually lasts four to seven days, and most people recover without treatment.

The latest recall comes amid heightened scrutiny of food safety in the U.S. restaurant industry, following last month’s outbreak of cyclosporiasis — a parasitic disease — linked to iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell restaurants that was reportedly sourced from central Mexico.

With reports from RTV Noticias, The Associated Press, the BBC and La Jornada

World.title: MND Local: Why is Puerto Vallarta so quiet right now?
World.content:
Walk around Puerto Vallarta right now and something feels different.

It’s not simply quieter in the way Vallarta is meant to feel during low season. There aren’t just shorter waits at restaurants, and there isn’t just a little more room on the beach.

It’s empty.

Restaurants have tables sitting unused. Tour operators are seeing smaller groups. Businesses that depend on visitors are wondering when the crowds will return.

More than just the ‘low season’

Anyone who has lived here for a while knows that summer is slower. That’s nothing new. But this one? This one feels different.

And the question being asked across the city is simple: “Where did everybody go?”

The events of Feb. 22 certainly didn’t help. The violence that followed the military operation against cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as El Mencho, brought roadblocks, burned vehicles, disruptions and international headlines. Several airlines temporarily suspended flights to Puerto Vallarta as the situation unfolded.

For those here at the time, the reality was more complicated than the images broadcast around the world. The immediate crisis passed quickly, and Puerto Vallarta reopened even faster.

But for people watching those images thousands of kilometers away, they may have been all they saw. Fear has a far longer memory than a roadblock.

A viewer in Canada or the United States doesn’t necessarily distinguish between what happened that day and what Puerto Vallarta was like the day after, let alone what it’s like six months later.

If your only knowledge of a place comes from television footage showing burning vehicles and blocked roads, you might think twice about booking a holiday there, too.

However, February isn’t the whole story.

Increased competition for travelers

Travelers have more choices now, and Puerto Vallarta is competing harder for holiday dollars. Airfares and promotions matter, and more destinations are competing for the same travelers than ever before.

People can visit somewhere new, find a cheaper flight, take advantage of a resort promotion elsewhere or simply decide after several trips to Vallarta that they would like a change of scenery.

For a family deciding where to spend a week, a few hundred dollars makes a big difference.

Travelers don’t owe Puerto Vallarta their vacation, which means the city has to keep earning their business. That includes offering solid value.

Some may point out the prices certain restaurants are charging right now.

There are places in Puerto Vallarta where prices have climbed to the point that visitors can legitimately ask whether the experience still represents good value for money, particularly when compared with other destinations.

Yet there is another side to that conversation.

The economics of tourism

Restaurant owners still have employees to pay. They have rent, electricity, ingredients, maintenance, taxes and a list of other costs that don’t disappear because it’s August and the tables are empty.

When fewer people come through the door, every customer matters more. That doesn’t make every price reasonable, nor does it mean visitors should simply pay whatever they are asked. But to encourage lower prices, businesses need both a reason and a way to reduce them.

Volume matters. A restaurant with full tables can afford to make a little less per customer. A tour operator with full boats can offer a better deal. A shop with steady foot traffic can move more product at a smaller margin.

When the customers aren’t there, the math changes. That’s where the impact of a quiet tourism season spreads far beyond the hotel lobby.

Tourism isn’t just hotels. It’s the taxi driver waiting for a fare. It’s the server whose income depends partly on tips. The boat captain. The tour guide. The massage therapist. The shop owner. The market vendor. The person cleaning vacation rentals. It’s an enormous economic ecosystem that most people don’t consider until something goes wrong.

Why locals matter

The question isn’t necessarily whether businesses have any customers. It’s whether they have enough to make the numbers work. That’s where full-time residents come in, because local residents have far more influence than they realize.

Foreign residents often fall into the trap of thinking, “I’m not a tourist. Tourism doesn’t really affect me.”

It does. Local restaurants employ neighbors. Local shops generate community income. Taxis, tours and business recommendations all drive the surrounding economy.

One response to a quiet summer is surprisingly simple: Go out.

Try the restaurant you’ve been meaning to visit. Use the independent shop with the quirky knickknack that caught your eye. Book the local tour you’ve thought about taking. Catch a bus and venture beyond the tourist zone.

Leave a review. Recommend a business. Spend money locally. And when someone back home asks whether Puerto Vallarta is still worth visiting, tell the truth.

A shared investment

Yes, there was violence on Feb. 22. Yes, Vallarta deals with crime, traffic, construction and infrastructure issues. But it also offers extraordinary natural beauty, remarkable food, generous people, neighborhoods full of character and a community that continues to evolve.

Both things can be true.

Don’t sell a fantasy. Tell people why you still live here. Long-term residents offer something tourism campaigns never will: personal credibility.

When a government campaign says Puerto Vallarta is wonderful, people expect it — it’s a sales pitch. But when someone who has lived here for five, 10 or 20 years says, “I know the problems. I know what happened. And I still think you should come,” that carries real weight.

Maybe this unusually quiet summer is a warning. Maybe it’s simply a blip. Either way, it would be foolish not to pay attention.

The question shouldn’t only be “Where did everybody go?” It should also be “What can residents do to make sure they want to come back?” That starts with remembering that tourism isn’t an entitlement; it’s an investment everyone shares.

When those tables sit empty, the impact doesn’t stop with the restaurant owner. It ripples out, eventually reaching everyone who calls Puerto Vallarta home.

And when home is hurting, no one is untouched.

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: Has Mexico reined in its inflation rate? Not yet, says Banxico chief
World.content:
Inflation in Mexico fell to just 0.12 points above the Bank of Mexico’s 3% target in July, but the central bank’s governor says it’s too early to declare victory in the fight against rising prices.

“At the Bank of Mexico, we’re not claiming victory yet,” Victoria Rodríguez Ceja told the newspaper El Financiero in an interview published on Monday.

Her remarks came after the national statistics agency INEGI reported on Friday that Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate was 3.12% in July, down from 3.37% in June.

Rodríguez noted that the headline rate in July was the lowest since May 2020. However, “even though inflation is practically at the [3%] target,” the Bank of Mexico will continue to seek low and stable price rises, the central bank governor told El Financiero.

INEGI’s 3.12% annual inflation reading in July was the product of 3.95% year-over-year core inflation and 0.29% non-core inflation. Annual core inflation remained reasonably high due to factors such as 4.85% year-over-year price rises for processed food, beverages and tobacco and 4.36% year-over-year increases for services.

The low non-core reading was the product of a 3.34% annual drop in prices for agricultural products (fruit, vegetables and meat) and a 3.31% increase in energy prices, including those for electricity and gasoline. Prices for agricultural products also declined on a month-over-month basis in July, falling 1.51%.

Rodríguez: Lower prices for agricultural products won’t last

Rodríguez’s interview with El Financiero came after Mexico’s headline inflation rate fell during four consecutive months from April to July. The headline rate last month was 1.47 percentage points below the 2026 peak of 4.59% in March.

Rodríguez said that the recent decline in inflation is explained, in part, by “changes in relative prices caused by favorable supply shocks.”

That was a reference to increased supply of fresh food, such as fruit and vegetables, and, as a result, lower prices for such products, as reflected in INEGI’s latest inflation data.

Rodríguez said that the Bank of Mexico doesn’t anticipate that lower prices for agricultural products will last due to “the unique characteristics of these prices and their exposure to meteorological phenomena.”

The easing of drought conditions in Mexico is a major reason why fresh food prices have recently come down, but there is no guarantee that weather-related factors won’t cause increases in the future.

Further explaining why the Bank of Mexico isn’t yet declaring victory in the fight against rising prices, Rodríguez noted that core inflation was 3.95% in July, while services were 4.36% more expensive than a year earlier. Inflation for services has recently trended down, but is still higher than the central bank would like. One factor driving the increase in prices for services was a 5.93% year-over-year increase in private school fees in July.

The Bank of Mexico’s inflation outlook

The Bank of Mexico (Banxico) forecasts that Mexico’s average annual headline inflation rate will be 3.5% in both the third and fourth quarters of 2026. In other words, the central bank anticipates that inflation will be higher between August and December than the 3.12% reading in July.

Banxico sees inflation declining in every quarter next year. It anticipates an average rate of 3.4% in Q1 of 2027, 3.3% in Q2, 3.2% in Q3 and 3% in Q4.

Those forecasts are included in a monetary policy statement released by Banxico last Thursday after its governing board voted in favor of maintaining the central bank’s key interest rate at 6.50%. Rodríguez told El Financiero that the bank’s current benchmark rate will contribute to the consolidation of “inflation’s downward path toward the [3%] target.”

However, she noted that the bank’s interest rate is subject to change based on “our assessment of the inflation outlook.”

In its Aug. 6 statement, the Bank of Mexico noted that headline inflation is “expected to converge to the target in the fourth quarter of 2027,” two quarters later than the bank anticipated when announcing its board’s interest rate decision in late June.

It said that its inflation forecasts “are subject to various risks.”

On the upside, they include “persistence of core inflation; disruptions due to foreign trade policies or to an inflationary impact from geopolitical conflicts; climate-related impacts; cost-related pressures, and a trend towards depreciation of the Mexican peso.”

On the downside, the risks include “lower-than-anticipated economic activity in Mexico and/or the United States; lower pass-through from increased costs, and lower pressures stemming from the appreciation that the national currency has been registering since last year.”

In her interview with El Financiero, Rodríguez stressed that the Bank of Mexico’s focus when making monetary policy decisions is the “inflation dynamic,” rather than economic growth, which had been very weak — or non-existent on a quarter-over-quarter basis — until a 1.5% sequential expansion in the second quarter of 2026.

With reports from El Financiero

Four of its governments are bidding for the same factories Mexico and Brazil want, and the money is moving faster than the heat allows anyone to work.

Southeast Asia – Bidding for the Factories You Want

Four national plans in three weeks

Thailand has unveiled a national plan to become a regional semiconductor hub, and Malaysia has committed more than 45 million dollars to advanced chip packaging. Vietnam has deepened cooperation with the regional semiconductor association, and the Philippines is debating the terms of a large chip and computing project.

These are national industrial strategies announced within three weeks of each other. The ambition across the region is unmistakable and unusually coordinated in its timing.

What it means for Latin America

This is a direct contest for the same nearshoring capital that Mexico and Brazil are courting. Every incentive package announced in Bangkok or Kuala Lumpur is one a board will weigh against Querétaro or Campinas.

The regional mood here is impatient ambition, a set of governments unwilling to be left as assembly floors. Their honest constraint was named in Bangkok last week, where the AI drive was described as limited by shortages of skilled people and access to data.

China – Building Machines, Buying Nothing

Two numbers that do not belong together

China’s artificial-intelligence industry reached 176.7 billion dollars in 2025, growing 40% in a year. Its consumer prices fell 0.1% in July and rose just 0.5% over twelve months, half the pace of June, while factory-gate prices fell 0.7% on the month.

A country can pour money into computing power and still not persuade its own households to spend. Its main large-company index fell 0.4% on Monday while most of Asia rose.

Read the demand picture carefully

Beijing’s statisticians attribute the weakness to imported international factors and note that core prices rose 0.3% on the month, while foreign analysts read the same figures as households declining to spend. Both readings come from the same release and the argument is unresolved.

For Latin American exporters this is the number that matters most this week. Copper, iron ore and soybean demand ultimately rests on whether Chinese consumption is pausing or contracting, and Monday’s data did not settle it.

The Region – El Niño Reaches the Order Book

A warning from Beijing’s own paper

China Daily reported last week that Asian economies face growing risks to food security. Southeast Asia is bracing for hot, dry conditions and heightened haze as El Niño strengthens, and Indonesia has already seen an early surge in wildfires.

In South Korea, heat illness cases have hit a record with two further deaths, the highest-level warning has been issued for greater Seoul, and workplaces are lengthening lunch breaks and adding rest periods. That is a heat that has started shortening the working day.

The same weather system, two continents

This is the El Niño the World Food Programme warned about days ago, when it said nearly 49 million more people could face acute hunger by the end of 2027. Asia and Latin America are exposed to the same event from opposite sides of the trade.

A tighter Asian harvest means a larger Asian import bill for soy, corn, beef, coffee and sugar. For Latin American producers that is a price story rather than a weather story.

Four Southeast Asian governments announced semiconductor strategies within three weeks, and in the same fortnight Korean employers began shortening the working day because of the heat — a region investing in 2030 while negotiating with 2026.

Japan – Cutting Tax and Capping Spending at Once

Ten trillion yen, and no named source

Tokyo has locked in a cut to the consumption tax on food, from 8% to 1% for two years from April 2027, at a cost of roughly 10 trillion yen. Its own press is asking the obvious question of how the lost revenue will be covered.

In the same week the government moved to rein in supplementary budgets, seeking to lift growth while reducing debt. Those two decisions pull in opposite directions and both were taken deliberately.

Why a Tokyo budget matters in São Paulo

Japan is a creditor nation and a long-standing direct investor across Latin America, in mining, autos and infrastructure. Its bond yields and its currency shape how much of that capital travels.

The temperament on display is a government trying to be generous and disciplined in the same breath. Its market closed 2.08% higher on Monday on American employment data rather than on anything it decided itself.

Japan, China and Korea – One Paper, Two Protests

A document nobody liked

China’s foreign ministry said last week that it deplores Japan’s latest defence white paper. Days earlier Seoul had lodged its own formal protest against the same document, over its restatement of a territorial claim.

Tokyo has managed to antagonise both neighbours with a single publication. It has withdrawn nothing.

Fragmentation is the whole reason nearshoring exists

Since Japan’s prime minister linked a Taiwan contingency to Japanese military action, Beijing has suspended cultural exchanges, halted Japanese seafood imports and restricted rare earths and dual-use goods. None of it has been lifted.

This is the environment that makes boards look for production sites outside North Asia altogether. Every month these measures stay in place strengthens the argument for Mexican and Brazilian capacity.

Energy – Asia Is the Gauge for What You Pay

Where the fuel bill is already visible

Thai AirAsia has suspended nine routes from Bangkok’s main airport because of fuel costs, and the Laotian government is acting to soften pump-price rises. Both the regional bloc and Beijing have called publicly for safe transit through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran said on Sunday that an agreement with Oman on new shipping lanes was in its final stages, while adding that the waterway reopens only once further conditions are met. Nothing about that is settled.

The number on your own screen

Asia imports most of its energy and shows the strain first, in cancelled routes and subsidised pumps. Latin American importers read the same barrel at a delay.

Brent was trading around 83 dollars and West Texas near 78 as this brief was written. What Bangkok cancels this month is what São Paulo pays for next quarter.

The Bigger Picture Asia is committing to the next decade while struggling with this one. Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam and the Philippines have all moved on semiconductors within three weeks, and China’s artificial-intelligence industry has reached 176.7 billion dollars while its consumer prices fall outright. Against that, the immediate environment is getting harder. El Niño is strengthening, food security warnings are coming from Beijing’s own newspaper, Korean employers are shortening the working day for heat, and airlines are cancelling routes over fuel. For Latin American readers there are three practical reads. Southeast Asia is competing for the same factories, Chinese household demand remains the swing factor for copper, iron ore and soy, and a tighter Asian harvest points to firmer prices for the region’s agricultural exporters. Frequently Asked Questions

Which Southeast Asian countries are bidding for semiconductor investment?

Thailand unveiled a national plan in late July to build a regional chip hub, Malaysia committed more than 45 million United States dollars to advanced chip packaging, Vietnam deepened cooperation with the Southeast Asia Semiconductor Association, and the Philippines is publicly debating the terms of a large computing project. Thai officials have also acknowledged that the country’s artificial-intelligence drive is constrained by shortages of skilled workers and limited access to data.

What did China’s July inflation data show?

Consumer prices fell 0.1% from June and rose 0.5% from a year earlier, down from 1.0% in June, while core prices excluding food and energy rose 0.3% on the month and producer prices fell 0.7% on the month while remaining 3.5% higher than a year ago. China’s statistics bureau attributed the softness to international imported factors, while foreign analysts read the same release as evidence of weak household demand.

How is El Niño affecting Asian economies?

China Daily reported last week that Asian economies face growing risks to food security, Southeast Asia is bracing for hot and dry conditions with heightened haze risk, and Indonesia has recorded an early surge in wildfires. In South Korea heat illness cases have reached a record with two further deaths, the highest-level warning has been issued for the greater Seoul area, and employers have begun extending lunch breaks and adding rest periods.

Why did both China and South Korea protest Japan’s defence white paper?

Seoul lodged a formal protest over the document’s restatement of Japan’s claim to disputed islets, and China’s foreign ministry subsequently said it deplores the paper. The wider context is that Beijing has maintained trade measures against Japan since November, including suspended cultural exchanges, a halt to Japanese seafood imports and restrictions on rare earths and dual-use goods, after Japan’s prime minister linked a possible Taiwan contingency to Japanese military action.

World.title: El Niño Puts 756 Latin American Hospitals at Risk as Dengue Cases Top 624,000
World.content:
Health: Latin America

Key Facts —Dengue surge. In epidemiological week 12 of 2026, the Americas reported 624,085 suspected dengue cases, a cumulative incidence of 62 per 100,000 population — a 64% decrease from the same period in 2025 but still elevated. —El Niño threat. PAHO’s July 2026 analysis warns that the 2026–2027 El Niño event could expose 756 emergency hospitals in the Americas to coastal-flooding risks and disrupt supply chains for medicines and medical supplies. —2025 baseline. The Americas recorded 4.46 million suspected dengue cases in 2025, down 66% from the record 13 million in 2024 but still above the pre-pandemic average. All four serotypes circulated simultaneously in Brazil, Colombia and Mexico. —Brazil lead. Brazil reported 1.66 million probable dengue cases in 2025, with an incidence rate of 775.7 per 100,000. In early 2026, 62,707 suspected cases were reported through epidemiological week 5. —Vaccine access. PAHO is advising member states on newly approved dengue vaccines and has expanded clinical-training networks, while warning that climate-related disruptions could delay immunization campaigns.

Latin America is entering the 2026–2027 El Niño cycle with dengue still circulating at scale and its health infrastructure — including hundreds of coastal hospitals — newly exposed to climate-driven flooding risks.

The Scale of the Dengue Burden in 2025–2026

The Americas experienced its largest dengue epidemic on record in 2024, with more than 13 million cases reported to the Pan American Health Organization. In 2025, the numbers fell but remained high: 4.46 million suspected cases and 1.68 million confirmed cases across the region, according to PAHO’s February 2026 epidemiological update. The decline of 66% from 2024 was partly seasonal, but the underlying transmission potential remains.

Brazil accounted for the largest share. In 2025, the country reported 1.66 million probable cases, 1.45 million of them confirmed, with 1,793 deaths. The incidence rate was 775.7 per 100,000 population. Colombia reported 125,119 suspected cases in 2025, including 86,881 confirmed and 124 deaths. All four dengue virus serotypes — DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4 — circulated simultaneously in Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Mexico, Panama and Puerto Rico.

In the first weeks of 2026, the pattern continued. Through epidemiological week 12, PAHO reported 624,085 suspected cases across the Americas. Brazil alone added 62,707 suspected cases in the first five weeks of the year. The figures represent a 64% decrease from the same period in 2025, but PAHO warned that the seasonal uptrend is consistent with expected behavior and that health systems should prepare for potential increases.

What El Niño Adds to the Health Risk

In July 2026, PAHO published a public-health situation analysis specifically on the El Niño climate event for 2026–2027. The document is not a forecast of certainty but a mapping of vulnerabilities. It identifies the same set of climate-sensitive diseases — dengue, Zika, chikungunya, malaria, cholera — and adds a new layer of infrastructure risk.

The analysis examined 756 emergency hospitals across the Americas and found them exposed to coastal flooding associated with sea-level rise, which El Niño can amplify through storm-surge and extreme-rainfall events. The risk is not theoretical: disruptions to supply chains for medicines, vaccines and medical equipment have already occurred during past climate emergencies in the region.

The report also notes that drought conditions can paradoxically increase dengue transmission. When water becomes scarce, households store it in open containers, creating breeding sites for the Aedes aegypti mosquito. The 2023–2024 El Niño contributed to severe drought in the Brazilian Amazon, disrupting healthcare access and increasing malaria incidence in states such as Rondônia. The same dynamics could recur.

Climate emergency response in the Americas. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

How Countries Are Responding

PAHO’s response has three pillars: surveillance, vector control and clinical training. The organization has deployed expert teams to affected countries, expanded its online clinical-diagnosis course for dengue, and established national networks of clinical specialists in arboviral diseases. In August 2025, PAHO held a workshop to update its Integrated Management Strategy for Arboviral Disease Prevention and Control, setting a roadmap for 2026–2030.

On the vaccine front, PAHO is advising member states on newly approved dengue vaccines, though access remains uneven. The organization emphasizes that vaccination is a complement to, not a replacement for, vector control and early clinical management. It also warns that climate-related disruptions could delay routine immunization campaigns, widening existing immunity gaps.

The bottom line is that Latin America’s health systems are facing a converging threat: endemic arboviral diseases that never fully receded, a new El Niño cycle that amplifies both drought and flood risks, and infrastructure that was not designed for either. The 756 hospitals in the flood-risk zone are a concrete measure of that vulnerability.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many dengue cases were reported in the Americas in 2025?

The Americas reported 4.46 million suspected dengue cases in 2025, including 1.68 million confirmed cases, 8,966 severe cases and 2,207 deaths. This was a 66% decrease from the record 13 million cases in 2024.

What does El Niño mean for healthcare in Latin America?

PAHO’s July 2026 analysis warns that El Niño could expose 756 emergency hospitals to coastal-flooding risks, disrupt medicine supply chains, and increase transmission of dengue, malaria and waterborne diseases through both flooding and drought-driven water-storage practices.

Which countries are most affected by dengue?

Brazil leads in absolute numbers (1.66 million probable cases in 2025), followed by Colombia, Mexico, Guatemala and Panama. All four dengue serotypes circulated simultaneously in Brazil, Colombia, Mexico and several Central American countries in 2025.

Africa Intelligence Brief — Monday, August 10, 2026

Key Facts —Uranium inquiry DR Congo will test its cobalt exports after research estimated that thousands of tonnes of uranium left the country as a by-product over two decades. —Sixty days Kinshasa has given itself sixty days to assess health and environmental risks, and will consult the international nuclear watchdog. —Zambia votes Zambians choose a president and parliament on Thursday, with copper providing about 70% of the country’s export earnings. —A fiscal gap Standard Chartered expects Zambia’s 2026 deficit near 5.0% of output, more than double the government’s 2.1% target. —Cape Town shootings Eleven people were killed in three separate mass shootings in Khayelitsha, Langa and Gugulethu, with no arrests reported. —Sall falters Macky Sall took six votes in favour, seven against and two abstentions in the first Security Council ballot for United Nations secretary-general.
