One country is counting its votes on whether copper has paid off, and the other is counting, for the first time, what has been leaving alongside it.

DR Congo – The Uranium in the Cobalt

A state that starts measuring

The Democratic Republic of Congo said on Friday it will test its cobalt exports for uranium. The decision follows research published on 30 July in the journal Nature Communications, examined by the Financial Times and Lighthouse Reports, which estimated that thousands of tonnes of the radioactive metal left the country as a by-product over roughly two decades.

Kinshasa will set up a working group, consult the International Atomic Energy Agency about a technical mission, and assess health and environmental risks within sixty days. It also plans to install radiation detectors on trucks leaving the country.

Contested, and taken seriously anyway

The government disputes the method, saying the estimates rest on modelling rather than direct measurements of exported material, and that uranium occurring alongside copper and cobalt in the region is natural and well documented. Chinese mining companies operating in the country reject the claims outright.

The head of the Congolese nuclear energy agency told the Financial Times it was technically possible and even probable that uranium had been extracted from exported ore, while stressing there is no direct evidence. The national mood is neither denial nor alarm but a wary insistence on checking, which is itself new.

Zambia – Three Days to the Copper Vote

Reform seeks its receipt

Zambians vote on Thursday for a president and parliament, with President Hakainde Hichilema seeking a second term against a fragmented opposition led by Brian Mundubile. The country is Africa’s second-largest copper producer and the world’s eighth, and copper supplies about 70% of its export earnings.

Hichilema steered the country through a punishing debt restructuring after it became the pandemic era’s first sovereign defaulter. The question this week is whether voters feel any of it in their own lives.

Stability without the receipts

The previous 1.7 billion dollar programme with the International Monetary Fund expired in January, and investors treat a successor as the real test of continuity. Standard Chartered expects this year’s deficit near 5.0% of output, more than double the government’s 2.1% target, partly because a record maize harvest obliges the state to buy heavily from farmers.

Drought has also undercut a power system that leans on hydro, forcing cuts that stall industry. Zambia’s temper is that of a country asked to be patient for five years and now being asked, politely, for proof.

South Africa – A Speech Against Violence, and Eleven Dead

Seventy years after the march

President Cyril Ramaphosa marked Women’s Day at the Union Buildings on Sunday, seventy years after thousands of women gathered there to protest against apartheid pass laws. He condemned those who try to justify abuse, saying how women dress or behave can never be an excuse.

He called on men and boys to take a stronger stand and on communities to stop turning away. He also urged more women into science and engineering.

The same weekend, in Cape Town

Eleven people were killed in three separate mass shootings in the city. Three men died in Khayelitsha, five in Langa, and three at the Barcelona settlement in Gugulethu, where two others were wounded.

Police have reinforced deployments and no arrests have been made, with motives still under investigation. The gap between the speech at the Union Buildings and the weekend in the townships is the country’s whole predicament in a single day.

Senegal – Six For, Seven Against

A candidacy that stalls at the first ballot

Former president Macky Sall took six votes in favour, seven against and two abstentions in the Security Council’s first informal ballot for United Nations secretary-general, held on 30 July. The polls are non-binding, and further rounds are expected through August and possibly into the autumn.

Two Africans are in the race, Sall and Uganda’s Olara Otunnu, who entered late. A former head of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa judges the continent’s chances this year to be low.

A prize Africa keeps not winning

Sall was nominated by Burundi rather than by his own country, and only secured Senegal’s endorsement later. At home the ruling party still holds him responsible for deaths during protests in 2021 and 2023.

The mood in Dakar is not wounded so much as unsurprised. A continent that supplies the world’s minerals is still waiting to supply its secretary-general.

One country is counting votes on whether its copper has paid off, and its neighbour has begun counting what has been leaving alongside the same ore — the Copperbelt, at last, taking its own inventory.

Kenya – The Arithmetic of 2027

A retreat at Naivasha

President William Ruto and Oburu Odinga led a broad-based parliamentary retreat at Naivasha, gathering legislators from across the governing arrangement. The subject is the shape of the coalition heading into the 2027 election.

Kenyan politics is already organising itself around that date. Alliances are being tested well before any campaign formally begins.

Governing and campaigning at once

The country’s mood is watchful and transactional, with everyone counting numbers a year and a half early. That leaves less attention for the cost of living that drove last year’s protests.

Kenya’s economy has held up better than many of its neighbours. Its politics is the part that never rests.

Sudan – The Students Who Kept Going

Education as refusal

Sudanese students are finding ways to continue studying through a conflict that has emptied universities and scattered families. United Nations accounts describe young people sitting examinations and resuming courses in displacement.

One of them said simply that it made him dream again. It is a small sentence carrying a great deal.

What persistence is worth

A generation losing its education is the slowest and most expensive damage any conflict does. Countries that keep teaching through disaster recover years faster than those that do not.

The mood here is stubbornness rather than hope, which may be more durable. Sudan’s students are protecting the one asset nobody can carry away.

The Bigger Picture The Copperbelt is one geological formation running under two countries, and this week it holds both of the continent’s largest stories. Zambia votes on Thursday on whether five years of reform have reached ordinary lives, with copper supplying about 70% of export earnings and a deficit heading for double its target. Across the border, DR Congo has begun testing what leaves alongside the same ore, after research alleged that thousands of tonnes of uranium were exported unmeasured for two decades. The claim is disputed by the government and by the Chinese firms involved, and Kinshasa is checking anyway, which is the part that matters. Elsewhere the day was about counting of a different kind. South Africa counted eleven dead in three Cape Town shootings on the weekend its president spoke against violence, Senegal counted six votes for Macky Sall and seven against, and Kenya’s politicians counted their numbers for an election still a year and a half away. Frequently Asked Questions

Why is DR Congo testing its cobalt exports for uranium?

Research published on 30 July in Nature Communications, examined by the Financial Times and Lighthouse Reports, estimated that thousands of tonnes of uranium left the country as a by-product of cobalt exports over roughly two decades, most of it destined for Chinese-owned entities. The government announced on 7 August that it would test exported cobalt hydroxide, form a working group, consult the International Atomic Energy Agency and assess health and environmental risks within sixty days, while disputing the study’s methodology and noting that uranium occurs naturally alongside copper and cobalt in the region.

What is at stake in Zambia’s election on 13 August?

President Hakainde Hichilema is seeking a second term against a fragmented opposition led by Brian Mundubile, in a vote widely seen as a test of whether his economic reforms have reached ordinary households. Zambia is Africa’s second-largest copper producer and copper accounts for roughly 70% of export earnings, while a 1.7 billion dollar International Monetary Fund programme expired in January and Standard Chartered expects the 2026 deficit near 5.0% of output against a 2.1% target.

What did President Ramaphosa say on Women’s Day?

Speaking at the Union Buildings on Sunday 9 August, seventy years after the 1956 march against pass laws, Ramaphosa condemned those who attempt to justify abuse, saying how women dress or behave can never serve as a justification, and urged men and boys to take a stronger stand while calling on communities not to turn a blind eye. Over the same weekend eleven people were killed in three separate mass shootings in Khayelitsha, Langa and Gugulethu, with police reinforcing deployments and no arrests reported.

How did Macky Sall perform in the first UN straw poll?

In the Security Council’s first informal ballot on 30 July, the former Senegalese president received six votes in favour, seven against and two abstentions, a result widely read as weakening his candidacy. The polls are non-binding, with further rounds expected through August and possibly into the autumn before a single candidate is recommended to the General Assembly, and the new secretary-general takes office on 1 January 2027.

São Paulo · Nightlife

São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 10, 2026

If You Only Go to One Place Last Days: Two World-Cinema Festivals Two rare film seasons run tonight and close Wednesday. CineSesc on Rua Augusta has the first-ever complete Aki Kaurismäki retrospective — all 18 features — while Cine Belas Artes is finishing its Festival Filmes Incríveis of unreleased world cinema. Both are open tonight, both are cheap (around R$20, US$4), and both end 12 August. On a quiet Monday, this is the move.

Tonight at a Glance —Kaurismäki retrospective · CineSesc All 18 of the Finnish director’s features, first time complete in Brazil, on Rua Augusta. Runs daily to 12 August. Around R$20 (US$4). —Festival Filmes Incríveis · Cine Belas Artes Unreleased films from festivals like Cannes and Berlin, on Consolação. Final days through 12 August. Check tonight’s exact showtimes on the site. —SP2B, Day 2 · Ibirapuera The innovation festival’s content day (from 1 pm) is credential-based — the Sunday opening with Esther Perel was Platinum-only and is done. But the park’s open areas stay free to walk through all week. —Monday forró & pagode · Pinheiros / Centro / Mooca São Paulo’s Monday music tradition: forró pé de serra at Remelexo Brasil (Pinheiros, from 11 pm) and Estúdio Lâmina (Centro), plus a Monday pagode night in Mooca. Confirm the night’s band on their socials. —CCBB São Paulo · Centro Open Mondays (closed Tuesdays) until 8 pm, with free exhibitions and film sessions. A good early-evening culture stop before dinner. Confirm the current programme on the site.

Tonight, Monday 10 August 2026, is a classic São Paulo Monday — slow for clubs, but the cinemas and a handful of Monday-night music rooms keep the city alive. The standout is timing: two exceptional film seasons, a Kaurismäki retrospective and the Festival Filmes Incríveis, both end this Wednesday, so tonight is one of your last chances. SP2B rolls into its business-content day at Ibirapuera, and Vila Madalena keeps its Monday forró going.

São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 10, 2026. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Aki Kaurismäki retrospective at CineSesc — Rua Augusta 2075, Cerqueira César. The first complete retrospective in Brazil of the Finnish master, gathering all 18 of his fiction features — dry humour, working-class characters, and that unmistakable deadpan style. It runs daily to 12 August, so tonight is a genuine last-chance window. Tickets are R$20 (US$4) full, R$10 (US$2) half, R$6 (US$1) with a Sesc card. Check the day’s specific titles and times.

Festival Filmes Incríveis at Cine Belas Artes — Rua da Consolação 2423, Consolação. The art-house festival of unreleased world cinema — 14 films from 14 countries, many straight from Cannes, Berlin and Rotterdam — is in its final days before closing 12 August. Tickets around R$20 (US$4) full, R$10 (US$2) half, with a five-film pass at R$45 (US$9). Confirm tonight’s programme on the site.

SP2B, Day 2 at Parque Ibirapuera — the innovation festival’s content programme begins around 1 pm on Monday and runs through the week. Access to the stages and talks requires a paid credential (Explorer from about R$1,180, US$232, up to Platinum at R$4,720, US$930); the Sunday Opening Night with Esther Perel was Platinum-only and has passed. Worth knowing: the park itself stays open and free, so you can still walk the grounds and catch the open-area atmosphere without a ticket. The festival is 18+.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Early evening (6 pm) — Start with a film. CineSesc on Rua Augusta and Cine Belas Artes on Consolação are a short walk apart, both in the Paulista corridor, so you can check both schedules and pick the session that fits.

Dinner (8 pm) — The Consolação/Augusta stretch is full of bars and restaurants. Grab a bite between or after screenings without moving far.

Later (10–11 pm) — For music, head to Pinheiros for the Monday forró at Remelexo Brasil (it gets going around 11 pm), to Estúdio Lâmina in Centro, or to Mooca for the Monday pagode. All are relaxed, local and danceable — the antidote to a quiet Monday.

Nightcap (11:30 pm) — Vila Madalena’s bars stay open on a Monday if the forró winds down. Keep it low-key; the big clubs are a weekend affair.

Alternative — Culture-first: CCBB in Centro closes at 8 pm, so catch an exhibition early, then move to Augusta for a late film.

Scenes & Sounds

Cinema — This is the Monday story. Two festivals in their final days: the Kaurismäki retrospective at CineSesc and Festival Filmes Incríveis at Cine Belas Artes, both closing 12 August. Nationwide, the Harry Potter and La La Land anniversary re-releases are also in cinemas this month. Where: CineSesc (Rua Augusta), Cine Belas Artes (Consolação), Cinemateca Brasileira (Vila Clementino).

Forró — Monday is forró night in São Paulo. Traditional forró pé de serra runs every Monday at a couple of dedicated houses, with dancing and a welcoming crowd. Where: Remelexo Brasil (Pinheiros), Estúdio Lâmina (Centro) — confirm the night’s band on their socials.

Pagode and samba — A Monday pagode night runs in Mooca, and samba turns up across the city midweek. Where: Bar Templo (Mooca) and neighbourhood bars — confirm the night’s act.

MPB and jazz — Small rooms like Centro da Terra (Perdizes) and Coringa (Vila Madalena) sometimes programme Monday sets. The bigger jazz and MPB houses skew to later in the week. Where: Centro da Terra, Coringa, JazzB — check listings.

Cultural and talks — SP2B’s business programme runs all week at Ibirapuera (credential required); the park’s open areas stay free. CCBB in Centro is open tonight with exhibitions and film sessions. Where: Parque Ibirapuera, CCBB (Centro).

Electronic and clubs — Not a Monday thing in São Paulo. Save the Barra Funda clubs (D-Edge, Clash Club) for Friday and Saturday. Where: Barra Funda, weekends.

Pick Your Night

See it before it’s gone: The Kaurismäki retrospective at CineSesc or Festival Filmes Incríveis at Cine Belas Artes — both close Wednesday.

Dance on a Monday: The Vila Madalena forró — social, danceable, and very São Paulo.

Culture first: CCBB São Paulo in Centro — free exhibitions, open Mondays until 8 pm.

Ideas and networking: SP2B at Ibirapuera, if you hold a credential — the business content runs from the afternoon.

Dance till sunrise: Not tonight. Save the Barra Funda clubs for the weekend.

Where to Go

CineSesc — Cerqueira César (Rua Augusta) A comfortable Sesc-run cinema on Rua Augusta with popular-priced tickets, hosting the first complete Aki Kaurismäki retrospective in Brazil. Tonight: Retrospectiva Aki Kaurismäki — all 18 of the director’s fiction features, running through 12 August. Check the day’s titles and times. Best time: Daily, roughly 1:15 pm to 9:30 pm during the retrospective. Cost: R$20 (US$4) full / R$10 (US$2) half / R$6 (US$1) with Sesc Credencial Plena. Address: Rua Augusta 2075, Cerqueira César Website: www.sescsp.org.br Getting there: Metro Consolação (green line), short walk up Rua Augusta. Good to know: Programme and tickets on the Sesc São Paulo site.

Cine Belas Artes — Consolação São Paulo’s beloved art-house cinema, finishing its Festival Filmes Incríveis 2026. A cultural anchor with a great courtyard café. Tonight: Festival Filmes Incríveis — unreleased world cinema, final days through 12 August. Confirm tonight’s exact showtimes on the site. Best time: Evenings. The courtyard café is open all day. Cost: R$20 (US$4) full / R$10 (US$2) half; five-film pass R$45 (US$9). Address: Rua da Consolação 2423, Consolação Website: www.cinebelasartes.com.br Getting there: Metro Paulista (yellow line), 10-minute walk. Good to know: Buy tickets online or at the box office.

SP2B — Parque Ibirapuera The city’s big new innovation and culture festival, spread across the park’s cultural buildings and open areas for eight days. Tonight: Day 2 — business-content programme from about 1 pm. Credential required for the stages and talks; the Sunday opening with Esther Perel has passed. Best time: The main content block runs Tuesday to Thursday; the free music and Experience Day land on the weekend. Cost: Credentials from about R$1,180 (US$232) Explorer up to R$4,720 (US$930) Platinum. The park’s open areas remain free to enter. Address: Parque Ibirapuera, Vila Mariana Website: sp2b.com.br Getting there: Rideshare best; buses from Paulista. It’s 18+ for the festival areas. Good to know: Check the app for the day’s stages and any free public activations.

Monday forró — Remelexo Brasil (Pinheiros) & Estúdio Lâmina (Centro) São Paulo’s Monday forró tradition. Remelexo Brasil is one of the city’s best-known forró houses; Estúdio Lâmina is a decades-old forrozeiro haunt near São Bento. Both keep a traditional pé de serra going every Monday, with dancing and a welcoming crowd. Tonight: Live forró at Remelexo Brasil (Mondays, from about 11 pm) and at Estúdio Lâmina (every Monday). Confirm the night’s band on their socials. Best time: Late — Remelexo runs into the early hours. Arrive earlier for a table. Cost: Remelexo cover around R$30 (US$6) in advance, R$50 (US$10) at the door, plus drinks. Card accepted. Address: Remelexo Brasil — Rua Ferreira de Araújo 1076, Pinheiros; Estúdio Lâmina — Av. São João 108, Centro Getting there: Remelexo: rideshare, or metro Faria Lima/Pinheiros. Estúdio Lâmina: metro São Bento, then rideshare out late. Good to know: No dance experience needed — locals are happy to show you the basic step.

CCBB São Paulo — Centro The Banco do Brasil’s cultural centre in a restored 1901 building in the historic centre. Free exhibitions, cinema and theatre — and open on Mondays. Tonight: Open until 8 pm with current exhibitions and film sessions. Confirm today’s programme on the site — the schedule turns over between shows this month. Best time: Wednesday to Monday, 9 am to 8 pm. Closed Tuesdays. Cost: Free, with timed tickets reserved online (bb.com.br/cultura) or at the box office. Address: Rua Álvares Penteado 112, Centro Histórico Website: ccbb.com.br/sao-paulo Getting there: Metro São Bento (blue line), short walk into the pedestrian centre. Good to know: Centro empties after office hours — use rideshare door-to-door at night.

Blue Note São Paulo — Paulista The São Paulo outpost of the New York jazz club, polished and central. A strong option for later in the week. Tonight: Typically no Monday show — Blue Note programmes shows Wednesday to Sunday. Check the site and plan for later in the week. Best time: Wednesday to Sunday. Arrive 30 minutes early — seating is first-come. Cost: Couvert from R$40 (US$8) to R$80 (US$16) depending on the act. Address: Av. Paulista 2073, 2º andar (Conjunto Nacional), Consolação Website: bluenotesp.com Getting there: Metro Consolação (green line), 200 m from the door. Good to know: Show seating is first-come; arrive early on show nights.

Casa de Francisca — Sé/Centro An intimate listening room inside the gorgeous Palacete Teresa, mixing MPB, jazz and instrumental. A hidden gem for another night. Tonight: Usually no Monday show — the Casa’s programme runs Tuesday to Sunday. Check the Instagram and plan for later in the week. Best time: Tuesday to Sunday, shows around 8 pm or 9 pm. Cost: Couvert around R$30 (US$6) to R$60 (US$12). Cash and card accepted. Address: Rua Quintino Bocaiúva 22, Sé (Palacete Teresa) Instagram: @casadefrancisca Getting there: Metro Sé (red/blue lines), 5-minute walk. Use rideshare after dark. Good to know: Tiny room — reservations strongly recommended when it’s open.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Paulista / Consolação / Augusta: The city’s spine — cinemas, bars and jazz clubs within a short walk. Safe and well-lit, and the natural base for a Monday film-and-dinner night.

Vila Madalena / Pinheiros: Bohemian and bar-heavy, and home to the Monday forró. Walkable and lively even early in the week.

Sé / Centro: Historic core with CCBB and hidden gems. Grand by day, very quiet after dark on a Monday — use a rideshare.

Ibirapuera / Vila Mariana: Leafy and upscale around the park, which hosts SP2B this week. A more relaxed, residential side of the city.

Barra Funda: The club district — empty on a Monday, alive at the weekend. Home to D-Edge and Clash Club.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Weekend-led scene — São Paulo’s big queer club nights, including the Barra Funda parties, are Friday-and-Saturday affairs. Mondays are quiet on that front.

Everyday-friendly spaces — The Augusta corridor and Vila Madalena bars are broadly mixed and welcoming any night. For a Monday, that’s your best bet; save the dedicated club nights for the weekend.

Money & How Paying Works Cinema tickets: Festival films run around R$20 (US$4) full, with half-price (meia) at R$10 (US$2) for students and others. Bring ID for meia. Couvert artístico: Music bars add a per-person music charge, not a tip — usually R$20 (US$4) to R$40 (US$8). It will be on your bill; ask before you sit. Cash, card and Pix: Cards and Pix are widely accepted, but carry R$100 (US$20) to R$200 (US$40) in cash for smaller bars and street vendors. Tipping: 10% is standard and often added as ‘serviço’. Check before you double-tip.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: The last trains leave between midnight and 12:30 am, depending on the line. Check the ViaQuatro and Metrô SP apps before you rely on it.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber are reliable and widely used. Wait in a lit, busy spot, especially leaving Centro late.

Centro at night: The Sé and República areas are very quiet after dark on a Monday. Stick to lit main roads and take a rideshare door-to-door.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

Augusta and Vila Madalena: Both stay busier and better-lit early in the week, but keep the usual city awareness late at night.

Frequently Asked Questions

I’ve just landed at GRU tonight. Can I still do something?

Yes — aim for a late film. CineSesc and Cine Belas Artes both run evening sessions and are about a 40-minute rideshare from the airport, in the well-connected Paulista corridor. For something livelier, the Vila Madalena forró runs late.

Can I just show up to SP2B tonight?

Only to the park itself, which stays open and free. The festival’s stages and talks require a paid credential (from about R$1,180, US$232), and Monday is a business-content day. The Sunday opening with Esther Perel was Platinum-only and has passed.

Do I need to speak Portuguese?

For the films, many are subtitled world cinema, so no. At the forró, the music and dancing do the work — a smile and a willingness to try the step are all you need.

What’s the dress code on a Monday?

Casual everywhere tonight. Comfortable clothes for the cinema and the forró; jeans are fine. Bring a light layer for air-conditioned screening rooms.

World.title: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — August 10, 2026
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — August 10, 2026

If You Only Go to One Place Samba do Trabalhador at Clube Renascença Monday looks quiet on paper, but Rio’s samba world is wide awake. Moacyr Luz’s Samba do Trabalhador has run every Monday for two decades at the Renascença Clube in Andaraí — gates from around 4:30 pm, samba from 5 pm. It is the most Carioca thing you can do on a Monday, and it’s cash-only, so come prepared.

Tonight at a Glance —Samba do Trabalhador · Andaraí The city’s most famous Monday roda, led by Moacyr Luz. Gates ~4:30 pm, samba from 5 pm, ends around 9 pm. About R$30 (US$6), cash only. —Roda de Samba da Pedra do Sal · Saúde Free open-air samba at the birthplace of Carioca samba, in the old port’s “Pequena África”. From about 7 pm on the stone steps. Bring cash for beer tokens. —CCBB Rio · Centro Open Mondays (closed Tuesdays) until 8 pm. Catch “Vik Muniz: A Olho Nu” before the port fills up — a strong culture warm-up in the historic centre. —Lapa The nightlife heart is quiet on a Monday — the big houses (Rio Scenarium, Circo Voador) run later in the week. Good for a low-key boteco nightcap under the Arcos, not a big night out. —Jazz TribOz in Lapa is the city’s dedicated jazz room, but it runs Wednesday to Saturday — not tonight. Note it for later in the week.

Tonight, Monday 10 August 2026, is a classic Rio Monday — slow on paper, but the samba is the whole point. The city’s two great weekly rodas run as they always do: Moacyr Luz’s Samba do Trabalhador in Andaraí and the free open-air roda at Pedra do Sal in the old port. Add an early exhibition at CCBB and you have a full, unhurried evening. They sit in different parts of the city, so realistically you pick one roda and commit.

Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — August 10, 2026. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Samba do Trabalhador, led by Moacyr Luz — at the Renascença Clube, Rua Barão de São Francisco 54, Andaraí. Now in its third decade, this Monday-afternoon-into-evening roda is one of Rio’s essential experiences: a long table on a raised platform, top-tier instrumentalists, and a crowd that sings every word. Gates open around 4:30 pm and the samba runs to roughly 9 pm. Entry is about R$30 (US$6) and the club takes cash only — there’s no card at the door or the bar. Go early for a spot.

Roda de Samba da Pedra do Sal — at Largo João da Baiana, Saúde, in the port district known as Pequena África. This free, open-air Monday roda takes place at the literal birthplace of Carioca samba: musicians set up at the foot of the old stone steps and the crowd spreads across the largo with cold beer and caipirinhas. Music from about 7 pm. It’s free to attend, but drinks work on a cash token (ficha) system, so bring small bills. Arrive early if you want a good spot on the steps.

Vik Muniz: A Olho Nu at CCBB Rio — Rua Primeiro de Março 66, Centro. The Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil is one of the few major culture houses open on a Monday (it closes Tuesdays), running until 8 pm. The Vik Muniz retrospective is the headline show and pairs well with an early-evening walk through the historic centre before you head to the port. Tickets are free but must be reserved online in advance.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Option A — The Andaraí night. Head to the Renascença Clube by around 5 pm for Samba do Trabalhador and stay put; this is an afternoon-into-evening event that winds down about 9 pm. Rideshare there and back — it’s a residential Zona Norte street.

Option B — The port night. Start at CCBB in Centro (before it closes at 8 pm), then walk or take a short ride to Pedra do Sal in Saúde for the 7 pm roda. Everything is within the revitalised port area, near Praça Mauá and the Museu do Amanhã.

Dinner (8 pm) — Around the port, grab petiscos and a cold beer at a botequim near the largo. In Centro, the Travessa do Comércio lanes near CCBB have old-school bars.

Late (10 pm) — Lapa is subdued on a Monday, but a boteco under the Arcos da Lapa is a fine, low-key nightcap. Don’t expect the weekend club crush.

Getting between them — Andaraí (Zona Norte) and the port (Centro) are far apart. Pick one roda; don’t try to do both in a night.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba — This is the Monday story. Samba do Trabalhador (Andaraí) and Pedra do Sal (Saúde) are the two great weekly rodas, both running tonight. Where: Clube Renascença (Andaraí), Pedra do Sal (Saúde). Trapiche Gamboa nearby runs live samba later in the week.

Choro — Rio’s intricate instrumental tradition turns up in bars and cultural centres, often mixed into samba nights and the port scene. Where: Pedra do Sal surrounds, Centro botecos, CCBB music programme.

MPB (Música Popular Brasileira) — Rio’s songbook lives in Lapa’s music houses and theatres, though most run Thursday to Saturday. Check listings for the week’s bigger names. Where: Lapa houses, Circo Voador, Theatro Municipal.

Jazz — TribOz in Lapa is the city’s dedicated jazz room, with two sets a night Wednesday to Saturday and a modest couvert. Not open Monday, but worth planning for. Where: TribOz (Lapa).

Electronic and clubs — Rio’s club nights are firmly a weekend affair. Save this energy for Friday and Saturday in Lapa and the port. Where: Lapa and the Gamboa/port district, Thursday to Saturday.

Cinema and culture — CCBB Rio is open tonight with the Vik Muniz show and an August cinema programme. Nationwide, the Harry Potter and La La Land anniversary re-releases are also in cinemas this month. Where: CCBB (Centro), Estação and Reserva Cultural (Botafogo), Cine Odeon (Cinelândia).

Pick Your Night

The most Rio thing tonight: Samba do Trabalhador at Renascença — a legendary weekly roda and a real slice of Carioca life.

Free and easy: Pedra do Sal — open-air, no ticket, feet on the cobbles, cold beer, and samba at the birthplace of the genre.

Culture first: CCBB Rio — the Vik Muniz exhibition, then a short walk to the port for the roda.

Quiet and cultured: A boteco in Botafogo or the Travessa do Comércio in Centro — petiscos, cold chope, conversation.

Dance till sunrise: Not a Monday thing in Rio. Save it for the weekend in Lapa or the port.

Where to Go

Clube Renascença (Samba do Trabalhador) — Andaraí A historic Zona Norte social club that hosts Rio’s most celebrated Monday roda, led by Moacyr Luz. A warm, community feel and superb musicianship. Tonight: Samba do Trabalhador. Gates around 4:30 pm, samba from 5 pm, ends about 9 pm. Best time: Mondays only. Arrive by 5 pm for a seat before it fills. Cost: Around R$30 (US$6) at the door. Cash only — no cards at the door or bar. Bring more cash for cold beer and bar food. Address: Rua Barão de São Francisco 54, Andaraí Getting there: Rideshare is easiest — it’s a residential street. Metro Uruguaiana or a ride from Zona Sul; go door-to-door after dark. Good to know: Loud and joyful. It’s a raised-platform roda, so sightlines are good, but come early on a busy Monday.

Pedra do Sal — Saúde (Pequena África) The stone steps in the old port where Carioca samba was born. A free, open-air Monday roda with a loose, spontaneous street-party energy. Tonight: Roda de samba from about 7 pm. Musicians at the foot of the steps; crowd across the largo. Best time: Mondays and Fridays are the big roda nights. Come early to grab a step. Cost: Free to attend. Drinks run on a cash token (ficha) system — carry small bills. Beers roughly R$8–R$12 (US$2). Address: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde Getting there: VLT to the port, or metro Uruguaiana and a short walk/ride. Rideshare to and from after dark. Good to know: Wear comfortable shoes — you’ll stand or perch on stone for hours. Keep an eye on your belongings in the crowd.

CCBB Rio — Centro The Banco do Brasil’s grand cultural centre in a neoclassical landmark. Free, high-quality exhibitions, cinema and music — and open on Mondays. Tonight: “Vik Muniz: A Olho Nu” plus other current shows. Open until 8 pm. Best time: Wednesday to Monday, 9 am to 8 pm. Closed Tuesdays. Cost: Free, but reserve timed tickets online in advance. Café on site. Address: Rua Primeiro de Março 66, Centro Website: ccbb.com.br/rio-de-janeiro Getting there: Metro Uruguaiana or Carioca, short walk. VLT to the port also close. Good to know: Centro empties after office hours — pair it with the port and use rideshare between stops at night.

TribOz — Lapa A tiny, Australian-run jazz room and the city’s dedicated home for the genre. Intimate, serious about the music, easy to miss (no sign outside). Tonight: Closed — TribOz runs Wednesday to Saturday, not Mondays. Note it for later in the week. Best time: Two sets Wednesday to Friday (around 6 pm and 9 pm); Saturday around 8 pm and 9 pm. Cost: Couvert roughly R$15–R$30 (US$3–US$6). Confirm the night’s act and times before going. Address: Rua Conde de Lages 19, Lapa Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, short walk into Lapa. Rideshare to the door — the street is small and easy to miss. Good to know: Small room — reserve ahead for the better nights.

Circo Voador — Lapa Rio’s beloved open-sided concert tent beside the Arcos da Lapa — a launchpad for Brazilian music since 1982. A key venue to check for the week ahead. Tonight: No Monday show — Circo Voador programmes concerts later in the week. Check upcoming dates. Best time: Show nights vary; most run Thursday to Sunday. Doors typically 8 pm. Cost: Varies by act. Buy through official channels. Address: Rua dos Arcos, s/n, Lapa Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, about a 7-minute walk. Good to know: Open-air sides — comfortable most of the year. Confirm the night’s line-up before heading over.

Trapiche Gamboa — Gamboa A characterful live-music bar in a restored port-district building, long loved for its samba and MPB nights and unpretentious crowd. Tonight: Likely closed on a Monday — Trapiche’s live nights skew midweek to weekend. Check before going. Best time: Wednesday to Saturday evenings for live samba and MPB. Cost: Couvert and drinks vary by night. Cash and card usually accepted. Address: Rua Sacadura Cabral 155, Gamboa Getting there: Near Praça Mauá; VLT to the port, then a short ride. Rideshare after dark. Good to know: Same port district as Pedra do Sal — handy to combine later in the week.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Centro / Saúde / Gamboa (Pequena África): The port revival and the cradle of samba. Alive on a Monday for Pedra do Sal, but largely deserted otherwise after dark — travel door-to-door by rideshare.

Lapa: Rio’s nightlife heart under the Arcos — but a weekend beast. On Mondays it’s quiet; good for a boteco, not a big night.

Santa Teresa: Bohemian hilltop of cobbled lanes and artist bars. Charming and low-key; take a rideshare up and down.

Andaraí / Grande Tijuca (Zona Norte): Residential and local, home to the Renascença Clube. Not a stroll-around area at night — rideshare to the door.

Botafogo / Zona Sul: Botafogo has a buzzy boteco and bar scene that ticks over any night; Copacabana, Ipanema and Leblon are relaxed and walkable, if quieter culturally on a Monday.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Weekend-led scene — Rio’s big queer parties, including the port-district clubs, are firmly Friday-and-Saturday affairs. Mondays are quiet on that front.

Everyday-friendly spaces — Lapa’s bars and the samba rodas are broadly mixed and welcoming. For a Monday, the rodas and Botafogo’s bars are your best bet; save the dedicated club nights for the weekend.

Money & How Paying Works Cash for samba: Clube Renascença is cash-only at the door and the bar, and street rodas like Pedra do Sal use cash tokens (fichas) for drinks. Carry R$100–R$200 (US$20–US$40) in small bills. Fichas (tokens): At many rodas and street bars you buy tokens first, then exchange them at the bar for drinks. Buy a few at a time and don’t lose them. Couvert artístico: Music houses like TribOz add a per-person artistic charge (roughly R$15–R$30, US$3–US$6). It’s not a tip; it will be on your bill. Cards and Pix: Cards and Pix are widely accepted in bars and restaurants, but the traditional samba venues are the big exception — assume cash there. Tipping: 10% is usually added to the bill as ‘serviço’. Check before adding more.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: MetrôRio runs roughly 5 am to midnight Monday to Saturday. Check the last-train time for your line before you rely on it.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber are reliable and widely used, and are the safest way home from Andaraí and the port at night. Wait in a lit, busy spot.

Port and Centro at night: The area is lively during the Pedra do Sal roda but empties fast once it winds down. Leave with the crowd or call a car to the largo rather than walking to quiet streets.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

Zona Norte logistics: Andaraí is residential and not a walk-around-at-night area. Go door-to-door by rideshare in both directions.

Frequently Asked Questions

I’ve just landed at GIG (Galeão) tonight. Can I still catch some samba?

On a Monday, yes — Pedra do Sal in the port runs until late and is roughly a 30–40 minute rideshare from Galeão. Samba do Trabalhador in Andaraí is closer to the airport side of town but winds down around 9 pm, so only if you land early. Either way, take a rideshare door-to-door and carry cash.

Do I need to speak Portuguese to enjoy a samba roda?

Not at all. The music does the work, and the crowds at both rodas are welcoming. Learn a couple of songs’ choruses if you can, but a smile, a cold beer and cash for the fichas are all you really need.

Is the port area safe at night for the Pedra do Sal roda?

During the Monday roda the largo is busy and lively, which makes it feel comfortable. The usual city sense applies: keep your phone and wallet secure, stay within the crowd, and take a rideshare to and from rather than walking out to empty streets afterwards.

What’s the dress code on a Monday night?

Casual and comfortable. Samba is relaxed — light clothes and shoes you can stand in for hours. There’s no dress code at the rodas; just bring cash and leave the valuables at home.

Sources: riotur.rio (Samba do Trabalhador), visitrio.com.br (Pedra do Sal), ccbb.com.br, Time Out Rio

Four days of toys, shows, and family fun at Parque San Vicente. Free entry, plus a good cause.

Looking for a free, family-friendly outing this week in Mendoza? The Mendoza toy fair, La Feria del Juguete, lands at Parque San Vicente in Godoy Cruz from Thursday, August 13 to Sunday, August 16, 2026. Entry is completely free, and there are more than 200 stands to explore.

The Mendoza toy fair features over 200 stands plus a food truck zone, making it a one-stop family outing. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What to Expect at the Mendoza Toy Fair

This isn’t just a toy market. You’ll find bicycles, clothing, electronics, books, baby items, and accessories spread across the park.

Food trucks line up for hungry visitors, and live shows run throughout the four days. Kids can enjoy recreational activities, children’s performances, and surprise raffles.

The fair is timed perfectly for Argentina’s Día del Niño, so it’s a great spot to pick up a gift without breaking the bank. With over 200 stands, there’s something for every age and interest.

You can stroll through aisles of traditional wooden toys, board games, and remote-control cars. Parents might spot vintage-style dolls and educational kits that spark nostalgia.

Beyond toys, look for handmade crafts and unique local gifts that you won’t find in shopping malls. The variety makes it easy to find a special present for a child or a treat for yourself.

Many vendors offer discounts on multiple items, and bargaining is welcome in a friendly way. Take your time to compare prices and chat with the sellers—they often have stories behind their goods.

Families often spend three or four hours here without noticing the time. There are benches and grassy areas where you can rest between adventures.

The fair is organized by the municipal government of Godoy Cruz, with support from local volunteers. They’ve arranged everything with families in mind, from stroller-friendly paths to clean restrooms.

Expect a lively mix of music and laughter as performers wander through the aisles. The atmosphere stays relaxed, so you won’t feel rushed as you browse.

Daily Schedule: Shows and Surprises

Thursday opens at 19:00 with Roquito, a family favourite. Friday brings Clasiclown at 16:00, followed by La leyenda de Mur… at 17:30.

Between 18:00 and 20:00, you can grab free popcorn and cotton candy. Friday night heats up with Robot Led at 21:00, Mandalina at 21:30, and Chakaymanta with folklore at 22:00.

Saturday repeats many favourites, starting with Miradas at 17:00, then more Mandalina, Roquito, and Chakaymanta. Each day brings a chance to see something new, so you can visit more than once without getting bored.

Keep an eye on the main stage schedule, which is posted at the entrance. Shows run on time, but arriving a few minutes early helps you secure a good spot.

Sunday: Powercon Takes Over

Sunday is all about Powercon, a comic, manga, and K-pop zone running from 15:00 to 18:00. Kids can join a drawing contest, compete in cosplay, or watch K-pop dance interventions.

There’s also a Japanese sword-fighting demonstration and more raffles. It’s a fantastic way to close the fair with something a little different.

The Godoy Cruz municipal government organises the fair, and they’ve packed the weekend with activities for all ages. The schedule comes straight from their official announcement.

How to Get There and Practical Tips

Parque San Vicente sits in Godoy Cruz, just south of Mendoza’s city centre. It’s easy to reach by bus or car, and the park has plenty of space for families to spread out.

Bring cash, as some stands may not take cards. You can also bring a non-perishable food item to donate to the Banco de Alimentos de Mendoza, a local charity that helps families in need.

Consider arriving early on weekends to avoid the biggest crowds. The park’s open layout means you can find a shady spot for a picnic if you want to stay for several hours.

If you’re driving, there’s free parking nearby, though it fills up fast on Saturday. Public buses stop right at the park’s main entrance, making it a simple trip.

A Day Out

Mendoza’s plazas and tree-lined streets are built for family outings. The city is compact and easy to explore on foot.

Free public events like this are common in Argentine cities. They are a low-cost way for families to fill a weekend.

Check local listings for exact times before you go. Programs can shift with the weather.

Bring cash for snacks and rides. Not every stall takes cards.

Sun protection helps for daytime visits. Mendoza is bright and dry for much of the year.

Strollers are welcome, but the busiest aisles get tight. Off-peak hours are easier with the very young.

Why You Should Care

If you’re living in or visiting Mendoza, this fair is a rare chance to experience local family culture without spending a peso. It’s also a perfect way to meet neighbours, practise your Spanish, and enjoy Mendoza’s warm community spirit.

The fair runs for four days, so you can pick a time that suits you. Whether you’re after a gift, a snack, or just a fun afternoon, this is a welcoming event for expats and locals alike.

Just note this fair is different from the smaller toy fair held at Plaza Tomás Godoy Cruz on August 7. That one has already passed.

The Parque San Vicente event is the big one, so mark your calendar. With so many activities and free entry, it’s an easy choice for a family day out.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Mendoza toy fair really free? Yes, admission is completely free. The official Godoy Cruz announcement says ’entrada libre y gratuita’ for all four days. What dates does the fair run? It runs from Thursday, August 13 to Sunday, August 16, 2026. Thursday opens at 19:00, while Friday to Sunday start earlier in the afternoon. Where exactly is the fair held? It’s at Parque San Vicente in Godoy Cruz, Mendoza. That’s a short trip from the city centre, and the park is easy to find. Can I buy toys there? Absolutely. There are over 200 stands selling toys, games, bicycles, clothing, electronics, books, and baby items. It’s a great place for Día del Niño gifts.

Sources: Godoycruz, Elnueve, Prensa, Tradeshowradar, Mendoza

Trace the 1809 uprising through the old town’s plazas and convents, with a self-guided route for Ecuador’s August 10 holiday.

If you’re in Quito on Monday 10 August 2026, you’re in for a treat. It’s Ecuador’s day of independence, and the old town is buzzing with history. Skip the crowds and do a self-guided walk that traces the dramatic events of 1809. The Quito August 10 historical route takes you from the house where patriots plotted, to the palace where they ousted a governor, and ends at a monument built to remember it all.

The Monumento a los Héroes del 10 de Agosto in Plaza Grande, inaugurated in 1906, stands at the route’s end. In the background, the Palacio de Carondelet. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The Story Behind the Date: Quito August 10 historical route

On 10 August 1809, a group of Creole patriots in Quito did something bold. They deposed the Spanish colonial authorities and formed their own governing junta.

It’s known as the Primer Grito de Independencia, the first cry for independence.

The uprising was short-lived. Colonial forces crushed it within months, and full independence only came in 1822 after the Battle of Pichincha.

But the date stuck as a symbol of Ecuador’s long fight for freedom.

Historians debate its exact significance. Some call it the first successful revolution in Latin America.

Others see it as the opening act of a longer emancipation process. Either way, the events of 1809 shaped the nation.

For visitors, the old town is a living history book. The route takes you through the same streets and plazas where the drama unfolded, over two centuries ago.

The patriots who met that night were mostly Creoles, people of Spanish descent born in the colonies. They were inspired by Enlightenment ideas and by the recent revolutions in the United States and France.

Their junta, though brief, set a powerful example for other regions. It also led to harsh reprisals from royalist authorities, who executed many of the leaders.

The Self-Guided Route, Step by Step

Start at the parish office of El Sagrario, on the edge of Plaza Grande. This is where Manuela Cañizares’ house once stood.

She hosted the secret meeting on the night of 9 August 1809, where the plot was hatched. She was a key figure, known for her sharp mind and her role in rallying the conspirators when they hesitated.

From there, walk a few steps to the Palacio de Carondelet. On the morning of 10 August, Antonio Ante informed the Spanish president, Manuel Urriés, that he was removed from office.

Imagine that tense scene in the palace halls, where the governor’s authority vanished overnight.

Next, head to the Iglesia y Convento de San Agustín. The formal installation of the junta happened here on 16 August 1809, in the Sala Capitular.

It’s a quiet, beautiful convent that packs a historical punch, with its grand cloisters and colonial art.

Finally, return to Plaza Grande and the Monumento a los Héroes del 10 de Agosto. This memorial was inaugurated in 1906, nearly a century later.

It stands as a proud tribute to the uprising’s leaders, with statues and plaques that tell their stories.

The whole walk is short and easy. You can do it in an hour or two, depending on how long you linger.

Wear comfy shoes and bring water, as Quito sits at 2,850 metres and the altitude can tire you out.

Optional Extensions for a Fuller Picture

If you have extra time, continue to the Museo de la Ciudad. It holds documents and objects that show the social context of those revolutionary years.

You’ll see beyond the famous names to how ordinary people lived, including indigenous and Afro-Ecuadorian communities.

A further option is to finish at San Blas, a historic neighbourhood on the edge of the old town. It’s a named extension in the route, but you’ll need to decide if the walk is worth it.

The views and colonial charm are a fine reward, and the area is less crowded than the centre.

The old town itself is a UNESCO World Heritage site. So even without a guide, you’re surrounded by history.

The route simply connects the dots in a meaningful way, giving you a thread to follow amidst the grand architecture.

On the holiday, the city adds its own events. Quito’s tourism office lists museum activities and history-themed programming in the centre.

Check their site before you head out, as some may require advance booking.

Commemorations and 2026 Events

This year marks 217 years since the 10 August 1809 uprising. The Asamblea Nacional, Ecuador’s legislature, held a solemn session to mark the occasion.

It included the entry of provincial flags and the national standard, a moment of silence, and the singing of the Himno a Quito.

You don’t need to be at the official ceremony to feel the weight of the day. Join locals at the plazas, listen to the speeches, or simply sit and watch.

The atmosphere is festive, with a mix of pride and reflection, as bands play and families gather.

If you’re in town for the long weekend, you’ll find concerts, food stalls, and museum specials. The city embraces the holiday with gusto, turning the old town into a stage.

Your self-guided walk fits neatly into the larger celebration, offering a quiet counterpoint to the public events.

Why This Walk Matters for Expats and Nomads

Living in Latin America means experiencing history up close. Ecuador’s independence isn’t just a date on a calendar.

It’s a story of courage and resistance that still defines the nation’s identity, from street names to political speeches.

For expats, this walk is a chance to understand the culture beyond the surface. You’ll see the places where history was made, not just read about them.

It makes for great stories to share back home, and it deepens your connection to your new country.

Plus, it’s free and flexible. You can go at your own pace, stop for coffee, or join a local guided tour.

The route works for solo travellers, couples, or families with older kids, as the distances are short and the sites are rich.

So on 10 August, lace up your shoes and step into 1809. The echoing plazas of Quito will do the rest, as you walk in the footsteps of those who dreamed of freedom.

More: Ecuador news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Quito August 10 historical route? It’s a self-guided walk through Quito’s old town that connects key sites of the 10 August 1809 uprising. It starts at El Sagrario, goes to Carondelet Palace, then San Agustín, and ends at the monument in Plaza Grande. How long does the walk take? About one to two hours, depending on your pace. The sites are close together, so it’s an easy walk. Add extra time for museums or resting in the plazas. Is there an entry fee for the churches or museums? The walk itself is free. San Agustín and the plaza have no entrance fee. The Museo de la Ciudad may charge a small fee, which is worth it for the collections. Check their current prices online. What else happens on 10 August in Quito? The city marks the date with ceremonies, events, and holiday programming. The Asamblea Nacional holds a solemn session. Museums and cultural spaces often have special activities. Check Quito’s tourism office for the latest schedule.

Sources: Expreso, Desacsetdeau, Kchcomunicacion, Turismo, Vistazo

World.title: Puebla Arts Venue Closure Stirs Gentrification Fears
World.content:
Mexico · Culture

Key Facts Venue closure — Foro Cultural Karuzo, a beloved independent arts space, has shut its doors.

— Foro Cultural Karuzo, a beloved independent arts space, has shut its doors. Gentrification debate — Locals link the closure to rising property values and tourist-led redevelopment.

— Locals link the closure to rising property values and tourist-led redevelopment. Festival fallout — The city’s Festival de la Memoria was cancelled, then rescheduled for autumn.

— The city’s Festival de la Memoria was cancelled, then rescheduled for autumn. Artist crackdown — Urban performers report harassment and shrinking performance spaces in Centro Histórico.

— Urban performers report harassment and shrinking performance spaces in Centro Histórico. City response — Puebla plans to expand its registered artist roster despite the tensions.

— Puebla plans to expand its registered artist roster despite the tensions. Historic centre — The Paseo del Río San Francisco project is a flashpoint for critics.

The reported closure of Foro Cultural Karuzo has ignited a wider debate about rising rents and cultural displacement in Puebla’s historic centre.

If you live in Puebla, you may have heard the whispers: Foro Cultural Karuzo, a scrappy independent arts venue in the heart of the city, has shut its doors. This closure isn’t official yet, but it’s already stirring a fierce debate about Puebla cultural venue gentrification. For expats and nomads drawn to the city’s street art and underground music, this feels personal. It’s a story about who gets to shape a city’s soul when money moves in.

A mural in Puebla’s Centro Histórico, where urban artists say performance spaces are shrinking amid redevelopment. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)
