World.title: Germany’s modern miracle: Churches are losing believers but gaining money
World.content:
Rising salaries have outweighed the cost of hundreds of thousands leaving the church.

German commentators are calling it a modern-day “miracle.”

Hundreds of thousands of worshippers are walking away from their churches each year. The money, however, keeps rolling in.

Some 660,000 people formally quit the country’s Catholic and Protestant churches in 2025, freeing them from a levy automatically charged to registered members as a percentage of their income tax bill.

Despite the exodus, the two institutions collected more than €12.5 billion through the church tax for the 2025 fiscal year, up from around €12.4 billion in 2024.

The apparent miracle has a decidedly earthly explanation: Rising wages and Germany’s progressive tax system mean the shrinking pool of members is paying more.

“At first glance, the development may seem contradictory,” a spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany — the umbrella organization representing Germany’s regional Protestant churches — said. “The reason is that church tax is calculated based on individual income tax.”





Members of Germany’s Catholic and Protestant churches and some Jewish communities pay an additional religious tax equal to 8 or 9 percent of their income tax liability, even if they don’t attend services.

In 2021, the most recent year for which comprehensive data is available, more than 29 million people paid church tax in Germany, amounting to almost half of all income taxpayers in Europe’s largest economy.

The German Finance Ministry’s 2025 payroll tax tables suggests that a single employee without children earning €50,000 gross a year pays approximately €600 in church tax annually on top of income tax, depending on the federal state. Someone earning €70,000 per year pays more than €1,000.

People are registered as part of their religious community at birth or at local government offices. To stop paying the church tax, they must formally leave through a process known as Kirchenaustritt, or “church exit.”

The procedure varies across Germany’s federal states but typically requires appearing in person at a registry office or local court to submit a declaration. Most states also charge an administrative fee.

While those who deregister can still attend services as a visitor and access some church services, they are not allowed to have a church wedding, be a godparent or be guaranteed a church burial.

In 2025, some 310,000 left the Catholic Church, while around 350,000 left one of Germany’s regional Protestant churches.

Church exit

The reasons people give for formally leaving their religious communities range from feeling less connected to the church to simply wanting to save money.

“People are leaving the Church because they feel it no longer plays a role in their lives,” said Matthias Kopp, director of communications for the German Bishops’ Conference.

“Added to this are the scandals of recent years, which have called the Church’s credibility into question,” he added. “There are also people — though this is by no means the primary reason — who leave the Church because of the church tax.”

“These are processes of alienation to which we must respond,” said Kopp.

For Jana Keil, a 33-year-old accountant from Berlin, the decision was both financial and moral. “I no longer wanted to support the system with church tax in light of the [child sex] abuse scandals,” she said.





Lukas Heinich, a 23-year-old working student, said he formally left after completing his apprenticeship because he “didn’t feel like paying the tax or supporting the church.”

That church tax revenues continue to rise despite the exodus is down to the types of taxpayers choosing to remain church members.

Those who are still paying church tax in Germany are “probably the higher earners,” said Zareh Asatryan, professor of empirical economics at the University of Münster. “Those that stay will naturally earn more income because of inflation plus real wage growth, and they will just generate more revenue.”

A miracle with an end date?

But the continued rise in church tax revenue masks significant long-term challenges — and raises questions about how long the trend can last.

While those revenues are going up, they are “relatively sluggish” and “haven’t been increasing by a lot,” said Asatryan.

The increase in revenue from the church tax is considerably lower than the increase in revenue from income tax. State revenue from wage and income taxes rose by 6.65 percent in 2025, said Kopp, whereas church tax revenue increased by 1.93 percent.

“Long-term projections indicate that church tax revenue will decline significantly over the coming decades as church membership continues to decrease,” said the spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany.

Protestant churches are already preparing for their income to decrease “through long-term planning processes,” said the spokesperson. “Without this system, the church’s religious, social and charitable work would not be possible on its current scale.”

World.title: EU opens channel with Meta, TikTok to tackle Ceuta migrant crisis
World.content:
That will serve as a point of contact for platforms, fact-checkers and the Commission to quickly flag content so that it can be reviewed and taken down if necessary. The effort comes amid concerns that disinformation is promoting further crossings into the territory on Aug. 15, according to Maldita.es. Maldita.es and the European Fact-Checking Standards Network attended Monday’s meeting.

The Commission operates a rapid response system under its code of conduct on disinformation, often triggered around elections. The new mechanism on Ceuta would bring a closer group of stakeholders together, two of the people said.

Another meeting has been set for later this week, one of those people and the third person confirmed.

Meta and TikTok said they were already actively monitoring the situation in line with their policies and had set up dedicated teams to monitor and respond to content in real time.

The crisis has divided EU countries and has reignited Europe’s long-running debate on illegal migration. Italy has since been one of the harshest critics of Spain’s left-wing government and its migration policies, and has implemented border controls for travelers arriving from Spain.

Former EU commissioner Thierry Breton, who was a force behind the EU’s online content rules, on Monday said the bloc should launch a disinformation inquiry into the Ceuta crisis in an interview with Italian newspaper La Stampa.

World.title: Greece’s aging power grid blamed for catastrophic wildfires
World.content:
Two deadly wildfires in late July — one in western Attica and one on the island of Crete —were also linked to the electricity grid in preliminary findings from the Greek fire brigade. The fires destroyed more than 36,000 acres and killed four people.

“Six out of 10 major fires and 55 percent of the area burnt in 2025 were caused by the power grid,” said Elias Tziritis, wildfires actions coordinator at World Wildlife Fund Greece. “Statistically speaking, the majority of fires may not start from the power grid, but these are the ones that cause the most major, devastating fires.”

Loose or sagging power lines, vegetation coming in contact with cables, dust buildup on transmission equipment and other such faults can all generate sparks. The risk rises during strong winds and periods of heavy electricity demand, when aging infrastructure is under greater strain.

Much of Greece’s electricity grid was installed decades ago and runs above ground through fire-prone forests and increasingly depopulated rural areas. In the 1960s, the country opted for an overhead network as a cheaper way to extend electricity across the country, while the prolonged financial crisis that began in 2009 further constrained investment in the system.

Critics say Greece has moved too slowly to bury distribution lines and adapt the network to increasingly severe fire conditions.

“We raised the issue years ago, calling for something to be done with the power grid urgently,” said Christos Kalogeropoulos, a retired lieutenant-general with the Fire Service and former director of the Arson Crimes unit. “We have been calling for urgent underground cabling.”

World.title: UK approves its second weight-loss pill while EU access lags
World.content:
However, with the arrival of the first GLP-1 pill Wegovy (semaglutide) from Danish competitor Novo Nordisk — which launched in the U.S. and U.K. this year and is soon expected in some EU countries — demand for the more-convenient tablet is expected to rise.

Novo Nordisk has been attempting to reach as many patients as possible with its pill to capture market share, said CEO Mike Doustdar last week.

Doustdar also said the company would soon launch in Germany at its chosen price, ignoring pressure from the U.S. administration to raise prices in Europe.

Washington has been pressuring EU countries to pay more for medicines to offset pharma revenue losses from lower U.S. drug prices. The U.K. is the only country to agree to pay more for medicines via a bilateral deal with the U.S.

Foundayo's arrival in the U.K. will initially provide competition in the private market. A decision on whether the National Health Service will cover the pill is not expected until Nov. 18, and will be made by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.

World.title: Europe’s scorching summer is erasing its economic growth, says report
World.content:
The biggest drag is expected to come from people struggling to work in extreme heat. Triodos estimates lost labor productivity alone could shave around 0.6 percent off EU GDP, while agricultural output could fall by between 3 and 7 percent.

“At first sight this might seem modest, but it is exactly the expected economic growth for the EU this year,” said the bank of the overall €180 billion blow.

And the summer is not over. France and Britain are bracing for their fifth heat wave of the season this week, with temperatures nearing 40 degrees Celsius in southeastern France and 36 degrees forecast in the U.K.

The bill is already mounting beyond GDP. POLITICO estimated at least 14,000 excess deaths across the six hardest-hit European countries during the record-breaking heat wave from mid-June to early July.

Drought has also hammered Europe’s energy system: Low water levels in the Danube in recent weeks have forced sharp cuts at Hungary’s Paks nuclear plant and pushed Romania to blast apart a rock to divert water toward its last operating reactor. Vessels on the Rhine and Danube have had to sail only partially loaded.

In Austria, meanwhile, drought has caused an estimated €1 billion in agricultural losses, according to Austrian Hail Insurance, after some regions received more than 75 percent less rain than normal since mid-June.

Triodos warned against treating this summer as a freak event, saying extreme heat “might become structural” as the planet warms. But governments can soften the damage through irrigation, insulation, cooling and shifting working hours, said the bank.

“Every year adaptation without mitigation is a year borrowed against a hotter baseline.”

World.title: Europe is running out of Patriot missiles as Ukraine braces for Russia’s winter attacks
World.content:
Germany, one of Ukraine’s top military aid donors, has already transferred Patriot systems and missiles to Ukraine. But Berlin must now balance Kyiv’s increasingly urgent needs against the minimum stocks required to protect Germany and meet its NATO commitments. Other European countries are also weighing whether to hang on to their interceptors or give them to Ukraine.

“We are really reaching our limits here,” Brig. Gen. Jürgen Schrödl, a senior German defense ministry official, said at a panel in Berlin shortly after last month’s NATO summit in Ankara. “We also have to ensure our own protection.”

Berlin and other Northern European capitals have urged counterparts elsewhere on the continent to examine what more military equipment and financial support they could release.

“I think it’s not sustainable for Europe in the long run,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik told POLITICO. “All the European countries have to step up.”

That's putting pressure on countries with stocks of Patriot interceptors like Poland, Spain and Greece. The shortage primarily concerns Patriot PAC-3 and PAC-2 missiles, which are among Ukraine’s few effective defenses against fast-moving Russian ballistic weapons.

Ukraine can use other, often cheaper, air-defense systems against drones and cruise missiles. The country is racing to develop its homegrown Freyja interceptor, but the anti-ballistic system still requires investment, engineering work and testing before it can fill that role.

World.title: Moldovan president condemns Russia over killer drone crash
World.content:
Maia Sandu participates in a press conference in Warsaw on Jan. 26, 2026. | Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images

Chișinău has recalled its envoy to Moscow after two incidents in recent weeks.

Moldovan President Maia Sandu has blamed Russia’s war in Ukraine for a recent drone crash in the southeast of her country.

A drone crashed and exploded in the village of Crocmaz on Sunday, causing a fire that damaged several properties but caused no casualties. After conducting preliminary analysis on the fragments, local police said it could be a “missile-like drone.”

“I strongly condemn the latest violation of our airspace,” Sandu wrote on X, adding: “This is a direct consequence of Russia’s war, and it endangers us all.”

World.title: Trump pushes overhaul of US childhood vaccine policy
World.content:
In an executive order, President Trump calls for fewer recommended childhood vaccinations and more spacing between shots. Medical experts warn the changes lack scientific backing and could leave children less protected.

US President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order seeking sweeping changes to childhood vaccine policy, including fewer recommended immunizations and more separate appointments for children to receive them.

The order calls for the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, to be separated into three single-disease shots. It also advocates administering childhood immunizations at separate medical visits whenever possible.

A healthcare worker prepares an MMR vaccination at a health center in Texas [FILE: April 8, 2025] Image: Annie Rice/AP Photo/picture alliance

Trump described the move as a "major victory for parents rights, religious and constitutional rights, and for the gold standard science."

What changes does Trump want for childhood vaccines?

The order says the federal government will support 11 core childhood vaccinations and advises states and territories to review vaccine requirements for school enrollment.

However, Washington cannot directly determine most school vaccine mandates, which are largely set by individual states. On those requirements, Trump's order is therefore primarily a recommendation.

The order also directs the Health and Human Services Department to improve vaccine research and develop a plan to make separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines available in the US. Such single-antigen vaccines are not currently licensed there.

US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has long questioned established vaccine recommendations and promoted a disproven link between vaccines and autism Image: Andrew Leyden/ZUMA/picture alliance

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. had already sought in January to remove vaccines against six of 17 diseases from the childhood schedule. A federal judge later blocked those changes while legal proceedings continue. Monday's order reaffirms much of that overhaul.

Why do experts oppose spacing out vaccines?

Public health experts say childhood vaccination schedules are based on extensive research into when and how vaccines can safely be administered together. Safety monitoring continues after vaccines are introduced.

They warn that spreading shots across more appointments can leave children vulnerable to preventable diseases for longer and increase the risk that later doses are delayed or missed.

Vaccine maker Merck said there was no published scientific evidence showing any benefit from splitting the MMR vaccine. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, estimated that developing and approving separate vaccines in the US could take more than a decade.

"We're advising that you continue to give children a vaccine that has decades of safety data," said Aaron M. Milstone, a member of the AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases.

What does Trump say about vaccines and autism?

Speaking in the Oval Office, Trump repeatedly suggested that the number or timing of childhood vaccines could be linked to rising rates of autism spectrum disorder.

Scientific consensus and decades of studies have found no link between vaccination and autism.

Kennedy has also repeatedly promoted the disproven connection. He founded an anti-vaccine nonprofit before joining the administration.

How have experts reacted to Trump's vaccine order?

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician and chairman of the Senate health committee, condemned the move.

"I'm a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The president does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy said, adding that splitting combination vaccines "will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots."

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy, a physician, has sharply criticized Trump's executive order on childhood vaccines, saying it could leave children less protected [FILE: May 19, 2026] Image: Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Cassidy cast the decisive vote to confirm Kennedy as health secretary in 2025 despite concerns over his vaccine skepticism. He lost his Republican primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger and is due to leave office in January.

New York City Health Commissioner Alister Martin said the order was based "in politics and conspiracy theories."

"Fortunately, vaccination recommendations are not set by the president, nor should they be," Martin said.

Why is the timing of Trump's vaccine push significant?

The policy shift comes as the United States experiences its worst measles outbreak in 35 years and children prepare to return to school.

Critics have accused Kennedy of contributing to vaccine hesitancy through years of questioning established immunizations.

The renewed focus on vaccines also marks a shift from the administration's recent emphasis on less divisive health policies, including healthy eating, drug price negotiations and efforts to combat medical fraud ahead of November's midterm elections.

World.title: Turkey MPs back historic law on reintegrating PKK militants
World.content:
Turkey's parliament has taken a major step toward ending four decades of conflict with the PKK. The new law sets out how some militants can return to civilian life, but leaves Abdullah Ocalan's future unresolved.

Turkey's parliament on Monday approved legislation offering a conditional pardon and legal protections to thousands of members of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK).

After around 12 hours of debate, lawmakers voted 468 to 88 in favor of the 12-article bill, with six abstentions. It was backed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's AK Party, its nationalist MHP allies and the pro-Kurdish DEM party.

What does Turkey's new PKK law provide?

The law sets out procedures for the PKK's disarmament and dissolution and the reintegration of some members into civilian life. The government has stressed that it is not a general amnesty.

Some prison sentences would be suspended, while investigations and trials could be postponed for five or 10 years depending on the offense.

If those covered commit no terrorism-related crime during that period, cases would be dropped and sentences considered served.

Turkish lawmakers debated the bill for around 12 hours before voting on the legislation Image: Mustafa Kaya/Xinhua/picture alliance

Around 3,500 PKK-linked detainees could initially be released, lawmakers said. Media reports suggest exiled members and fighters in Iraq and Syria could also benefit.

People convicted of intentional killings and some serving life sentences are excluded.

When will the law take effect?

The measures will only come into force once Turkey's National Security Council confirms that the PKK has dissolved and surrendered all weapons.

Those seeking to benefit would then have six months to apply. Ministerial and parliamentary committees are also due to monitor the process.

Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz hailed the vote as a 'historic step' toward ending the decades-long conflict with the PKK [FILE: March 27, 2026] Image: Ahmet Okur/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Turkey’s Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz called the vote a "historic step", saying "the 468 'yes' votes are of the utmost importance in terms of political consensus".

What happens to Abdullah Ocalan?

The law does not cover imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan, 77, who has been held on Imrali island near Istanbul since 1999.

Yilmaz said Ocalan's case "does not fall within the scope of this law", but added that he could remain "in a position to contribute to the peace process".

Ocalan has been central to the initiative. In February 2025, he urged the PKK to disarm and dissolve and pursue Kurdish rights through democratic means.

This latest image of imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan was provided by the pro-Kurdish DEM party [FILE: February 27, 2026] Image: DEM

The PKK announced its dissolution in May 2025. Two months later, militants symbolically burned weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq and the group said it was withdrawing fighters from Turkey.

What does the PKK say?

The PKK has called the legislation a "beginning" but said it contains "serious shortcomings and deficiencies."

It has demanded Ocalan's release and said the process can move forward only if he "lives and works freely."

The group also said fighters would not return without guarantees that they could engage in politics without prosecution over their views or organizations.

Pro-Kurdish DEM lawmaker Gulistan Kilic Kocyigit said: "The people of Turkey, who have paid a heavy price for many years, now have an opportunity to consolidate peace and build democracy."

Why is the bill controversial?

Nationalist opposition lawmakers accuse the government of making concessions to the PKK.

"How can you negotiate with terrorists? You said they would be laying down their weapons unconditionally," said Turhan Comez, a lawmaker with the nationalist opposition Iyi party.

Turkey: An end to the Kurdish conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iyi Party leader Musavat Dervisoglu also said the law "would pave the way" for Erdogan to remain in power. Erdogan could run again if parliament calls an early election during his current term.

Why does the conflict matter?

The PKK launched its insurgency in 1984. More than 40,000 people have been killed, and the conflict has caused major economic damage in Kurdish-majority southeastern Turkey and fueled decades of political and social division.

The PKK initially sought an independent Kurdish state but later shifted toward demands for autonomy and expanded rights.

It is designated a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States and the European Union.

Previous peace efforts failed, most recently in 2015.

The initiative could also have regional effects, including closer Turkish-Iraqi ties and implications for efforts to integrate areas in Syria administered by the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) with Damascus.

The SDF's dominant militia, the People's Defense Units (YPG), is seen as an offshoot of the PKK, and is considered by Ankara to be a terrorist organization.

World.title: Russia: Top court bans opposition anti-war party from vote
World.content:
Yabloko, Russia's only anti-war party, has been barred from September's parliamentary elections. The motion to bar Yabloko was filed by the nationalist pro-Kremlin party Rodina.

The Supreme Court of Russia on Monday ruled in favor of the nationalist pro-Kremlin Rodina (Motherland) party and barred Yabloko (Apple) — Russia's only anti-war party — from participating in September parliamentary elections.

Rodina accuses Yabloko of receiving undeclared financial support from Western sources, among other things.

Arguing before the court, Yabloko vehemently denied the accusations and railed against Rodina's lack of supporting evidence.

The nationalist pro-Kremlin Rodina party brought the case, accusing Yabloko of receiving foreign funding, yet without providing evidence to support the claim Image: Pavel Seleznev/TASS/picture alliance

On Monday, Judge Vyacheslav Kirillov said, "The claims seeking to annul the registration of the federal list of candidates for the State Duma of the ninth convocation, nominated by the Yabloko political party, were granted."

The court's decision means citizens opposed to Russia's four-and-a-half-year invasion of Ukraine — or "special military operation" as it has been legally deemed under penalty of imprisonment — have no opportunity to vote for representatives willing to articulate that opposition.

Yabloko leader Nikolay Rybakov told the hundred or so supporters gathered outside the court, "Excluding Yabloko from the election means refusing dialog with people who ask questions that are uncomfortable for the authorities."

"We have a long road ahead and we have a big and important task — to stop deaths and bring back peace. Everything we do should be dedicated to that," Rybakov added, vowing to appeal the decision.

Yabloko — the only liberal party still operating in Russia since most of President Vladimir Putin's opponents have been jailed, exiled or murdered — has received the backing of several exiled opposition figures, including Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny.

Yabloko was once a strong liberal force in Russia but like other opposition outfits it has been systematically sidelined by the Kremlin.

The party is currently only polling around three percent — short of the five percent threshold for entry into parliament — and has not won a seat in the federal State Duma since 2003.

Putin-backing United Russia has won every single election since then and that is expected to again be the case in September.

Yabloko supporters ignored the threat of repression to show support for the party's anti-war stance at the Supreme Court Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance

But despite barring political opposition to the war, public opinion toward the conflict has soured, more so since Ukraine has intensified its attacks on energy and logistics infrastructure inside Russia.

The non-governmental Levada Center — which is on the Kremlin's "foreign agents" list — charts support at around 66%, the lowest since Russia launched its attack against neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022.

The Kremlin has cracked down on opposition to the war with strict censorship rules and mass arrests, with many activists and journalists preferring to flee than to face potentially deadly persecution by staying in Russia.

World.title: Colombia earthquake: Death toll rises to over 100
World.content:
A powerful earthquake, measured at magnitude 7.4, has struck Colombia, killing dozens of people and trapping many under rubble. Cities including Cali, Pereira and Manizales were among the hardest-hit.

A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.

Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country.

Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.

The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.

What is the latest?

Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency.

He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency.

"As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota.

Multiple deaths after major earthquake in Colombia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU stands "ready to provide more support" to Colombia. The bloc's satellite service, Copernicus, has already been mobilized to aid rescuers.

"Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia," she wrote on social media.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia."

What's happening on the ground?

The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.

"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."

Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, said that at least 27 people had died in the quake, in numbers issued prior to the president's address.

Officials in Risaralda had said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor.

The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were 12 dead and 84 wounded in her district as of lunch time local time.

And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira.

Residents in Cali tried to rush to safety in the aftermath of Monday's earthquake Image: Santiago Saldarriaga/AP Photo/picture alliance

Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.

"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list.

What do we know about the quake's size and location?

The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.

The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.

One of the towers at the Cathedral of Manizales was damaged by the quake Image: John Jairo Bonilla/AP Photo/picture alliance

The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.

The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.

The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors .

Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.

USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.

The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

World.title: Why the Rhine drought is bad news for Germany's recovery
World.content:
Germany’s inland waterways still move around 5% of the nation's goods. With the Rhine at a critically low level, DW explores how the drought is hitting the economy where it hurts most.

Water levels on the Rhine River — a small but critical artery for goods vital to Germany’s industry — remain critically low as a result of weeks of drought.

At one of the river's shallowest stretches, Kaub — between Mainz and Koblenz — the water level stood at around 16 centimeters (6.3 inches) at Monday lunchtime, according to the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration (WSV).

Although the real navigable channel is roughly a meter deeper, 40 centimeters is regarded as the lowest for standard commercial vessels at Kaub.

Ship operators use the reading at Kaub to decide how much cargo their barges can safely carry and whether a passage is feasible at all.

According to local media, in recent weeks, carriers have significantly cut their cargoes along the Rhine — in many cases to as little as one-fifth of normal capacity.

The problem isn't just limited to the Middle Rhine, the 130-kilometer (80-mile) stretch between Mainz and Bonn that is the narrowest and shallowest section of the river.

Areas around Cologne, Düsseldorf, Duisburg-Ruhrort and Emmerich are also at historic lows.

Jens Schwanen, the head of the BDB association of inland shipping, told the Rheinische Post newspaper on Monday that the Rhine may become impassable at Kaub before the end of the week.

This would effectively split the river in two for commercial traffic.

What effect will the drought have on the German economy?

The drought could not come at a worse time for Germany’s economy, which is already grappling with weak growth, high energy costs and fading industrial competitiveness.

Germany still relies on its long rivers and waterways to transport some 5% of goods around the country, most of them bulk materials, including iron ore, coal, sand and petroleum products.

Out of 3.28 billion tons of goods transported in 2024, 173 million tons were carried by inland water, including the Rhine, according to BDB.

Eurostat, the European Union's statistics agency, calculated in 2023 that the Rhine corridor — from the Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands to the German-Swiss border — accounts for around 40% of freight by ton-kilometers.

After two previous droughts, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy calculated in 2023 that for every 30 days of low water on the Rhine, Germany's industrial production declines by about 1%.

In an economy that has barely grown for the past two years, even a temporary 1% hit to industrial output is highly damaging.

The German Economic Institute (IW) now predicts a 0.4% drop in gross domestic product, effectively wiping out this year's economic growth, which was expected at 0.5%.

"A prolonged disruption of navigability on the Rhine could completely stifle the tiny seed of growth we have," warned IW economist Thilo Schäfer in an interview with Bild newspaper last week.

Other experts have warned of losses of €1 to €2 billion ($1.2 to $2.3 billion) in the third quarter alone, with the steel, chemicals and energy sectors hit especially hard.

What happens if the River Rhine is effectively split in two?

The BDB's Schwanen warned that "due to the lack of rainfall, a single-digit reading is forecast for the first time this week at the Kaub gauge."

"In principle, this means the Rhine is no longer navigable along its entire length and is therefore effectively divided in two," he told the Rheinische Post.

This would result in two separate areas. On the one hand, shipping traffic would continue between the North Sea ports of Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and Antwerp and the Cologne region via the Rhine and the Western German canal system.

Further south, shipping would operate on the tributaries of the Neckar, Moselle, and Main, as well as the Main-Danube Canal, which is regarded as a key global link on the route to and from Southeast Europe.

Between the two sections, shipping companies would then try to move cargo onto trucks and freight rail services.

However, Germany's roads cannot absorb the typical 50 to 150 truckloads that a single large barge can handle without severe congestion and substantially higher costs.

Baden-Württemberg said Monday it would join four other German states in easing restrictions on truck movements on Sundays to help ease congestion.

Following urgent talks last Thursday, Transport Minister Steffen Bilger announced several other measures to shore up Germany's supply chain.

These include cutting red tape for heavy loads shifted to the road network, stopping unnecessary roadworks and better coordination with DB Cargo, the rail freight arm of Deutsche Bahn.

Many vessels are carrying a fifth of their normal cargo volumes Image: Rüdiger Wölk/IMAGO

Are regular droughts a new reality for Europe's waterways?

Extremely low water on the Rhine and other major European rivers used to be rare events.

Yet, many scientists believe climate change is now making them more frequent, longer and more severe.

According to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, western Europe has just experienced its warmest June and July on record, with exceptionally low rainfall driving much lower than average water levels on the Rhine, Danube and Seine.

The current crisis marks the third major low‑water episode in eight years, after major droughts in 2018 and 2022.

The Rhine has traditionally been supported during dry summer months by meltwater from Alpine snow and glaciers. As those glaciers retreat and snow cover declines, this natural buffer is weakening.

Germany’s Federal Institute of Hydrology (BfG) projected in 2023 that severe low-water events like 2018 could strike every five to 10 years by mid-century.

Can shipping adapt as Germany's busiest river runs dry? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: India news: Jharkhand police use tear gas, water cannons to disperse student protesters
World.content:
08/10/2026 August 10, 2026 Assam flood toll climbs to 100

As floodwaters recede in some areas, residents are returning to homes buried under thick layers of silt Image: Pitamber Newar/ANI

The situation in India's northeastern Assam state remained critical on Monday, with the death toll in the floods reaching 100, officials said.

Two more people died overnight on Sunday after weeks of heavy monsoon rain inundated villages, damaged roads and farmland and disrupted livelihoods.

More than 700,000 people have been displaced since the floods began last month, while about 49,000 remain in 125 relief camps and distribution centers, officials said.

Authorities are warning that, several rivers, including the Brahmaputra, remained above danger levels, raising the risk of further flooding in vulnerable areas.

Farukuddin Ahmed, a 47-year-old trader from Nazira town in Assam's worst-hit Sivasagar district, that in a nearby village of 100 houses only a few remain.

"The residents, mainly dairy farmers, have to rebuild their lives from scratch having lost all their cattle," he said, according to the Associated Press.

Authorities are assessing the damage and providing financial assistance to affected residents. According to the government about 50,000 people had already received interim compensation.

While flooding is a recurring problem in Assam during the monsoon, experts warn that climate change is making rainfall increasingly erratic and extreme.

World.title: Which country is the new Mecca defense pact targeting?
World.content:
Observers suggest the new alliance between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan won't result in any of the countries fighting for each other. Instead it's about preventing Iran and Israel from regional dominance, they say.

Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia sealed a historic defense pact on Friday, signing an agreement "intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression."

The so-called "Mecca Joint Defense Agreement" between the three Sunni Muslim-majority states is meant to increase cooperation during regional uncertainty and threats from the Iran war.

The agreement was signed in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

The alliance has been likened to a NATO-style alliance and on Friday, the Pakistani foreign ministry said that an attack on any member would be regarded as an attack on all.

But experts and analysts have been quick to point out that the deal is unlikely to work that way — at least at first.

On Saturday, Yemen's Houthi group targeted Saudi Arabian oil facilities in Jizan. A July attack on the same facility is seen here Image: Social Media/REUTERS

For example, on the weekend the Houthi rebel group in Yemen fired at Saudi Arabian oil facilities again. The Houthis consider Saudi Arabia their enemy and are also aligned with Iran. The latter has also targeted Saudi Arabia after the US and Israel attacked it, starting a war in late February, because it sees the Saudis as a US ally.

But following the Houthi attack on the weekend, neither Turkey nor Pakistan sprang to the Saudis' defense. Nor are they likely to attack Iran, analysts say. In fact, Pakistan is acting as a mediator between Iran and the US currently.

Mecca agreement an 'elastic defense pact'

This arrangement is meant as more of a deterrent and as an "elastic defense pact," Dania Thafer, executive director of the Washington-based think tank the Gulf International Forum, or GIF, told DW late last week.

"If you look at the parties in this agreement, you have Saudi Arabia, which is in the middle of this conflict. But you also have Turkey and Pakistan, who both have relations with Iran and both have relations with the US. So I think it's an extra layer of deterrence, if you will, for Saudi Arabia," Thafer explained. "I think Saudi Arabia is looking at a layered deterrence approach to regional threats as they emerge."

This new alliance is likely to work out in various stages with the short-term goal being a "stabilized region," Kamran Bokhari, a senior fellow at the Middle East Policy Council in Washington, told DW.

Technology transfer and investment

Longer term goals will involve defense cooperation rather than fighting, other experts have said.

"The three countries complement each other unusually well," Andreas Krieg, a lecturer in security at King's College London, told news agency Agence France-Presse last week.

Saudi Arabia has oil wealth but limited defense technology and has been reliant on the US up until now. Meanwhile Turkey and Pakistan need investment and have strong armed forces, and in Turkey's case an advanced defense-industrial sector, Krieg explained. Pakistan is the only one with nuclear weapons of the three.

"Turkey has technology and production capacity but needs markets and investment. Pakistan has a workforce, military institutions and nuclear deterrent, but needs financing and industrial capabilities," Krieg noted.

Who does the Mecca pact target?

A Turkish official cited by Reuters said the agreement was purely defensive in nature and open to any regional neighbors who might want to sign on. Egypt is thought to be a potential partner but also has other allies to consider, including the United Arab Emirates. The latter have not joined and relations between the UAE and Saudi Arabia are currently strained.

The Turkish official also said the pact does not replace or negate previous bilateral or multilateral agreements between signatories, nor is it directed at any one actor or threat.

Yet there's no doubt the agreement has been understood as a deterrent, mainly against two other nations, Iran and Israel.

The Mecca pact's objectives are not about some kind of military victory, Khalid al-Jaber, director of the Doha-based Middle East Council on Global Affairs wrote in a Sunday op-ed for Qatari news outlet, Al Jazeera . "It is the prevention of hegemony."

"Diminished American weight could leave the region inside an order whose rules are set by two actors alone: Israel and Iran," he continued. "The Mecca pact is best understood as an early attempt to build a third pole — a bloc that does not need to fight either power, but one that has enough weight to deny either a monopoly over the region."

Damage in Iran: The country was attacked by the US and Israel in late February and the war is ongoing, although peace talks also continue Image: Morteza Akhoondi/MEI/SIPA/picture alliance

How does Israel feel about it?

Two of the signatories to the agreement — Pakistan and Saudi Arabia — don't recognize Israel and have no official relations with it, even though at least in Saudi Arabia's case there are likely some covert ties. Turkey does recognize Israel but the relationship is strained at the moment, due to Israel's activity in Gaza that Turkey has called genocide.

Turkish leader Erdogan said last week that Israel's actions in Syria and Lebanon also constitute a threat to Turkish security.

"The development [of the Mecca pact] poses significant challenges for Israel, pushes the prospect of normalization with Riyadh further out of reach and cuts short the vision of a 'new Middle East'," Oshrit Birvadker, a research fellow at the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security, wrote in a Saturday editorial for the outlet Israel Hayom .

Birvadker also believes that the new trilateral alliance will increase the growing rivalry and tensions between Turkey and Israel.

Mixed reactions in Iran

The Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University looked at how the Iranians were reacting.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi did not seem too upset by the agreement. On the social media platform, X (formerly Twitter) he posted that "when Muslims stand together, we can face every challenge by malicious outsiders head-on."

Observers took this to be a positive, part of Iran's argument for pushing the US out of the region.

Some Iranian observers thought that the Saudis might be trying to leverage the better relations that the Turkish and Pakistanis have with the Iranians, to make itself safer from Iranian attacks. But other Iranian politicians were more critical, saying that Saudi Arabia wasn't safe with the US as an ally and wouldn't be safe with Turkey and Pakistan either.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: How climate change is reshaping Africa's malaria risk
World.content:
Researchers say warming temperatures are altering malaria transmission patterns across Africa, creating new challenges for health systems and disease control.

For decades, global efforts towards the eradication of malaria, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, have focused essentially on West and Central Africa, where the disease is most endemic.

The WHO African Region accounts for about 95% of global malaria cases and deaths. More than half of all malaria deaths in the region occur in Nigeria (31.9%), the Democratic Republic of Congo (11.7%) and Niger (6.1%). Children under 5 years of age account for about 76% of malaria deaths in the region.

To stem the tide of malaria cases across Africa, the global health body has recommended a wider use of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine among children living in regions with moderate to high malaria transmission by the Plasmodium falciparum — a parasite that causes 95% of all malaria infections in Africa. It's transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

The WHO warned in April 2025 that recent funding cuts were jeopardising malaria control efforts, with more than half of malaria-endemic countries surveyed reporting moderate or severe disruptions to malaria services.

A study published in The Lancet found that the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine reduced all-cause mortality among vaccine-eligible children by 13.2% in pilot programs in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi.

A changing disease landscape

Malaria transmission is most efficient within temperature ranges common across many tropical regions of West and Central Africa, according to a new study published in the journal Nature .

Tanzania's bold experiment against malaria To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Malaria transmission by mosquitoes usually peaks at temperatures of around 25 degrees Celsius (77 Fahrenheit) and becomes much less likely when temperatures drop below 16 degrees or rise above 34 degrees Celsius, largely because the malaria parasite must complete part of its life cycle inside the mosquito — a process that is highly temperature-dependent.

Because of this, malaria transmission has historically been most favourable across many tropical parts of West and Central Africa, where temperatures frequently fall within the range most suitable for transmission.

In contrast, some parts of Southern Africa and the highlands of East Africa have historically remained cool enough to keep the spread of malaria at bay, preventing the disease from becoming a major public health burden.

That, however, is beginning to change. The Nature study found that rising temperatures are making parts of southern Africa and high-elevation areas of East Africa increasingly suitable for malaria transmission, while parts of West Africa are becoming too hot for optimal transmission.

What does this mean for the continent?

Climate change is not only heating up the continent, it's redistributing risks, says Olugbenga Mokuolu, professor of pediatrics at Nigeria's University of Ilorin.

Although West African countries like Nigeria fall under areas that are "too hot for malaria to thrive, this is not good news to celebrate either, because a world that's too hot for malaria is not a good world for children's health overall," Mokuolu, who also serves as an advisor to the Nigerian Minister of Health on malaria elimination, told DW.

"The same heat that's inconvenient for mosquitoes is dangerous for people," he added, noting that climate is "not the primary driving factor of malaria. Funding, drug and insecticide resistance, and health system strength still matter more."

Olugbenga continued that the elimination and prevention of malaria on the continent could become "a story of two very different regions: West and Central Africa may get a small, unplanned assist from climate, while East and Southern Africa, historically lower-burden areas, face a growing new threat that could undo hard-won gains."

Are African health systems keeping pace?

Climate change is fundamentally changing the geography of disease on the continent, Olumide Idowu, founder of the International Climate Change Development Initiative, told DW.

Malaria research in Germany targets parasite’s life cycle To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Idowu added that many African countries have developed adaptation plans but implementation has lagged behind the pace of climate change.

Although Africa is one of the lowest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions, it remains one of the most vulnerable regions to climate change — posing systemic threats to the economy, infrastructure, and even its fragile health systems.

Idowu mentioned that without a significant increase in "investment at home, reinforcement of local institutional capacity and embedding health as a core pillar of climate resilience, many African countries risk being unprepared for the changing epidemiological landscape that climate change is creating."

The regions expected to be hardest hit are also regions less accustomed to fighting malaria today, the study revealed.

"Governments, health systems and communities must adapt to this evolving threat, including getting ready now to run more aggressive anti-malaria programs in cooler areas where risk is rising," Olugbenga said.

He also urged countries in West and Central Africa to sustain malaria elimination efforts, warning that resistance to insecticides and drugs, funding gaps and weak health systems could easily negate any reduction in malaria transmission associated with rising temperatures.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Colombia amanece bajo el estado de emergencia por el terremoto que deja más de 130 muertos
World.content:
Colombia todavía cuenta sus muertos. El país amanece este martes bajo el estado de emergencia nacional, después de que un terremoto de magnitud 7,4 sacudió la víspera durante cuatro eternos minutos el oeste del país, y se sintió hasta Panamá y Ecuador. Los coletazos del temblor –el de mayor magnitud desde 1979– han dejado hasta el momento más de un centenar de muertos y más de 500 heridos, con decenas de edificios completamente colapsados. Al menos 132 personas han fallecido, de acuerdo con el más reciente balance de la Asociación Colombiana de Ciudades Capitales (Asocapitales). Las cifras todavía se consideran preliminares.

Una gran parte de las muertes se concentra en la ciudad de Pereira, en el eje cafetero. También ha quedado muy golpeada Cali, la capital del Valle del Cauca y la tercera ciudad más poblada del país, donde se declaró un toque de queda y se han militarizado varios puntos, especialmente las zonas donde aún se desarrollan acciones de rescate entre los escombros. Quibdó, la capital del Chocó, donde se ubicó el epicentro en San José del Palmar, así como Manizales y Armenia, vecinas de Pereira en la región cafetera, son otras de las urbes más afectadas, con edificios colapsados, aeropuertos cerrados y servicios intermitentes.

En Cali, que se preparaba para celebrar el popular festival de música del Pacífico Petronio Álvarez este fin de semana, los rescatistas todavía escarban entre los escombros en busca de sobrevivientes. Mientras que en la región cafetera el temblor ha revivido el trauma de otro terremoto, el que devastó Armenia en enero de 1999 y dejó a su paso casi 1.200 muertos.

Vista aérea de edificios colapsados por el temblor de este lunes, en Cali, Colombia ALEJANDRO MELÉNDEZ (EL PAÍS)

El desastre se ha desencadenado cuando el presidente, Abelardo de la Espriella, cumplía apenas tres días en el cargo, después de que se posesionó el viernes en un auditorio de Cali y pronunció su primer discurso desde una instalación militar, en el que prometió gobernar desde las regiones y para las regiones. “Le encomiendo nuestro país al señor Jesucristo”, dijo después del mediodía, cuando transmitió el primer reporte del Gobierno y declaró la emergencia nacional desde Bogotá, a donde voló por primera vez como mandatario desde la caribeña Barranquilla, la ciudad que propone convertir en capital alterna de un país con una geografía muy compleja.

En su primer lunes en el poder, cuando apenas ajusta su talante como gobernante, el presidente aseguró que “los compatriotas afectados” saldrán adelante “con la ayuda de Dios”, del Gobierno y de la cooperación internacional, e hizo un llamado a la unidad nacional: “Hoy todos los colombianos, sin distinciones ideológicas, tenemos que unirnos frente a una sola causa: las víctimas de este desastre natural”. Aseguró que asumía “directamente el liderazgo” de la atención de la emergencia. Un enorme primer desafío, en un momento prematuro para un Ejecutivo que apenas da sus primeros pasos.

En la tarde, realizó una fugaz visita al Chocó junto a parte de su gabinete, y de allí partió al Valle del Cauca. El presidente instaló un Puesto de Mando Unificado (PMU) nacional en Bogotá, y otros en Quibdó, Cali y Armenia. También decidió desplegar equipos liderados por varios de los ministros recién nombrados en algunos de los lugares más afectados.

Habitantes y autoridades buscan entre los escombros este lunes en Quibdó. Jean Arriaga (EFE)

Tanto el vicepresidente, José Manuel Restrepo, como el ministro del Interior, Rodrigo Lara, se encuentran en el eje cafetero, mientras que el de Defensa, el general retirado Jorge Eduardo Mora, y la de Salud, Ana María Vesga, están en Cali. Más allá del gabinete, y de su círculo más cercano, De la Espriella todavía no ha reemplazado las cabezas de algunas entidades clave para la atención de desastres, aunque ha anunciado que este martes designará al ingeniero geólogo David Suárez Tamayo en la cabeza de la Unidad Nacional de Gestión del Riesgo. Esa coyuntura se agravó por la ruptura del tradicional empalme con el anterior gobierno, en cabeza del izquierdista Gustavo Petro.

La solidaridad internacional se ha dejado sentir, a menos de dos meses de los terremotos de junio que devastaron a la vecina Venezuela con un saldo de más de 6.000 muertos. Estados Unidos anunció una ayuda de 15,5 millones de dólares, destinada a refugio de emergencia, alimentos, protección y evaluaciones de los daños causados por el sismo. También el Banco de Desarrollo de América Latina y el Caribe (CAF) dará una donación de 500.000 dólares a Colombia para atender la emergencia. Hace apenas unas semanas, CAF había anunciado un paquete financiero de 9.000 millones de dólares para impulsar el desarrollo del país en el periodo 2026-2030, que coincide con el cuatrienio de De la Espriella.

Otros socios cercanos ideológicamente al nuevo Gobierno colombiano expresaron su apoyo y disposición a ayudar, como el argentino Javier Milei, el chileno José Antonio Kast o el ecuatoriano Daniel Noboa. Los tres asistieron el viernes pasado a la posesión de De la Espriella en Cali. También ofrecieron ayuda desde la otra orilla ideológica mandatarios como el brasileño Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, la mexicana Claudia Sheinbaum o el español Pedro Sánchez. La Organización de Naciones Unidas (ONU), con una larga historia de presencia en el país, se manifestó preparada para ayudar en lo que haga falta.

World.title: Última hora del terremoto en Colombia, en directo | Al menos 132 muertos y 570 heridos por el terremoto de magnitud 7,4 en Colombia
World.content:
El presidente Abelardo la Espriella visita Chocó, el epicentro del sismo | Estados Unidos destina 15,5 millones de dólares para la emergencia | Avanzan las tareas de rescate en las ciudades afectadas

Al menos 132 personas han muerto en Colombia por el terremoto de magnitud 7,4 que ha sacudido el oeste del país este lunes a las 7.34 de la mañana (hora local), según el último balance entregado por la Asociación Colombiana de Ciudades Capitales a las 19.00. El presidente colombiano, Abelardo de la Espriella, ha cifrado en más de 1.500 las viviendas afectadas y ha elevado a 61 el número de edificios completamente colapsados. “Le encomiendo nuestro país al señor Jesucristo”, ha dicho el mandatario, que ha declarado la emergencia nacional y se encuentra en Bogotá. Gran parte de los fallecidos se concentra en el área metropolitana de Pereira y también se han producido graves destrozos en la ciudad de Cali, la capital del Valle del Cauca, donde el regidor, Alejandro Eder, ha comunicado que al menos una treintena de estructuras se han derrumbado “con personas atrapadas”. Los aeropuertos de Cali, Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago y Buenaventura suspenden sus operaciones tras sufrir daños por el seísmo.
