The party pledged stronger labor protections for medical workers, including the creation of a national AI-powered medical quality control system designed to reduce bureaucracy and improve healthcare oversight. It also proposed higher salaries, particularly for rural doctors.

Other initiatives include targeted training programs based on regional workforce needs and expanded support for medical graduates through relocation grants, employer-provided housing and preferential mortgage programs.

For patients, the party proposed creating a unified digital health portal that would provide secure access to medical records, test results, prescriptions and treatment history. According to the party, the system would protect personal data, improve transparency and prevent unauthorized changes to medical records. It also called for greater transparency in the Social Health Insurance Fund and the expansion of palliative care services, particularly for children with severe illnesses.

Respublica Party

The Respublica held two major public forums in Shymkent on Aug. 7 and Almaty on Aug. 8, where party leaders reviewed the results of the party’s three and a half years of activity.

The party also focused its campaign on visits to manufacturing enterprises, arguing that industrial development is essential for creating jobs, increasing household incomes and strengthening the national economy.

According to the party, meetings at production facilities provide direct insight into workers’ concerns and help translate practical challenges into policy solutions.

Voting to the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral parliament, is due on Aug. 23.

World.title: Kazakhstan Household Deposits Near $54 Billion as Savings Rise 20.9%
World.content:
ALMATY – Household deposits in Kazakhstan’s banks approached nearly 25 trillion tenge (US$53.5 billion) by the end of June 2026, increasing by 20.9% over the year, reported the Finprom financial and analytical agency. While the overall volume of savings continues to grow, deposits remain concentrated in several major cities and regions, revealing significant differences in household savings across the country.

Of the total, 84% or 21 trillion tenge (US$44.9 billion) was held in deposits denominated in the national currency, while foreign-currency deposits accounted for 16%. The predominance of tenge deposits is partly linked to the difference in returns. Interest rates on foreign-currency deposits cannot exceed 1%, while tenge deposits have offered comparatively high returns amid the elevated base rate.

Term deposits dominate

Term deposits accounted for 90% of all household deposits, making them by far the most common form of savings. Savings deposits represented 9.7%, while demand deposits accounted for only 0.05%. The concentration of deposits is particularly pronounced geographically.

The city of Almaty remained the country’s largest center for household savings, with 9.6 trillion tenge (US$20.5 billion) deposited in banks as of the end of June. This represented almost 40% of all household deposits in Kazakhstan. Astana followed with 3.2 trillion tenge (US$6.8 billion), while the Karagandy Region held 1.4 trillion tenge (US$3 billion). West Kazakhstan and Shymkent ranked fourth and fifth, with 1.2 trillion (US$2.6 billion) and 1.1 trillion tenge (US$2.4 billion) respectively.

The smallest overall volumes of household deposits were recorded in the Ulytau, Almaty and Zhetisu Regions.

Savings gap exceeds 25 times

The regional differences become even more pronounced when deposits are calculated per resident. As of July 1, Kazakhstan had an average of 1.2 million tenge (US$2,570) in household deposits per person. However, only five regions exceeded the national average.

Almaty ranked first, with more than 4 million tenge (US$8,570) per resident, followed by Astana at 1.9 million tenge (US$4,070). West Kazakhstan recorded 1.7 million tenge (US$3,640) per resident, while the Karagandy and Kostanai Regions each recorded nearly 1.3 million tenge (US$2,780).

In contrast, average deposits per resident amounted to just 144,000 tenge (US$310) in the Almaty Region and 161,000 tenge (US$345) in the Turkistan Region.

Overall, 12 of Kazakhstan’s 20 regions had less than 1 million tenge (US$2,139) in deposits per resident. The difference between the highest and lowest regional figures therefore exceeded 25 times.

The figures point to a banking sector in which household savings are expanding, but where the ability to accumulate financial assets remains closely linked to regional economic conditions. The concentration of almost two-fifths of all household deposits in Almaty, alongside substantially lower savings in several regions, underscores the continuing gap between Kazakhstan’s major economic centers and less affluent areas.

World.title: Comic Con Astana 2026: How Kazakhstan Turns Pop Culture into Creative Industries
World.content:
ASTANA — Comic Con Astana 2026 drew more than 76,000 visitors from 40 countries over four days, underscoring the growing popularity of pop culture in Kazakhstan and the festival’s expanding international profile.

Held from Aug. 6 to 9, the festival brought together fans of films, TV series, comics, gaming and cosplay across two venues: Barys Arena and Alau Ice Palace. The program included meetings with international stars, Q&A sessions, an international cosplay competition with a 20 million tenge ($42,930) prize pool, gaming tournaments, workshops and other activities.

This year’s international headliners included “Game of Thrones” star Nikolaj Coster-Waldau, “Peaky Blinders” actor Paul Anderson, and “One Piece” stars Iñaki Godoy and Taz Skylar.

International stars discover Kazakhstan

For several international guests, Comic Con Astana marked their first visit to Kazakhstan.

Mexican actor Iñaki Godoy, known for playing Monkey D. Luffy in Netflix’s “One Piece” adaptation, shared his first impressions of Astana.

Godoy said he was particularly impressed by Astana’s distinctive architecture, mentioning the Nur Alem pavilion at EXPO and Khan Shatyr.

“I haven’t seen much of Astana yet. But when I went into one of the shopping malls, I saw this huge sphere right next to it. I also got to see the giant tent. It’s really impressive. I’d love to see even more interesting places,” the actor said.

During his Q&A session, Godoy also spoke about working on One Piece and said he would like to see Kazakhstan become one of the filming locations for the series. He noted that some storylines in One Piece feature nomadic themes, which could make Kazakhstan an interesting location for future productions.

“I would really love to come back here, and I would really love to film here,” Godoy said.

British actor Paul Anderson, known for his role as Arthur Shelby in “Peaky Blinders”, also visited Kazakhstan for the first time.

“I was really impressed when we drove in from the airport to the hotel. What I saw outside the window… I honestly thought I’d landed in Los Angeles,” Anderson said.

One of the festival’s main headliners was Danish actor Nikolaj Coster-Waldau, internationally known for playing Jaime Lannister in “Game of Thrones”.

His visit to Kazakhstan was also his first.

“This is my first visit to Kazakhstan, to Astana. I have to say, it’s a very big country. Wonderful food, especially the meat. Today I ate more of it than I have in the last three years,” Coster-Waldau said.

When asked where Kazakhstan might fit into the world of “Game of Thrones”, Coster-Waldau drew a parallel with the two powerful sides of the fictional universe.

“If we’re thinking in “Game of Thrones” categories, Kazakhstan would probably be kind of in the middle between two very powerful neighbours. So it would kinda be somewhere between the Lannisters and the Dothraki lands, like very diplomatic. And making each side believe that they are their best friends,” he said.

Coster-Waldau also expressed interest in discovering Kazakh cinema and praised the landscapes of the Mangystau region. His conversation with fans also touched on artificial intelligence, a technology that is increasingly becoming part of Kazakhstan’s creative landscape.

When asked about the use of AI in filmmaking, Coster-Waldau said he sees it primarily as a tool rather than a replacement for human creativity.

“I think AI can be used as a tool, and it should be used as a tool,” the actor said.

At the same time, he stressed that key creative decisions should remain in the hands of artists.

“When we talk about filmmaking, the entire creative process should remain in the hands of the creators, in the hands of artists,” Coster-Waldau said.

That discussion found a practical continuation at Comic Con Astana 2026 with the presentation of “Tengrida: Cyber Steppe”, a Kazakh art film created with AI as one of its production tools.

Tengrida: from a cosplay character to a new universe

The festival hosted the first public screening of a three-minute AI-animated episode titled “Arena,” which introduces a new original fictional universe.

The story follows Tengrida, a young woman who enters a techno-clan arena to fight for justice. In a future where technology has replaced much of human memory and brutal fights have become mass entertainment, she faces a warrior named Kanjar while trying to help people see the truth again.

The character was created by Almaty-based cosplayer Aruzhan Zhunusova, known as Aruvibez. Tengrida’s story began in 2025, when Zhunusova presented the original cosplay character at Comic Con Astana, combining elements of Kazakh national style with a futuristic aesthetic.

According to Zhunusova, the audience’s reaction was the moment she realized the cosplay character could become something much bigger.

“So many people came up to me, took photos and wrote to me. And I realised that I had found some kind of response in people’s hearts. I didn’t want to limit it to just one festival. I wanted to create something much bigger, ” Zhunusova told The Astana Times.

This led to the idea of developing an entire universe around the character.

“In the end, we decided to start with an animated video using AI, as we want to take part in the AI film festival, and then gradually reveal the character and her universe. It could be comics, games, feature films. So I think this is only the beginning,” she said.

Zhunusova describes Tengrida as a “Kazakh warrior from the future” who fights for justice and truth.

The production of “Tengrida: Cyber Steppe” took around four to five months. For the directors, the project was also their first major experience working with AI animation and a fantasy aesthetic. According to Zhunusova, the first two months were spent developing the project’s visual language and experimenting with the technology.

Despite the use of AI, the film was not created with a single automated process. Individual scenes were generated in short fragments, after which the team manually reviewed and approved the material.

“We didn’t generate it all at once. We worked in five-second fragments. Then we approved everything, put it together, edited it and worked on the sound design,” Zhunusova explained.

Zhunusova believes AI does not replace the creative team in the project, but expands its possibilities.

“I believe that if AI is in the hands of a professional, it can be used as a great tool,” she said.

From fan festival to creative industry platform

The festival has steadily expanded its international profile, welcoming stars such as Mads Mikkelsen, Andy Serkis, Pilou Asbæk, Scott Adkins, Esai Morales, Michael Rooker, Sean Gunn, Percy Hynes White and Alexander Kuznetsov over the years.

Its international cosplay competition has also become a major part of the program, attracting participants from more than 20 countries. This year, 64 finalists competed across 20 categories for a total prize pool of 20 million tenge ($42,930).

According to the festival’s General Producer Natalia Abrashkina, Comic Con Astana is increasingly becoming a platform for the development of the creative industries.

“Comic Con Astana is much more than a festival. It is an international platform that brings the industry together, creates new opportunities for talented people and contributes to the development of Kazakhstan’s creative economy,” Abrashkina said.

She stressed that the festival aims not only to attract international stars, but also to promote Kazakh authors, artists, cosplayers and content creators internationally.

The story of Tengrida offers one example of this shift. A character created for a cosplay competition has, within a year, evolved into a screen project using AI and the foundation for a potential universe that could eventually extend beyond animation into comics, games and film.

For Comic Con Astana, that trajectory points to a broader evolution: from bringing global pop culture to Kazakhstan to giving local creators a platform to build stories and intellectual properties of their own.

World.title: Abai’s Legacy Endures as Nearly 19,000 Kazakh Citizens Carry His Name
World.content:
ALMATY – Nearly 19,000 people in Kazakhstan bear the name Abai, according to the Bureau of National Statistics, as the country marks Abai Day on Aug. 10, commemorating the 181st anniversary of the birth of Abai Kunanbayev, who was born in 1845. The figures highlight how the name of the country’s renowned poet, philosopher and thinker continues to resonate across generations.

A total of 18,961 people in Kazakhstan are named Abai. The largest number live in Astana, with 2,186 people, followed by the Turkistan Region with 2,008 and Almaty with 1,740.

The name remains in use among younger generations. During the first half of 2026 alone, 91 newborns were given the name Abai. Although traditionally regarded as a male name, national statistics also record nine women named Abai.

The oldest Kazakhstan resident with the name was born in 1932, while the largest age group is people aged 30–34, numbering 3,267. The name is also reflected in Kazakhstan’s geography. One region, one city, three districts and 26 villages are named after Abai.

Abai’s legacy in national identity

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, in his message marking Abai Day, described the poet’s intellectual and creative heritage as an important part of Kazakhstan’s cultural legacy. He also linked Abai’s ideas about knowledge, diligence, responsibility and unity to contemporary efforts to strengthen social values and national identity.

Abai’s influence has also extended beyond the country’s borders. Monuments dedicated to the poet have been erected in more than 20 cities, including Beijing, Budapest, Istanbul, Moscow, Tashkent, Baku, Tehran and Vitebsk.

In 2016, monuments were unveiled in Cairo and Rennes, France, further expanding the international presence of the Kazakh thinker. In 2021, President Tokayev took part in the opening of a 2.2-metre monument to Abai in Seoul during his official visit to South Korea.

Abai’s international recognition also has a longer history. UNESCO declared 1995 the Year of Abai to mark the 150th anniversary of his birth, placing his literary and philosophical legacy within a broader international cultural context.

For Kazakhstan, the continued spread of the name Abai, from newborn children to towns and cities and monuments abroad, reflects how a historical figure has become part of both the country’s cultural memory and its contemporary identity.

World.title: Kazakhstan Emerges as Firebird AI Market With Data Center Valley Project in Ekibastuz
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has emerged as the second market for US-based AI infrastructure company Firebird, which is developing a 125-megawatt computing facility in Ekibastuz as part of the country’s broader effort to build domestic artificial intelligence infrastructure and attract a larger share of the global AI economy.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev announced the development during the official opening of the first phase of Firebird’s AI campus in Hrazdan, Armenia, on Aug. 8. The event brought together Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang, NVIDIA Vice President Rev Lebaredian, US government representatives, technology companies, investors and industry experts.

Firebird’s Armenian facility is described as the region’s largest operational AI factory based on NVIDIA’s DSX architecture. The company plans to expand its Armenian infrastructure to more than 70,000 NVIDIA Rubin and Blackwell GPUs and 300 MW of computing capacity by the end of 2027.

Kazakhstan is becoming the company’s second major market. In Ekibastuz, Firebird, together with Kazakhtelecom as project operator, is developing the Data Center Valley, with an initial capacity of 125 MW.

The project has received the necessary approvals from the Kazakh government as well as an export authorization from the US Bureau of Industry and Security for the supply of relevant technologies.

Kazakhstan targets global AI infrastructure market

Huang highlighted Kazakhstan alongside Armenia as part of Firebird’s expanding infrastructure network.

“Together with Firebird, we are building AI infrastructure in Armenia and Kazakhstan that will provide researchers, startups and industry with the computing foundation to develop artificial intelligence within their countries, attract international innovators and participate in the global AI economy,” Huang said.

According to Madiyev, the project forms part of Kazakhstan’s efforts to develop domestic computing capacity rather than rely exclusively on external infrastructure.

“Kazakhstan has the necessary energy base, territory and developed digital ecosystem to host large computing capacities. Our task is not only to attract global technology partners, but also to create a complete environment within the country for the development of artificial intelligence, research, startups and new digital services,” he said.

The Data Center Valley builds on plans announced earlier this year to develop a large-scale computing hub in Ekibastuz. Kazakhstan has been discussing the project with major international technology and investment companies, including Microsoft, OpenAI, G42 and Mubadala. The project has been envisioned as capable of eventually scaling to up to one gigawatt of computing capacity and attracting around $30 billion in investment.

Why Ekibastuz matters

Kazakhstan’s energy resources therefore provide one of the main potential advantages for developing large computing facilities. At the same time, the government is seeking to upgrade the digital infrastructure needed to connect these facilities to international markets.

One such project is the Trans-Caspian Fiber Optic Cable, which is being built between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan. The new submarine connection is expected to establish an additional high-speed data route toward Europe, strengthening the infrastructure supporting international cloud and AI services.

Together, the projects point to a broader approach in which Kazakhstan is attempting to develop several layers of an AI ecosystem simultaneously: electricity and data centers on one side, international connectivity and computing capacity on the other, and regulation, talent and startups to build applications on top of that infrastructure.

Firebird plans to continue expanding internationally and aims to bring its total global AI infrastructure capacity to 2 gigawatts across Armenia, Kazakhstan and other markets by the end of 2028.

The company has also announced plans for NVIDIA to invest in Firebird, while CoreWeave has previously invested in the company. The new funding is expected to support the accelerated development of Firebird’s global AI infrastructure.

World.title: AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov on How AIFC is Preparing for Next Era of Finance
World.content:
ASTANA — When Renat Bekturov first joined what would become the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), the institution existed only as an idea. There were no success stories to point to and no guarantee that an international financial center could take root in the heart of Eurasia. Nearly a decade later, the conversation has shifted. The AIFC has grown into an ecosystem with its own exchange, court, arbitration centre, business-friendly regulatory framework and growing international reputation.

“It was just an idea. Now this is a real jurisdiction with real working institutions,” he recalled.

That philosophy of institution building runs through nearly every initiative the AIFC pursues. Whether discussing Islamic finance, critical minerals, creative industries or digital assets, Bekturov repeatedly returns to one belief: institutions matter because they outlive the people who create them.

“I believe people create institutions, institutions create policy or culture, and culture affects people again. We’re trying to create an institution that will live beyond us and serve the economy and investors for many years ahead,” he said.

The vision has since translated into tangible results. Nearly a decade after its launch, the AIFC hosts more than 6,000 companies from over 90 countries, including companies from the United States, the United Kingdom, China, Türkiye, Singapore, and the UAE, has attracted more than $25 billion in investment, and has ranked as the leading financial center in Eastern Europe and Central Asia for three consecutive years in the Global Financial Centres Index. Those milestones reflect not only the center’s growth but also the institution-building philosophy Bekturov believes is essential for long-term success.

That long-term perspective also shapes how the AIFC identifies new areas for growth. Rather than focusing exclusively on traditional banking or capital markets, the center is building financial infrastructure around sectors where Kazakhstan has long-term competitive advantages.

Islamic finance is one example. While still developing in Kazakhstan, Bekturov believes it represents a significant opportunity for both the country and the wider Central Asian region, where many practicing Muslims remain underserved by conventional financial products.

“They have fewer opportunities than people who are not practicing Muslims. They can use current accounts and bank cards, but they cannot use deposits, which means they cannot earn returns on their money. And they cannot leverage financing to buy assets or make investments in the same way that others can,” he said.

Critical minerals are another strategic priority. As global demand rises for rare earth elements used in renewable energy, electric vehicles and advanced technologies, Kazakhstan’s vast mineral wealth is attracting growing international interest. But natural resources alone are not enough.

“The opportunities and ideas are nothing if they don’t have capital,” Bekturov said.

To connect promising exploration projects with investors, the AIFC will launch a dedicated Junior Mining Pitch Day during this year’s Astana Finance Days, taking place inSeptember and borrowing a format familiar from the venture capital world.

“We’ve learned it from the venture capital industry. The founders present their projects to investors. We want to organize the same kind of pitch day for junior miners,” Bekturov explained.

The same approach is now extending to Kazakhstan’s creative economy. Rather than financing films or music directly, the AIFC is building the legal and investment framework that allows private capital to support creative businesses.

“One of the biggest assets Kazakhstan has is its people — the talent and creativity of its people,” Bekturov said.

This year’s Astana Finance Days will also feature a Creative Pitch Day, bringing together filmmakers, producers and investors as part of the AIFC’s broader effort to open new sources of financing for the country’s creative industries.

Looking ahead, Bekturov believes the next transformation of finance will be driven by technology, particularly digital assets. While cryptocurrencies often dominate public discussion, he argues that the real breakthrough lies in tokenization: turning physical assets into digital ones that can be traded more efficiently. He illustrates the idea with a simple example. Gold is a physical asset that requires storage and security, but its ownership can be represented digitally through tokens, making transactions faster and easier.

“I really believe that digital assets will be transformative for the financial industry,” he said.

The technology, however, is only part of the equation. According to Bekturov, the problem is not technology but its adoption. Financial institutions and regulators, he said, will ultimately determine how quickly these innovations become part of the global financial system.

Artificial intelligence presents another challenge. Rather than focusing on whether AI will replace people, Bekturov is more interested in where responsibility should remain.

“We’re already discussing at what time we will give AI the role of a decision-maker and should we ever give that role?” he said.

For him, technology should strengthen financial markets rather than replace human judgment. That balance between innovation and institution building reflects the broader vision behind the AIFC. While the center continues expanding into new areas, from Islamic finance and critical minerals to creative industries and digital assets, its long-term objective remains unchanged: creating a trusted platform that connects global investors with Kazakhstan and Central Asia.

Bekturov often describes the AIFC as a bridge rather than a destination in itself.

“We’re basically a bridge that connects the world with the island of Kazakhstan, or Central Asia wider. People don’t use the bridge because it’s there. They use it because they want to get to a particular location,” he said.

For now, that bridge serves investors seeking opportunities in Kazakhstan and the wider region. Over time, Bekturov hopes it will evolve into a financial hub where international transactions are structured regardless of geography. Ultimately, however, his definition of success extends beyond financial indicators.

“For me, if in 10 years the AIFC is recognized among the world’s top 30 international financial centers, that would definitely be a success. Equally important is seeing a new generation of leaders moving the center forward, ensuring that the institution lives beyond its founders and the people who started it,” he concluded.

World.title: How PSG Academy’s Arrival Reflects Kazakhstan’s Rise as Football Talent Hub
World.content:
ALMATY – Paris Saint-Germain’s decision to open its first football academy in Kazakhstan this September is more than another international expansion for the French club. It reflects Kazakhstan’s growing attractiveness as a destination for elite youth football development, following a series of milestones that have elevated the country’s profile.

Located in Astana, the new PSG Academy Kazakhstan will welcome up to 300 boys and girls aged six to 14 during its inaugural season. Training will follow the official Paris Saint-Germain methodology, modeled on the club’s renowned youth academy in France and emphasizing technical excellence, game intelligence, discipline and teamwork.

While the academy’s opening marks Kazakhstan as the 24th country in PSG’s global network, it also fits into a broader pattern that has accelerated over the past two years: the country is increasingly positioning itself not only as a participant in international football, but as a place where future talent can be developed.

A broader football ecosystem is taking shape

The arrival of PSG follows several developments that together suggest Kazakhstan’s football strategy is evolving beyond isolated infrastructure projects or individual success stories.

Earlier, Atlético Madrid announced the creation of its football academy at the Akbulak Olympic Center in the Almaty Region. The project aims to introduce the Spanish club’s training methodology while improving the qualifications of Kazakh coaches and developing young players capable of competing at the highest international level.

Institutionally, Kazakhstan also reached an important milestone when the Kazakhstan Football Federation’s national academy became only the ninth association in the world and the second UEFA member to receive official FIFA Talent Academy recognition. The designation confirms that the country’s youth development system meets international standards and places Kazakhstan among a small group of national federations participating in FIFA’s global talent development initiative.

From exporting talent to building pathways

The growing interest from international clubs coincides with increased visibility of Kazakh football talent abroad. Earlier this year, teenage player Dastan Satpayev completed a record transfer to Chelsea, becoming one of the country’s most promising young exports.

Kazakhstan’s domestic football also enjoyed a breakthrough season. FC Kairat became the first Kazakh club to qualify for the UEFA Champions League group stage after eliminating Scotland’s Celtic FC in a dramatic penalty shootout in Almaty.

The club was later ranked among the world’s top 500 football clubs by the International Federation of Football History and Statistics (IFFHS), becoming the only Kazakh representative on the list.

Another milestone came when goalkeeper Anarbekov became the first Kazakh footballer to be named UEFA Champions League Player of the Match following his performance against Olympiacos. UEFA awarded him a 9.2 rating, while two of his saves were selected among the competition’s best moments of the round.

Taken individually, these achievements represent important milestones. Together, they suggest Kazakhstan’s football system is becoming increasingly visible within international scouting and development networks.

Why Kazakhstan?

For PSG, Kazakhstan offers more than a new commercial market. Football participation has grown steadily in recent years, accompanied by increasing investment in sports infrastructure and youth development. The Astana academy will initially operate from Air Arena, a modern indoor complex with a FIFA-standard pitch that allows year-round training despite Kazakhstan’s climate.

PSG also announced plans to expand beyond Astana, signaling that the project is intended as a long-term investment rather than a standalone academy.

“We are proud to bring the PSG Academy to Kazakhstan and provide young players with access to the Club’s world-class training methodology and football philosophy, “ said Almaz Alsenov, founder of PSG Academy Kazakhstan.

“Through this partnership, we aim to contribute to the long-term development of youth football in Kazakhstan by creating an environment where children can grow both as athletes and as individuals,” he added.

PSG officials similarly described Kazakhstan as part of the club’s strategy to broaden access to its football methodology worldwide while strengthening its international academy network.

Beyond international recognition

The arrival of another European football giant does not, by itself, transform Kazakhstan into a football powerhouse. Elite player development depends on far more than academy brands. Coaching quality, domestic competition, scouting systems and clear pathways from youth football to professional clubs remain equally important.

Yet the sequence of recent developments, from FIFA recognition and international partnerships to the emergence of players attracting attention from Europe’s top clubs, suggests Kazakhstan is gradually building many of those foundations.

If these initiatives continue to reinforce one another, the opening of PSG Academy Kazakhstan may come to represent more than the expansion of one of Europe’s biggest clubs. It could mark another step in Kazakhstan’s evolution from a country that occasionally produces exceptional footballers into one that is increasingly recognized as part of football’s global talent development ecosystem.

World.title: ‘Regional stability is main achievement’: assessing Washington peace summit one year on
World.content:
Washington peace summit: one year on

“The peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan is visible and tangible to everyone,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said in a statement marking the events of 8 August.

A year ago, on this day, Washington hosted a historic peace summit, with US President Donald Trump acting as mediator. Yerevan and Baku initialled a peace agreement, signed a declaration on the TRIPP project – a transit route through Armenia connecting Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan (the “Trump Route”) – and signed a number of bilateral documents with the United States.

Pashinyan said the peace agreement “awaits signing and ratification”. He added that practical work on TRIPP would begin in the near future and become a “major regional and international event”.

The prime minister congratulated the people of Armenia and Azerbaijan on the landmark date of 8 August.

“Finally, we have a day that brings peace rather than stirs up our emotions,” he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also issued a statement, highlighting the “courage and foresight” shown by both countries over the past year.

“We look forward to further progress towards lasting and durable peace in the South Caucasus,” the secretary of state said.

Pashinyan held phone calls with Donald Trump and Ilham Aliyev.

Armenian analysts said the main outcome of the Washington summit was the establishment of stability in the region.

They noted positive developments despite what they described as Baku’s “aggressive agenda”, including its calls for Azerbaijanis to return to what it calls “Western Azerbaijan”. The term refers to almost the entire sovereign territory of Armenia.

Pashinyan on unresolved issues and how to make “peace irreversible”

In his address to the nation, Pashinyan once again said that peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan had been established.

“But this, of course, does not mean that we have already reached the end of the road in implementing the peace agenda,” he added.

According to the prime minister, the following issues remain unresolved:

signing and ratifying the peace agreement,

delimiting the Armenian-Azerbaijani border,

“the continued detention of our compatriots in Azerbaijan” [referring to 19 Armenian prisoners held in Baku].

He also said that 8 August 2025 had marked a turning point, dividing Armenia’s history into the periods “before and after this date”. Pashinyan described the period before 8 August as a dead end, while the period since then has offered “limitless opportunities”.

Pashinyan said the main political and social-psychological result of the Washington summit was that “the wheel of our history has once again fallen into our hands”.

He identified the implementation of the “Trump Route” project as another major outcome:

“It will not only end Armenia’s blockade in the very near future and become the backbone of Armenia’s and the region’s economy, but will also help Armenia and Azerbaijan start seeing each other not as an obstacle, but as a route and as a neighbour.”

The transit route was named the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” after the mediator, as the Armenian and Azerbaijani authorities had been unable to reach an agreement on the issue for several years.

Pashinyan also outlined steps that Armenia and Azerbaijan should take to make the peace between them irreversible:

“We need to put an end to discussions about the ‘right of Armenians to return to Nagorno-Karabakh’ and the ‘return of Armenian refugees from Azerbaijan’. Azerbaijan, for its part, needs to end discussions about ‘Western Azerbaijan’ and the ‘right of Western Azerbaijanis to return’. This is an issue that both Armenia and Azerbaijan must resolve in the name of our generations’ right to live together in peace.”

“We hope to see further progress”, Rubio says

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stressed that over the past 12 months, the United States had continued to work with Armenia and Azerbaijan. He highlighted the importance of the TRIPP project. According to Rubio, the transit route is gradually becoming a reality:

“Engineering work on the railway has already begun in Armenia, while construction of the highway and railway linking Azerbaijan with Armenia is nearly complete.”

He stressed that TRIPP is not simply an infrastructure project but also an important link in the Trans-Caspian trade route. It could drive new trade opportunities for the United States and other countries.

“It is a factor that opens up new trade opportunities for the United States and other countries. It is also an example of how economic cooperation can strengthen peace after long-standing disputes have been resolved,” Rubio said.

He added that peace had created an opportunity to deepen relations between the United States, Armenia and Azerbaijan. This, he said, would contribute to the economic prosperity of all three countries.

Thanks to Trump

In a phone call with US President Donald Trump, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan thanked him for organising the peace summit and for signing the peace declaration adopted by the Armenian and Azerbaijani leaders as a testament to the agreement. He also stressed “the significant role of Trump’s personal efforts” in establishing peace.

“The two leaders welcomed the fact that the Washington Peace Summit had led to real peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan, which people in both countries can see and feel. […] Prime Minister Pashinyan and President Trump reaffirmed their determination to begin work on the construction of TRIPP in the near future. They also discussed other issues on the bilateral Armenian-US and international agendas,” the Armenian prime minister’s office said.

Talks with Aliyev

According to the prime minister’s office, Pashinyan and Aliyev discussed progress in normalising relations over the past year. They also focused on the development of trade and economic ties between the two countries.

“In this context, the sides highlighted Azerbaijan’s exports of petroleum products to Armenia, as well as the transit of goods through Azerbaijan to Armenia and from Armenia to other destinations. They also exchanged views on the implementation of the TRIPP project in line with the agreements reached in Washington. They stressed the importance of continuing efforts to advance the peace process and ensure long-term peace, stability, connectivity and economic cooperation in the region.”

Comment

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan says:

“The main result of the Washington summit is that it brought a period of relative stability to the region. For a year now, we have not had to discuss possible escalations or security risks coming from Azerbaijan.

The second positive factor is that the atmosphere has changed to some extent and shifted towards cooperation. “As for Azerbaijan, it continues to promote certain aggressive strategies, such as its ‘Western Azerbaijan’ narrative. But it is also taking steps aimed at establishing peace. Opening its territory for transit is one example, along with other similar measures.

Naturally, it is better for Azerbaijan to open its territory, establish contacts and start trade than for the region to face the risk of escalation.

But, as we have repeatedly pointed out, we will only be able to assess the final results of this process not when the TRIPP project becomes operational, but after we see what else follows TRIPP. Our assessment in the coming years will depend on these developments.

If TRIPP is implemented, and Armenia also gains access to Iran and Russia through Azerbaijani territory, and if the Armenian-Turkish border opens, then we will certainly be able to consider the process a success. If none of this happens, or only some of it is achieved, the assessment could be different.

But once again, the stability that came to the region as a result of the Washington summit is extremely important for Armenia. From 2020 to 2025, security threats dominated our lives. Progress on security, without a doubt, also gives us an opportunity to focus on other issues.”

Washington peace summit: one year on

World.title: Eight Turkish parliamentary parties call for ending Abkhazia’s isolation
World.content:
Eight parliamentary parties in Turkey have called for an end to Abkhazia‘s isolation. The initiative primarily calls for Turkey to recognise the Abkhaz passport as a valid document for crossing the Turkish border, as well as for direct sea and air links between Turkey and Abkhazia to open.

Representatives of opposition factions announced the initiative at a joint press conference in the Turkish parliament. The initiative forms part of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” public campaign, which the local diaspora launched in early July 2026. The diaspora organised the campaign.

“Just imagine: hundreds of thousands of people of Abkhaz origin and their relatives live in Turkey, yet the Abkhaz passport is not valid here. Abkhaz people cannot travel to Turkey to attend the funerals of their relatives, while young people cannot enrol in universities.

These are the realities of international relations. Sometimes states are prepared to turn a blind eye to tragedies and anti-democratic practices that affect their own citizens’ relatives.

We are saying openly: Abkhaz passports must be recognised as valid documents at our border crossings. This disgrace must come to an end,” said Tuncer Bakırhan, an MP from the Democratic Party.

The eight parliamentary parties calling for an end to Abkhazia’s isolation represent a broad range of political forces, from the far right to the far left. What unites them is that they are all in opposition. The largest of them is the Yeni Parti (“New Party”), which has 91 MPs in the current parliament. Together, the eight parties hold 166 of the 600 seats in parliament.

The support from the opposition parties was not welcomed by the leadership of the Federation of Abkhaz Cultural Centres in the Republic of Turkey. More precisely, the Federation’s leadership appears to have objected not to the MPs themselves, but to the organisers of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” campaign.

The Federation does not dispute the campaign’s demands: recognition of Abkhaz passports and the opening of transport links between Abkhazia and Turkey. Its objections concern the “right to represent” and the “right to initiate” such efforts.

In Abkhazia, the Federation’s reaction was met with strong criticism from both politicians and civil society representatives.

“If any Abkhaz person in Turkey or elsewhere makes progress on our common cause, we should all support them and, if possible, join them, rather than argue over who is authorised to do what.

If our representatives in Turkey focus solely on preserving the language and culture, they should not interfere with those working to advance the political cause. If they consider such advocacy part of their remit, they should join them. That is how it looks from Abkhazia,” said Duat Khutaba, head of the Abkhaz parliament’s Committee on Legislation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation

World.title: “Free the regime’s prisoners” – March in Tbilisi | Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
What’s happening at Tbilisi rallies

On August 8, Tbilisi saw its 34th Saturday pro-European march. Its main demand was the release of dozens of protesters who have been detained during marches and rallies.

According to Transparency International Georgia, 90 political prisoners are currently held in Georgian prisons.

Many marchers also carried signs reading, “We will never accept Russian occupation.”

August 8 marks another anniversary of the Georgian-Russian war over South Ossetia, which began on August 8, 2008.

In 2008, Russia recognized South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent states. The UN and the overwhelming majority of countries consider the two regions part of Georgia, under Russian occupation.

It was the 619th consecutive day of protests in Georgia, with the main demand being for the country to return to the path of European integration. The march ended with a rally outside the government building.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners, new parliamentary elections – as they do not recognize the results of the 2024 vote – and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

News in Georgia

World.title: Is Wildberries moving to Kazakhstan?
World.content:
Wildberries is building warehouses in Kazakhstan

Based on reporting by Novaya Gazeta Europe

Wildberries is building warehouses in Astana and Almaty with a combined area of more than 260,000 square meters, Kazakhstan’s Minister of Trade and Integration, Arman Shakkaliyev, said.

Details.According to the minister, Wildberries is building a warehouse of more than 100,000 square meters near Almaty. Another facility, covering 160,000 square meters, is under construction in Astana. Both are scheduled to begin operations in the first quarter of 2027.

The company also already leases about 46,000 square meters of warehouse space in Kazakhstan.

Shakkaliyev said the ministry had received no formal request from Wildberries regarding the opening of new warehouses in Kazakhstan. He added that companies can negotiate directly with warehouse owners without government involvement.

Confirmation from Russia’s foreign ministry. Moscow and Astana began working to integrate their online marketplaces before Ukrainian attacks on Wildberries warehouses, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said.

According to Galuzin, hundreds of thousands of Kazakh suppliers are already registered on Ozon and Wildberries.

Galuzin did not provide details of the deals, instead suggesting that questions about the companies’ specific plans be directed to their representatives.

Context. On July 29, Kommersant reported that Wildberries was looking for warehouse space in Kazakhstan following drone attacks on logistics centers in Russia. According to the newspaper’s sources, the company was prepared to take virtually all available warehouse space in Kazakhstan, where supply is generally limited. The move would allow the online retailer to shield part of its logistics capacity from drone strikes.

According to Kommersant, Wildberries is also continuing to search for new warehouse space in Russia. But owners of vacant facilities are currently reluctant to sign new leases with the company because of the risk of drone attacks.

World.title: Relatives of missing Russian soldiers demand that the state search for them. In response, they are accused of working for Ukrainian intelligence
World.content:
Missing Russian soldiers

The Russian state sends soldiers to fight in its war against Ukraine, but once they go missing, it effectively disclaims responsibility for their fate. Families spend months trying to determine whether their loved ones have been killed, taken prisoner or are being treated in hospitals, only to encounter a closed and dysfunctional system for tracing the missing.

When relatives band together and demand answers, the authorities respond not with assistance but with pressure and accusations that they are cooperating with Ukrainian intelligence services.

Based on reporting by Novaya Gazeta Europe

A grassroots initiative called The Missing Regiment is gaining traction on Russian social media. Launched in the Yaroslavl region in the spring of 2026, it brings together relatives of Russian servicemen who have gone missing in the war against Ukraine. They are demanding that the state make a genuine effort to find the soldiers it sent to the front and tell their families what happened to them.

Although Russian law provides a mechanism for tracing missing servicemen, in practice it barely functions. Relatives say the agency responsible has no website, telephone number or publicly accessible address where families can submit inquiries. They believe it exists largely on paper.

A reporter for Veter spoke with activists from The Missing Regiment. Their stories illustrate how the Russian state leaves the families of missing soldiers without information — and what happens to those who publicly speak out about the system’s failure to act.

Missing in action

Groups dedicated to finding missing soldiers have existed on social media since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The information is typically posted by soldiers’ mothers, wives and sisters, who hope their messages will reach someone who knows what happened to their missing relatives.

Thousands of names and photographs have been posted in groups on VKontakte and Telegram. The images show former factory workers, security guards, prisoners, older men and men barely out of their teens.

Roman Artamonov, a 19-year-old from Saratov, began his compulsory military service on June 23, 2025. His unit was stationed in Borzya, a town near Russia’s borders with China and Mongolia. Two months later, he signed a military contract. After four months of training in Rostov, Roman was sent on a combat mission in the Donetsk region. Two days later, his family lost contact with him.

“Three months later, my son’s military unit declared him dead, citing Certificate No. 1421,” his mother, Elena Pisakina, said. “The document states that neither his body nor my son himself has been found. Searches among prisoners of war and in hospitals have yielded no results.”

Under Russian law, military commanders are required to declare a serviceman who has disappeared missing in action. The search must continue for six months. Only after that period can a court formally declare the person missing.

A serviceman can be declared dead immediately only if there is compelling evidence that the circumstances of his disappearance were life-threatening. The distinction also has financial consequences: during the six-month search period, the serviceman’s family continues to receive his military pay.

In practice, commanders therefore often seek to have missing soldiers declared dead as quickly as possible. Families do not always object. Once a serviceman is officially declared dead, relatives may be eligible for payments of about 10 million to 15 million rubles, depending on the region.

According to Mediazona, Russian courts received 90,000 such claims between 2023 and 2025, seeking to have servicemen legally declared missing or dead. Military unit commanders filed 26,000 of the claims, while agencies under the Defense Ministry filed another 20,000. In nearly 40,000 cases, information about the plaintiffs was withheld.

But having a soldier declared dead does not mean the search will continue, that the body will be returned or that a funeral will take place. Roman Artamonov’s family has still not been able to bury him.

Elena appealed to the military prosecutor’s office but received no explanation. She then took her story to social media. Her video was published by The Missing Regiment on its Telegram channel.

The movement emerged in April 2026 as an association of families of missing servicemen. Residents of other Russian regions soon joined the activists in Yaroslavl.

Members of the initiative help relatives draft appeals to Russia’s Investigative Committee, the presidential administration, the Red Cross and other organizations. Lawyers they know provide free consultations, and the activists also work with veterans’ groups.

On May 9, the movement organized small demonstrations in several cities, where relatives gathered holding photographs of missing soldiers.

But a grassroots initiative cannot search for people in a combat zone. It lacks both the authority and the resources to do so. Instead, activists collect names and photographs, building a virtual database of the missing. They say more than 9,000 people have already contacted them.

“An assault soldier is just a number”

After a serviceman disappears, commanders are required to determine whether he went missing during a mission or left his unit without authorization. In the first case, the military must conduct an internal investigation. In the second, the soldier can be placed on a wanted list, face criminal charges and have his payments suspended.

But commanders have used this provision as a loophole. According to Important Stories, soldiers who disappear during combat missions are routinely classified as having left their units without authorization — even when there is evidence that they were killed in battle.

If a serviceman is officially declared missing in action, his information is entered into a centralized database, including the location where he disappeared and witness testimony. Special search teams are then supposed to work alongside civic and volunteer organizations to locate the missing.

Bodies that are recovered are evacuated and identified visually, through fingerprints or DNA testing. Military enlistment offices are then supposed to inform relatives of the results.

In practice, the system works differently. According to Verstka, soldiers are warned before being sent to the front that they may not be evacuated — whether they are wounded or killed.

The recovery of bodies depends on conditions on the battlefield and on commanders’ decisions. The speed of the search also depends on the dead soldier’s rank. Officers are searched for and evacuated more quickly.

“How do they treat some assault soldier who gets killed somewhere? He’s just a number. We report the number to the division and forget about him,” a military source told Verstka.

Relatives often have no way of finding out who is searching for their loved ones, where the searches are taking place or how they are being conducted. Their only options are to contact military enlistment offices and wait for news from volunteers.

In the fall of 2025, the Defense Ministry established a Main Coordination Center. Formally, it is responsible for coordinating the work of government agencies, civic organizations and volunteers.

Families are advised to contact military enlistment offices, the Defenders of the Fatherland Foundation, the human rights ombudsman or the military prosecutor’s office. They can also submit an electronic request through the Defense Ministry’s website. But there is no way to contact the coordination center directly.

Activists believe the center exists only on paper. It publishes no reports and has no dedicated website, telephone number, email address or public office where families can seek help.

Members of the movement say the Defense Ministry has effectively shifted responsibility for the searches to regional military enlistment offices, which lack the necessary equipment, specialists and access to up-to-date DNA databases.

Still, ombudsmen have reported some results. In 2025, they helped locate more than 300 servicemen, and about 100 more were found in the first half of 2026. Most were either prisoners of war or soldiers being treated in hospitals.

Photo: Unknown Regiment / Telegram

Vladimir Putin has claimed that the creation of the center improved the situation. In December 2025, he said the number of servicemen being sought had fallen by 50 percent and had dropped threefold since the beginning of the year. But the source of those figures is unclear. Russian authorities conceal the true scale of the country’s military losses, including the number of soldiers who are missing.

The Ukrainian project I Want to Find accepts inquiries from relatives of Russian servicemen and checks the information against its own database of prisoners of war and the dead. According to Verstka, the project received more than 84,000 requests over the course of a year.

Going It alone

Anna, whose name has been changed, joined the movement after her brother went missing. He was serving under contract with the 119th Guards Airborne Regiment.

In June 2026, Anna found The Missing Regiment on social media and became an activist. She stresses that the movement does not oppose the war or criticize the authorities. Its sole aim, she says, is to determine what happened to missing servicemen.

“Women come to memorials and say that their son, husband or brother is missing,” Anna said. “They want to know what happened to him. Government agencies should be doing this work instead of sending relatives from one office to another. On paper, there is a system in place, but in reality it either does not work or works poorly.”

Within a few months, activists had emerged in many regions across Russia. The movement has been particularly active in the Lipetsk, Yaroslavl and Rostov regions.

A community event by the Unknown Regiment. Photo: Unknown Regiment / Telegram

One of the movement’s organizers is believed to be Mikhail, a businessman from Yaroslavl whose name has also been changed. He describes himself simply as an active participant.

Mikhail’s friend Sergei went missing in the combat zone. Sergei’s elderly mother was left to navigate the bureaucracy on her own and was unable to do so.

Mikhail and Sergei’s mother repeatedly contacted his military unit but received no answers. Unit officials said Mikhail was not a relative of the missing soldier and therefore had no standing to seek information. The local military enlistment official avoided both Mikhail and Sergei’s mother. When Mikhail tried to stop the official to speak with him, he was threatened with police action and a fine.

There were many similar stories. What began as meetings with relatives eventually grew into a broader initiative. Activists started publishing video appeals, portraits of missing servicemen and announcements of public gatherings.

They sought support from political parties and state-affiliated organizations, but United Russia showed no interest in the initiative.

The activists also tried to work with the Defenders of the Fatherland Foundation, which is headed by Anna Tsivileva, a relative of Vladimir Putin. But according to Mikhail, the foundation is seeking to monopolize the issue without providing an effective system for finding the missing.

The movement then approached Communist Party branches in the Krasnodar region and the Chelyabinsk region. The party had previously provided meeting space to wives of mobilized soldiers from The Way Home movement.

But the authorities have cracked down hard on attempts by soldiers’ relatives to organize. The movement of mobilized soldiers’ wives initially supported both the war and Putin. Later, its most active members were designated “foreign agents” and faced criminal prosecution, while others were intimidated into silence.

Cooperation with the Communist Party also came to nothing. Its branch in the Chelyabinsk region said it had not worked with the organization, while the Krasnodar branch did not respond to a request for comment.

The party tried to involve the movement in its campaign against internet restrictions. But the issue had nothing to do with the search for missing soldiers, and the cooperation ended.

A local branch of the New People party in the city of Shakhty initially expressed interest in the initiative. Soon afterward, however, its representatives stopped responding. Some activists believe this happened after consultations with law enforcement agencies. The party did not respond to a request for comment from Veter.

“Give people hope”

Despite the stance taken by political parties and state-affiliated foundations, interest in the initiative continues to grow. Mikhail says the movement is receiving an enormous number of requests for help.

“We want the search effort to be taken to a new level and for officials to stop withholding information,” he said. “Commanders and military enlistment officials need to stop sending relatives from one office to another. Right now, if we want to find out what happened to someone close to us, we are treated as enemies of the state.”

Mikhail says the uncertainty is tearing families apart. Sergei’s mother begins to cry every time someone asks whether there has been any news.

The activists believe the system cannot be changed without the state’s involvement. Political parties, they say, could appeal directly to the president and the government, paving the way for legislative changes.

But military enlistment offices have little interest in conducting searches, while commanders are focused on the war. Without a clear legal obligation to act, the activists say, the system will not work.

A prank that spun out of control

Even these nonpolitical demands are treated by the Kremlin as a threat. Pro-government outlets quickly portrayed the movement as a project run by Ukrainian intelligence services.

In June 2026, War on Fakes, Lapsha Media and Southern News Service claimed that the initiative was part of an information operation. According to their account, Ukrainian intelligence services were collecting relatives’ personal information in order to hack their accounts and extort money from them.

Southern News Service claimed that those behind the effort were seeking to instill a sense of abandonment and helplessness among relatives. The supposed goal, it said, was to spread the idea that the state was not searching for the missing and that only grassroots organizing and public demonstrations could help.

Ahead of May 9, schools in several Russian regions held lessons titled “The Missing Regiment: Memory Cannot Be Blocked.” The classes focused on missing servicemen and contained no political appeals.

Several days later, schools began removing information about the lessons. The Sota project then reported, citing an anonymous source, that the campaign had supposedly been a prank.

None of Russia’s well-known pranksters claimed responsibility. Activists insist that the lessons had been organized by teachers through prior arrangements. They say educators began facing punishment after the events and that the initiative was subsequently portrayed as a prank in an effort to discredit it retroactively.

According to Mikhail, the movement faces pressure not only from pro-government media but also from law enforcement agencies.

On June 6, activist Irina Chebotareva in Lipetsk stopped responding to calls and messages. She had spent a long time searching for her missing husband and was regarded as the movement’s local coordinator. Members of the initiative believe she may have been in police custody. Veter was unable to determine what happened to her.

In Shakhty, in the Rostov region, members of the movement joined a May 9 motorcade carrying portraits of their missing relatives. On June 12, they organized a small demonstration of their own.

Shortly before the event, police summoned the movement’s local coordinator, Valeria Klyuchnikova, and questioned her over possible involvement in terrorist activity. Officers told her that the motorcade had to be approved by the city administration and law enforcement authorities.

Klyuchnikova was later detained while picking up a package containing the movement’s flag and several T-shirts. Police confiscated the flag and one T-shirt before releasing her.
