World.title: How a director’s love of the speccy turned into a film about a Chinese football team
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 How a director’s love of the speccy turned into a film about a Chinese football team Andrew Wu Updated August 11, 2026 — 2:27pm ,first published 11:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In David Gung’s first season of senior football in 1968, the speedy rover arrived at games well into the first quarter due to his work at a Chinese church on Sundays. When he won the best and fairest award that year, the club president presented him with an electric clock. “I got that to remind me to play on time,” Gung said. From left: David Gung, Peter Louey and Harold Chin Quan were members of the Chinese footy team depicted in a new film, Carn the Chinese! Joe Armao Harold Chin Quan was the centreman in that team. At 52 kilograms, he was built to be a jockey rather than negotiating the chaos after a centre bounce. “I played scared for the first two years,” joked Chin Quan, a third-generation Australian whose grandfather came to the country in 1897.



Peter Louey was the ruckman. Standing 5′10 (178 centimetres), he was undersized. The trio formed the heart of the midfield of a team called the Young Chinese League, a social football side consisting of Chinese Australians whose story of resilience and love of the game during the White Australian policy era has been turned into a short film by director Angela How. The Young Chinese League football team in 1966. Premiering on Wednesday at the Melbourne International Film Festival, Carn the Chinese! explores how sections of Melbourne’s Chinese community embraced the game long before names such as Barassi, Jesaulenko and Silvagni became synonymous with the code. How, a Singapore-born Australian, first saw the game after her family moved to this country in the 1990s. She was captivated by the speccy.



“What intrigued me was you climbed on someone else to get to the ball,” How told this masthead. “I’d never seen anyone jump so high. It was quite a sight.” Because of the lack of Chinese or Asian involvement in the sport, “I didn’t feel like the game belonged to me culturally”, How said. So she set about finding stories of Chinese Australians playing the sport. Though Chinese immigrants have been in Australia since the days of the gold rush, very few have reached the top level. Wally Koochew played for Carlton in 1908. George Tansing played five games for Geelong that year, Ernie Foo represented St Kilda four times in 1913. More recently, Fremantle’s Bailey Banfield is the most prominent men’s footballer with Chinese heritage, while Darcy Vescio is the torchbearer in the AFLW. They are also an executive producer of the film.



Though the YCL played for about 50 years from the 1930s to 1986, not much is known about the team beyond a chapter in author Patrick Skene’s book Celestial Footy, which chronicles the participation of Chinese immigrants in the game. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘They hid it away’: The DNA test that revealed an Australian cricketer’s family secret Formed in the 1930s after a merger between the Chinese Progress Association and the Chinese Athletics Association, the YCL was not part of an official league. They quickly made an impression. “By 1938, weekly Young Chinese League matches in Albert Park were a much-anticipated fixture on the calendar of the Melbourne Chinese community; a meeting point to build friendships and keep community strong,” Skene wrote. The YCL played all around Melbourne and in the bush, arranging games against companies such as Ford, Holden and Kraft.



How cannot remember how she came across the YCL, but the more she learnt, the keener she was to tell its story. Filming started in 2022, but other projects took up How’s time until last year. “I wanted it to be done and them to be celebrated while they’re here,” How said. “That was really important to me and I felt a responsibility to do the work and finish it. Gung, now 78, was a talented footballer for the Young Chinese League, the team featured in the short film Carn the Chinese! “Because they played through the White Australia Policy era, the thing that struck me was they were quintessentially Aussie with their larrikinism and attitude to life. “Peter warmed to the game so naturally and played really well. By embracing the game, he became accepted. Just the fact he was good at sport, it broke a lot of barriers for him.”



Louey, 88, came to Australia on a boat at the age of 12. He lived in West Melbourne, became a North Melbourne supporter, and was a good enough footballer and cricketer to captain Brunswick Tech’s school team in both sports. He also led the YCL. In 2016, he was awarded an OAM as part of the Queen’s Birthday Honours for service to the Chinese community in Victoria. “In Australia, if you’re a good sport, they admire you,” he said in the film. High-flying marks were what first drew director Angela How to Australian rules football. Chin Quan is a third-generation Australian whose grandfather arrived in the country in 1897 and settled in Darwin. His grandfather grew vegetables on a farm that now sits on a golf course and the Darwin Botanic Gardens. The road dividing the two – Chin Quan Road – is named after him. Born and raised in Melbourne, Chin Quan lived in St Kilda as a child. After playing little sport at school, he was introduced to the YCL by two cousins from Western Australia.



A metallurgist for the defence department, Chin Quan played more than 250 games for the club from 1964 to 1986. “I could run all day,” Chin Quan, who was a lightly-built rover, said of his playing style. “I got a lot stronger. I learned how to tackle, dodge elbows. Over 20-odd years, I had a broken thumb and collarbone – that was it, other than the odd hammy. I stayed out of the way a little bit.” Gung still has a feel for football. Joe Armao Gung was one of the team’s better players. As a junior, he played for North Melbourne’s under-15 and under-17 teams, and tried out with Essendon, where he was zoned. “When I played with North Melbourne, I had empty beer bottles thrown at me, all sorts of racist remarks: ‘Go home you chink’,” Gung said.



Related Article AFL 2026 Emails between Cats, AFL at the centre of club’s Kolodjashnij defence “The coach was a former North Melbourne player, Cole Spratling – he was a very good person. He pulled me aside after the game and he said, ‘Look Dave, if you’re going to play football at that level you have to learn to live with it’. “There weren’t rules and regulations to deal against racist remarks like they do today.” Disillusioned after being given just five minutes by the Bombers, he gave up on a league career. “I don’t think I was given a fair go,” Gung said.



At University High, he played alongside future league footballers Robert Peterson and John Scholes. Scholes also played cricket for Victoria, and later coached the state team. Playing against University High’s old boys team, Gung crossed paths with Allen Aylett, who played 220 games for the Kangaroos, then – as chairman of the VFL – oversaw the league’s expansion outside of Victoria to Sydney. In an attempt to slow him down, Aylett stomped on his Gung’s toes. Worse was to come. An archival image of the Young Chinese League team in action. “To rub salt in the wound, he got the ball facing the boundary, kicked it over his shoulder and scored a goal,” Gung said. Gung reminded Aylett of the incident when the pair ran into each other decades later at Marvel Stadium.



“We had a good laugh about it,” Gung said. For a team of Chinese Australians that played when the White Australia policy was still active, racism was surprisingly not a big issue for the YCL, whose players won admiration from opponents for their tenacity. “After a while, the guys realised we were a team that loved our footy,” Chin Quan said. “We played the right way – hard – and we got a lot of respect for that. We got along really well most of the time. “There were a few incidents with people who were a bit ignorant, but by and large it was not a problem for me.” Despite his family’s long history in the country, football made Chin Quan feel more Australian.



“Very much so, I met so many guys on the footy field,” Chin Quan said. “We’d have a barbecue afterwards and have a drink.” Related Article Analysis

AFLW Why the AFL has booted men’s footy from its most lucrative timeslot Forty years after the team’s last game, the ties that bind remain strong. They’re too old to lace the boots now, but several gather for a hit of tennis and to reminisce over a meal. Gung takes Louey to the gym twice a week. “When he was captain and I was at uni, I wasn’t earning any money and couldn’t afford the end-of-year trip to Stawell,” Gung said. “He said, ‘I’ll pay for your weekend away, accommodation and here’s a few pounds pocket money’. I’ve never forgotten that.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: I’m making good money. So why does everything still feel like a slog?
World.content:
August 11, 2026 — 2:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I had a business which I successfully sold. I was pretty burnt out by the end of it. Now, I’m self-employed, I’ve kept my team small, I make good money. I could be making more, but also I’m doing okay – I have decent savings and investments. My problem is that it just never feels like it gets any easier? Over the past five years, my wealth has been growing, but I still feel like I’m slogging away. I’m not afraid of hard work. I’m proud of my work ethic. But sometimes I just feel like it’s meant to get easier at some point. Or do I just keep grinding until I get there, and then retire? Until you change your mindset, your finances may always feel like a struggle. Simon Letch Here’s the short answer – it won’t start to feel easier, until you let it. We are often sold this idea that “ease” exists at a specific milestone in the future. It starts with small milestones – when I get a certain amount in savings, when I can stop living pay-to-pay, when I finally get out of debt – then, life will feel easier. But it doesn’t end there.



Then it becomes when I buy a house, when I pay off the mortgage, when my business/income hits $X milestone … then I’ll be able to relax and enjoy my life. But that’s not really how it works. Sure, financial progress can alleviate specific stressors. Having a reliable car, being able to easily afford your bills, having financial buffers for emergencies – if you didn’t have these things before, then you will experience a certain level of ease when you do finally get them. As a society we don’t love it when it looks like it was ‘easy’ for someone. We almost treat hardship as a form of justification. However, as you’ve noted, that relief is often temporary. Eventually, there is another milestone around the corner – and suddenly, you’re working hard again to make it happen. Soon, you start to wonder – when does this end? You start to think that maybe, the relief is right at the end of the road. Maybe, if you work really hard to make lots of money now, then you’ll be able to finally relax when you can retire. But the harder you work, the harder it feels, and soon the experience of hardship starts to become something of a habit.



Here’s the thing: the experience of ease is not just about what’s happening outside of you, it’s also about what’s happening inside you. This is clearer when you separate your external circumstances from your experience of those circumstances. You grew and sold a business before. That felt hard. You now have a leaner business. It still feels hard. You had less wealth a few years ago. That felt hard. Today, you have more wealth. It still feels hard. The common denominator isn’t the circumstances – it’s your experience of them. So, at some point the question isn’t “why are things hard?”, but rather, “why am I experiencing things as hard?” Here’s what I commonly see in my high-performing clients: You consider the experience of “hardship” normal and even a prerequisite. Everyone talks about how “hard” it is, how hard one must work, no pain, no gain, you have to make sacrifices, you have to struggle – that’s what they tell you is the path to success, right? So, you work hard. You hustle, hard. You do everything, hard, because you assume hard is the prerequisite. There is no other option. You couldn’t enjoy your way to success … or could you?



You have glorified struggle and hardship. It’s not your fault – we all love a good underdog story. In many ways, as a society we don’t love it when it looks like it was “easy” for someone. Editor's pick Opinion

Money psychology Three money habits that can keep you stuck financially Paridhi Jain Money contributor We almost treat hardship as a form of justification. We want to be able to say: “I deserve this because I worked hard for it.” But as long as you need hardship to justify your success, you’ll cling to it. So, can you let go of the badge of honour that comes with hardship? Those who experience more enjoyment and ease aren’t focused on how much they struggled, or even how hard they worked. They’re focused on how much they’re enjoying the journey. You notice the hardship more than the ease. There is an abundance of “ease” available for you to experience in your life right now. Maybe it’s easy for you to pay the bills. Maybe saving and investing comes easily to you.



How much do you enjoy and fully appreciate the ease that is available to you? If you are habituated to noticing hardship, you won’t notice (let alone be able to experience) the ease that is available for you right now. So, perhaps the question isn’t “when does it get easier?” but rather “what’s stopping me from experiencing more ease right now?” and “how can I increase my capacity and willingness to notice and enjoy more ease in my life, as it is?” Paridhi Jain is a money and mindset coach who combines practical strategies with mindset transformation to help clients create more freedom and fulfilment in wealth, work and life. World.title: Work-from-home law delayed by Carroll weeks before planned start
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian Parliament Work-from-home law delayed by Carroll weeks before planned start Angus Delaney Updated August 11, 2026 — 2:11pm ,first published 11:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victorians will not have a legal right to work from home until at least July next year, after Labor delayed its plan to introduce the controversial law following an eleventh-hour plea from business groups. Premier Ben Carroll announced on Tuesday that as part of his government’s “reset with the business community”, the law would not come into effect until July 1, 2027, 10 months after the original intended September start date. Premier Ben Carroll, pictured last month, has delayed Labor’s work-from-home legislation. Justin McManus “I support work from home. I support flexible work. It is good for working families,” Carroll said. But he said the state’s economic health was important, and he wanted business to thrive in Victoria. “That is why I’ve delayed these changes,” he said.



The bill was expected to pass parliament’s upper house on Thursday, but the government will now delay its passage, although Carroll promised it would still pass before the November state election. He said he would consult on any “commonsense amendments”. The move to delay the legislation has been welcomed by industry and business groups, which on Monday joined forces to call for the bill to be scrapped, and warned that it risked increasing unemployment and driving investment out of the state. Tim Piper, Victorian head of the Australian Industry Group, said businesses were still concerned the legislation was going ahead at all, but there was now at least opportunity for the government to consider amendments and improvements. Piper said the government should use the delay to consider scrapping the bill entirely and conduct an economic impact statement on the potential fallout.



“When you have an economic impact statement, you can understand whether ... it’s likely to be detrimental or not. We think it is,” Piper said. Labor’s promise to legislate a right to work from home two days a week has angered business groups, which say it will send jobs and investment interstate. Getty Images The concession from Labor is a sign Carroll is following through on his commitment to be a more pro-business premier than predecessor Jacinta Allan. Though the government and opposition have reaffirmed their support for employees’ work-from-home rights, the business lobby is still pushing Labor to ditch the policy altogether, believing a face-to-face meeting with Carroll will encourage him to scrap the policy. “What we’re going to be asking him is to listen to our issues … when we give him the reasons, the rationale, the economic benefits of not doing it, we hope that he will change his mind,” Piper said.



Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Sally Curtain said the decision to pause the debate over the “divisive legislation” and listen to industry was a good start, but maintained the bill should be scrapped. Related Article Victorian Parliament Coalition to support working-from-home laws but want changes to protect businesses “The premier has been in touch with us directly and indicated he is willing to meet with us,” Curtain said in a statement. “We hope to persuade him to abandon this destructive course.”



Bran Black, chief executive of the Business Council of Australia, said while Carroll was taking the first steps towards listening to industry, the bill in any form would “compound Victoria’s economic decline”. “Already, Victoria has the highest unemployment rate in the country and the Victorian economy cannot afford another policy that drives investment and jobs away, which only hurts Victorians through lower living standards,” Black said. Cath Evans, Victorian executive director of the Property Council, said the government should use the delay to consult deeply on the legislation and examine its potentially dire economic consequences.



“This needs serious attention,” Evans said. The Coalition under Opposition Leader Jess Wilson decided not to oppose Labor’s bill and was seeking to introduce amendments to protect businesses. Related Article Victorian election Pay for the desk or pay a penalty: Inside Victoria’s strict new work-from-home rules The proposed amendments include capping “reasonable costs” an employer must pay at $1000, limiting the right to employees who primarily work in Victoria and will continue to do so (unless mutually agreed to), and delaying an employee’s right to appeal a company’s decision until next year. Shadow attorney-general James Newbury said that by pushing the promised start of the legislation back 10 months Carroll was creating instability for businesses and workers.



“His government committed to a guarantee of working from home on the first of September – he’s broken that guarantee,” Newbury said. “Victorians should know they cannot trust this man, and they cannot trust this government, despite what he guarantees, despite what this government has promised.” Major business groups warned on Monday that the proposed overhaul was another layer of red tape that would result in companies deserting Victoria and expanding their businesses interstate. Business groups have not ruled out launching or joining a potential High Court challenge against the legislation if it passes. Legal experts have cast doubt over the state government’s ability to legislate a right to work from home, as most workplace laws are under the jurisdiction of the federal government. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Court hears brother of complainant ‘J’ received gifts from 2GB broadcaster as alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day six of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Jacqueline Maley will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

Last week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Sam Mooy

Our live coverage was paused on Wednesday after Local Court Judge Glenn Walsh temporarily imposed a non-publication order on the cross-examination of the complainant, known as “J”, by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC. That order was lifted on Thursday afternoon.

“J”, now in his early 40s, denied under questioning by Bashir that he had a financial motive for making the allegations against Jones, and denied that they were a fabrication.

He has given evidence that Jones groped him as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls farm. “J” has also told the court that Jones had indecently assaulted him at the property after telling him to wear “a robe and nothing else”.

The complainant said he came forward to police after seeing reports about Jones’ arrest in November 2024 because he wanted justice.

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box for a sixth day. He will be re-examined by prosecutor Georgina Wright, SC, after his cross-examination concluded on Friday.

A man known as “C” will be the next complainant to give evidence.

Bashir asked “J” a series of questions about whether he read media reports containing similar allegations about Jones in 2023 before he spoke to police the following year. He said he did not.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing, and Bashir said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to the court.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: RBA keeps rates on hold as major bank warns of 15% property price slump
World.content:
The Reserve Bank has kept interest rates on hold as it weighs a slowing economy, dragged down by a weaker-than-expected housing market, against risks that inflation could be pushed up by an “AI boom” and continued conflict in the Middle East. On Tuesday, the bank kept the official cash rate at 4.35 per cent – broadly in line with economists’ expectations – after releasing its updated forecasts for key metrics including economic growth, inflation and unemployment. Financial markets believe there is a 50-50 chance of a further rate rise late in the year, with rate relief not expected before the second half of 2027. House prices are falling in Labor’s marginal Melbourne seats but local MPs say community supports it. Joe Armao The bank expects economic growth to be slightly stronger for the rest of the year than it did in May, although it notes the figure is likely to remain below the long-run rate of 2 per cent. The RBA’s latest forecasts show growth of between 1.4 per cent by Christmas and 1.6 per cent by December next year.



The decision comes after ANZ economists on Tuesday morning warned that property prices could slump by almost 15 per cent over this year and next, citing interest rates, low levels of affordability and the federal government’s property tax changes. The RBA said household consumption has eased “gradually”, with spending on discretionary items including electric vehicles remaining relatively strong. Meanwhile, business investment had been much stronger than expected, the bank said, largely driven by data centre construction. While price growth across the economy remains above the RBA’s target range of 2 to 3 per cent – inflation was 3.8 per cent in June – the inflation figures were substantially lower than the 4.8 per cent figure the RBA forecast in May. Unemployment, at 4.4 per cent in June, is still below the rate the bank considers “full employment”: the level at which it believes inflation pressures will not be stoked as people looked for more work in response to cost-of-living pressures. Meanwhile, ANZ, which had been the most bearish about the property market of all the major banks, said it believed capital city prices would fall by 4.3 per cent this year and by 3.4 per cent in 2027 before staging a recovery the following year.



Combined, the falls would mean a drop of 10.6 per cent from the peak in prices to their trough. Editor's pick Census Completing the census is compulsory. Skipping it can result in a hefty fine The biggest hit is expected in Sydney, where the median value is now $1.5 million, with house prices tipped to fall by 14.5 per cent from their peak at the start of the year. Melbourne prices are tipped to fall by 12.8 per cent from their peak. Prices in both cities are expected to recover by almost 5 per cent in 2028. Smaller hits are expected in other capitals, with drops of 7.9 per cent forecast in Brisbane, 5.2 per cent in Perth and 9.8 per cent in Adelaide. In these three cities, prices have climbed by more than 15 per cent over the past two years.



ANZ senior economists Madeline Dunk and Adam Boyton said the market was slowing quicker than they had expected. Loading “It is clear the combination of restrictive interest rates, recent tax policy changes and global uncertainty have dampened sentiment in the market,” they said. “Auction clearance rates are very soft, coming in below 50 per cent for the past 10 weeks across the capitals.” Dunk and Boyton said interest rate settings, and ongoing pressures on the construction sector, meant prices were unlikely to fall for too long. They are tipping a nationwide increase of 4.3 per cent in 2028.

World.title: The doctor who helped the one player return from a pec injury without surgery is backing Isaah Yeo
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 The doctor who helped the one player return from a pec injury without surgery is backing Isaah Yeo Christian Nicolussi August 11, 2026 — 2:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The doctor who helped the only NRL player to return from a pec injury without surgery is backing Penrith co-captain Isaah Yeo to do likewise this finals’ series. Dr Ameer Ibrahim, who will be working for the Sydney Roosters when they play against Yeo’s Panthers on Thursday night, played a key role in Michael Gordon returning from a high-grade partial tear of his pectoral in 2017. Isaah Yeo has delayed surgery in the hope of returning for the NRL finals. Getty Images Gordon had the option of undergoing surgery, but the earliest he would have been back was 10 weeks. But he was edging towards the back end of his career, and was desperate to resume playing fullback for the Roosters in their run to the finals. So Ibrahim and the club’s medical team mapped out a plan to have Gordon back playing without surgery. It was successful.



The Panthers confirmed on Monday their inspirational forward Yeo would not require “immediate surgery” on a pec muscle injury he suffered against the Warriors last Friday night. The club said he had already started “rehabilitation in a bid to return to the field” this season. The plan is to have Yeo back for the start of the NRL finals in five weeks. A better scenario, according to a club spokesperson not authorised to speak publicly, would be for Yeo to return in the final round of the regular season against Wests Tigers – in four weeks – so he can get a run under his belt before the more rigorous tests in September. Ibrahim was unaware of the extent of damage Yeo had done to his chest, but using Gordon’s recovery as an example, explained what the Penrith leader’s next month might entail. “Because Michael Gordon was getting towards the end of his career, we rolled the dice a bit delaying surgery, even though surgery was what he ultimately needed,” Ibrahim said.



“If you operate on a tendon, it was a 10-week return to play, so surgery would have all but ruled Michael out of the finals. Michael Gordon returned for the back end of the 2017 NRL season after delaying pec surgery. NRL “There was research that said we could rehab the pec and get them to 80 to 85 per cent in terms of strength and function. “He was also playing in the backs, which was another factor in Michael’s favour. “He did very well in the end when he returned. He had about 85 per cent strength after six weeks.



Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Isaah Yeo’s scans delivered good news. This is when the Panthers hope he can return “Stretching is the worst thing you want to do. You want the inflammation to settle down, and once that settles, by about day 10, you can start isometric exercises to engage the muscle without ripping the muscle tendon. That includes band work, electric muscle stimulators, basic inner range strengthening exercises to avoid straining the tendon. “By two weeks, he’ll be back running and doing cardio. “It can definitely be done. You can’t needle the pec, and you just have to hope the rehab is good – and that is lasts. It will definitely go again. “This isn’t something you’d do at the start of the season, you’d only consider it at the end.”



Ibrahim was also the doctor at Manly when Tom Trbojevic flirted with the idea of trying to play on without pec surgery at the end of 2019, for the sake of featuring in the finals – and potentially Australia’s end-of-year Tests against New Zealand and Tonga – but given Trbojevic’s age, and early part of his career, “Turbo” elected to have surgery. Yeo, 31, not only wants to help Penrith chase a fifth title in six seasons, but also be fit to captain Australia at the World Cup in October and early November before committing to surgery.

World.title: They beat the flag favourites and have a finals berth sewn up, now the Dees welcome back a favourite son
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 They beat the flag favourites and have a finals berth sewn up, now the Dees welcome back a favourite son Oliver Caffrey August 11, 2026 — 2:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne vice-captain Jack Viney will play his first game in almost a year as he tries to be part of the surging Demons’ finals campaign. Having dealt with complex back and Achilles injuries, Viney hasn’t played a match at any level this season. After a month of training Jack Viney is set to make his return to the playing field in Melbourne’s VFL team this weekend. Getty Images The strong-bodied midfielder’s most recent game was Melbourne’s round-24 loss to Collingwood last August, before Steven King took over as Demons coach. But the premiership hero will return via the VFL on Sunday when the Casey Demons face Box Hill.



“He’s been full training now for nearly a month ... so we finally get a game into him,” King said on Tuesday. “He’s obviously chomping at the bit, vice-captain of our footy club and the ultimate competitor and the type of player you want to run out with. Loading “We’ve got to make sure that we do what’s right for Jack and right for the footy club. “But if he can get through that game, then he’ll put his name up in lights and make himself available and see what happens from there.”



After a stunning four-point win over premiership favourites Fremantle last Saturday, Melbourne locked in their finals spot. Having an experienced player like Viney slot into a September campaign makes the Demons a dangerous prospect. Viney stretches out at training. Getty Images But King has cautioned against expecting too much from the 32-year-old. “We have to respect what he’s been through,” King said of Viney.



“But I feel like you can’t just get given a game on reputation and your standing. “The first thing is just to get through a whole competitive game, and make sure he pulls up OK. “I want him to actually make sure of the long term as well and that he leaves this year well, ready for next season.” Complicating any AFL return for Viney, Casey’s VFL campaign will come to an end this Sunday as they have not qualified for finals.



King expressed his frustration at the inconsistent scheduling of the VFL, with numerous byes during the season making it hard for reserves players to build momentum. “We’ve got professional athletes that need to play games and develop, and that’s what I feel like the VFL competition is for – it’s for us to develop young men to play and be ready to play AFL,” King said “For every week they have off, that’s a missed opportunity where they get to develop and grow and learn. “It’s something I feel like the AFL certainly needs to look at aligning the seasons.” Youngster Latrelle Pickett will also return via the VFL this weekend after recovering from a concussion.

World.title: How a director’s love of the speccy turned into a film about a Chinese football team
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 How a director’s love of the speccy turned into a film about a Chinese football team Andrew Wu Updated August 11, 2026 — 2:27pm ,first published 11:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In David Gung’s first season of senior football in 1968, the speedy rover arrived at games well into the first quarter due to his work at a Chinese church on Sundays. When he won the best and fairest award that year, the club president presented him with an electric clock. “I got that to remind me to play on time,” Gung said. From left: David Gung, Peter Louey and Harold Chin Quan were members of the Chinese footy team depicted in a new film, Carn the Chinese! Joe Armao Harold Chin Quan was the centreman in that team. At 52 kilograms, he was built to be a jockey rather than negotiating the chaos after a centre bounce. “I played scared for the first two years,” joked Chin Quan, a third-generation Australian whose grandfather came to the country in 1897.



Peter Louey was the ruckman. Standing 5′10 (178 centimetres), he was undersized. The trio formed the heart of the midfield of a team called the Young Chinese League, a social football side consisting of Chinese Australians whose story of resilience and love of the game during the White Australian policy era has been turned into a short film by director Angela How. The Young Chinese League football team in 1966. Premiering on Wednesday at the Melbourne International Film Festival, Carn the Chinese! explores how sections of Melbourne’s Chinese community embraced the game long before names such as Barassi, Jesaulenko and Silvagni became synonymous with the code. How, a Singapore-born Australian, first saw the game after her family moved to this country in the 1990s. She was captivated by the speccy.



“What intrigued me was you climbed on someone else to get to the ball,” How told this masthead. “I’d never seen anyone jump so high. It was quite a sight.” Because of the lack of Chinese or Asian involvement in the sport, “I didn’t feel like the game belonged to me culturally”, How said. So she set about finding stories of Chinese Australians playing the sport. Though Chinese immigrants have been in Australia since the days of the gold rush, very few have reached the top level. Wally Koochew played for Carlton in 1908. George Tansing played five games for Geelong that year, Ernie Foo represented St Kilda four times in 1913. More recently, Fremantle’s Bailey Banfield is the most prominent men’s footballer with Chinese heritage, while Darcy Vescio is the torchbearer in the AFLW. They are also an executive producer of the film.



Though the YCL played for about 50 years from the 1930s to 1986, not much is known about the team beyond a chapter in author Patrick Skene’s book Celestial Footy, which chronicles the participation of Chinese immigrants in the game. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘They hid it away’: The DNA test that revealed an Australian cricketer’s family secret Formed in the 1930s after a merger between the Chinese Progress Association and the Chinese Athletics Association, the YCL was not part of an official league. They quickly made an impression. “By 1938, weekly Young Chinese League matches in Albert Park were a much-anticipated fixture on the calendar of the Melbourne Chinese community; a meeting point to build friendships and keep community strong,” Skene wrote. The YCL played all around Melbourne and in the bush, arranging games against companies such as Ford, Holden and Kraft.



How cannot remember how she came across the YCL, but the more she learnt, the keener she was to tell its story. Filming started in 2022, but other projects took up How’s time until last year. “I wanted it to be done and them to be celebrated while they’re here,” How said. “That was really important to me and I felt a responsibility to do the work and finish it. Gung, now 78, was a talented footballer for the Young Chinese League, the team featured in the short film Carn the Chinese! “Because they played through the White Australia Policy era, the thing that struck me was they were quintessentially Aussie with their larrikinism and attitude to life. “Peter warmed to the game so naturally and played really well. By embracing the game, he became accepted. Just the fact he was good at sport, it broke a lot of barriers for him.”



Louey, 88, came to Australia on a boat at the age of 12. He lived in West Melbourne, became a North Melbourne supporter, and was a good enough footballer and cricketer to captain Brunswick Tech’s school team in both sports. He also led the YCL. In 2016, he was awarded an OAM as part of the Queen’s Birthday Honours for service to the Chinese community in Victoria. “In Australia, if you’re a good sport, they admire you,” he said in the film. High-flying marks were what first drew director Angela How to Australian rules football. Chin Quan is a third-generation Australian whose grandfather arrived in the country in 1897 and settled in Darwin. His grandfather grew vegetables on a farm that now sits on a golf course and the Darwin Botanic Gardens. The road dividing the two – Chin Quan Road – is named after him. Born and raised in Melbourne, Chin Quan lived in St Kilda as a child. After playing little sport at school, he was introduced to the YCL by two cousins from Western Australia.



A metallurgist for the defence department, Chin Quan played more than 250 games for the club from 1964 to 1986. “I could run all day,” Chin Quan, who was a lightly-built rover, said of his playing style. “I got a lot stronger. I learned how to tackle, dodge elbows. Over 20-odd years, I had a broken thumb and collarbone – that was it, other than the odd hammy. I stayed out of the way a little bit.” Gung still has a feel for football. Joe Armao Gung was one of the team’s better players. As a junior, he played for North Melbourne’s under-15 and under-17 teams, and tried out with Essendon, where he was zoned. “When I played with North Melbourne, I had empty beer bottles thrown at me, all sorts of racist remarks: ‘Go home you chink’,” Gung said.



Related Article AFL 2026 Emails between Cats, AFL at the centre of club’s Kolodjashnij defence “The coach was a former North Melbourne player, Cole Spratling – he was a very good person. He pulled me aside after the game and he said, ‘Look Dave, if you’re going to play football at that level you have to learn to live with it’. “There weren’t rules and regulations to deal against racist remarks like they do today.” Disillusioned after being given just five minutes by the Bombers, he gave up on a league career. “I don’t think I was given a fair go,” Gung said.



At University High, he played alongside future league footballers Robert Peterson and John Scholes. Scholes also played cricket for Victoria, and later coached the state team. Playing against University High’s old boys team, Gung crossed paths with Allen Aylett, who played 220 games for the Kangaroos, then – as chairman of the VFL – oversaw the league’s expansion outside of Victoria to Sydney. In an attempt to slow him down, Aylett stomped on his Gung’s toes. Worse was to come. An archival image of the Young Chinese League team in action. “To rub salt in the wound, he got the ball facing the boundary, kicked it over his shoulder and scored a goal,” Gung said. Gung reminded Aylett of the incident when the pair ran into each other decades later at Marvel Stadium.



“We had a good laugh about it,” Gung said. For a team of Chinese Australians that played when the White Australia policy was still active, racism was surprisingly not a big issue for the YCL, whose players won admiration from opponents for their tenacity. “After a while, the guys realised we were a team that loved our footy,” Chin Quan said. “We played the right way – hard – and we got a lot of respect for that. We got along really well most of the time. “There were a few incidents with people who were a bit ignorant, but by and large it was not a problem for me.”



Despite his family’s long history in the country, football made Chin Quan feel more Australian. “Very much so, I met so many guys on the footy field,” Chin Quan said. “We’d have a barbecue afterwards and have a drink.” Related Article Analysis

AFLW Why the AFL has booted men’s footy from its most lucrative timeslot Forty years after the team’s last game, the ties that bind remain strong. They’re too old to lace the boots now, but several gather for a hit of tennis and to reminisce over a meal. Gung takes Louey to the gym twice a week. “When he was captain and I was at uni, I wasn’t earning any money and couldn’t afford the end-of-year trip to Stawell,” Gung said.



“He said, ‘I’ll pay for your weekend away, accommodation and here’s a few pounds pocket money’. I’ve never forgotten that.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: I’m making good money. So why does everything still feel like a slog?
World.content:
August 11, 2026 — 2:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I had a business which I successfully sold. I was pretty burnt out by the end of it. Now, I’m self-employed, I’ve kept my team small, I make good money. I could be making more, but also I’m doing okay – I have decent savings and investments. My problem is that it just never feels like it gets any easier? Over the past five years, my wealth has been growing, but I still feel like I’m slogging away. I’m not afraid of hard work. I’m proud of my work ethic. But sometimes I just feel like it’s meant to get easier at some point. Or do I just keep grinding until I get there, and then retire? Until you change your mindset, your finances may always feel like a struggle. Simon Letch Here’s the short answer – it won’t start to feel easier, until you let it. We are often sold this idea that “ease” exists at a specific milestone in the future. It starts with small milestones – when I get a certain amount in savings, when I can stop living pay-to-pay, when I finally get out of debt – then, life will feel easier. But it doesn’t end there.



Then it becomes when I buy a house, when I pay off the mortgage, when my business/income hits $X milestone … then I’ll be able to relax and enjoy my life. But that’s not really how it works. Sure, financial progress can alleviate specific stressors. Having a reliable car, being able to easily afford your bills, having financial buffers for emergencies – if you didn’t have these things before, then you will experience a certain level of ease when you do finally get them. As a society we don’t love it when it looks like it was ‘easy’ for someone. We almost treat hardship as a form of justification. However, as you’ve noted, that relief is often temporary. Eventually, there is another milestone around the corner – and suddenly, you’re working hard again to make it happen. Soon, you start to wonder – when does this end? You start to think that maybe, the relief is right at the end of the road. Maybe, if you work really hard to make lots of money now, then you’ll be able to finally relax when you can retire. But the harder you work, the harder it feels, and soon the experience of hardship starts to become something of a habit.



Here’s the thing: the experience of ease is not just about what’s happening outside of you, it’s also about what’s happening inside you. This is clearer when you separate your external circumstances from your experience of those circumstances. You grew and sold a business before. That felt hard. You now have a leaner business. It still feels hard. You had less wealth a few years ago. That felt hard. Today, you have more wealth. It still feels hard. The common denominator isn’t the circumstances – it’s your experience of them. So, at some point the question isn’t “why are things hard?”, but rather, “why am I experiencing things as hard?” Here’s what I commonly see in my high-performing clients: You consider the experience of “hardship” normal and even a prerequisite. Everyone talks about how “hard” it is, how hard one must work, no pain, no gain, you have to make sacrifices, you have to struggle – that’s what they tell you is the path to success, right? So, you work hard. You hustle, hard. You do everything, hard, because you assume hard is the prerequisite. There is no other option. You couldn’t enjoy your way to success … or could you?



You have glorified struggle and hardship. It’s not your fault – we all love a good underdog story. In many ways, as a society we don’t love it when it looks like it was “easy” for someone. Editor's pick Opinion

Money psychology Three money habits that can keep you stuck financially Paridhi Jain Money contributor We almost treat hardship as a form of justification. We want to be able to say: “I deserve this because I worked hard for it.” But as long as you need hardship to justify your success, you’ll cling to it. So, can you let go of the badge of honour that comes with hardship? Those who experience more enjoyment and ease aren’t focused on how much they struggled, or even how hard they worked. They’re focused on how much they’re enjoying the journey. You notice the hardship more than the ease. There is an abundance of “ease” available for you to experience in your life right now. Maybe it’s easy for you to pay the bills. Maybe saving and investing comes easily to you.



How much do you enjoy and fully appreciate the ease that is available to you? If you are habituated to noticing hardship, you won’t notice (let alone be able to experience) the ease that is available for you right now. So, perhaps the question isn’t “when does it get easier?” but rather “what’s stopping me from experiencing more ease right now?” and “how can I increase my capacity and willingness to notice and enjoy more ease in my life, as it is?” Paridhi Jain is a money and mindset coach who combines practical strategies with mindset transformation to help clients create more freedom and fulfilment in wealth, work and life. World.title: Work-from-home law delayed by Carroll weeks before planned start
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian Parliament Work-from-home law delayed by Carroll weeks before planned start Angus Delaney Updated August 11, 2026 — 2:11pm ,first published 11:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victorians will not have a legal right to work from home until at least July next year, after Labor delayed its plan to introduce the controversial law following an eleventh-hour plea from business groups. Premier Ben Carroll announced on Tuesday that as part of his government’s “reset with the business community”, the law would not come into effect until July 1, 2027, 10 months after the original intended September start date. Premier Ben Carroll, pictured last month, has delayed Labor’s work-from-home legislation. Justin McManus “I support work from home. I support flexible work. It is good for working families,” Carroll said. But he said the state’s economic health was important, and he wanted business to thrive in Victoria. “That is why I’ve delayed these changes,” he said.



The bill was expected to pass parliament’s upper house on Thursday, but the government will now delay its passage, although Carroll promised it would still pass before the November state election. He said he would consult on any “commonsense amendments”. The move to delay the legislation has been welcomed by industry and business groups, which on Monday joined forces to call for the bill to be scrapped, and warned that it risked increasing unemployment and driving investment out of the state. Tim Piper, Victorian head of the Australian Industry Group, said businesses were still concerned the legislation was going ahead at all, but there was now at least opportunity for the government to consider amendments and improvements. Piper said the government should use the delay to consider scrapping the bill entirely and conduct an economic impact statement on the potential fallout.



“When you have an economic impact statement, you can understand whether ... it’s likely to be detrimental or not. We think it is,” Piper said. Labor’s promise to legislate a right to work from home two days a week has angered business groups, which say it will send jobs and investment interstate. Getty Images The concession from Labor is a sign Carroll is following through on his commitment to be a more pro-business premier than predecessor Jacinta Allan. Though the government and opposition have reaffirmed their support for employees’ work-from-home rights, the business lobby is still pushing Labor to ditch the policy altogether, believing a face-to-face meeting with Carroll will encourage him to scrap the policy. “What we’re going to be asking him is to listen to our issues … when we give him the reasons, the rationale, the economic benefits of not doing it, we hope that he will change his mind,” Piper said.



Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Sally Curtain said the decision to pause the debate over the “divisive legislation” and listen to industry was a good start, but maintained the bill should be scrapped. Related Article Victorian Parliament Coalition to support working-from-home laws but want changes to protect businesses “The premier has been in touch with us directly and indicated he is willing to meet with us,” Curtain said in a statement. “We hope to persuade him to abandon this destructive course.”



Bran Black, chief executive of the Business Council of Australia, said while Carroll was taking the first steps towards listening to industry, the bill in any form would “compound Victoria’s economic decline”. “Already, Victoria has the highest unemployment rate in the country and the Victorian economy cannot afford another policy that drives investment and jobs away, which only hurts Victorians through lower living standards,” Black said. Cath Evans, Victorian executive director of the Property Council, said the government should use the delay to consult deeply on the legislation and examine its potentially dire economic consequences.



“This needs serious attention,” Evans said. The Coalition under Opposition Leader Jess Wilson decided not to oppose Labor’s bill and was seeking to introduce amendments to protect businesses. Related Article Victorian election Pay for the desk or pay a penalty: Inside Victoria’s strict new work-from-home rules The proposed amendments include capping “reasonable costs” an employer must pay at $1000, limiting the right to employees who primarily work in Victoria and will continue to do so (unless mutually agreed to), and delaying an employee’s right to appeal a company’s decision until next year. Shadow attorney-general James Newbury said that by pushing the promised start of the legislation back 10 months Carroll was creating instability for businesses and workers.



“His government committed to a guarantee of working from home on the first of September – he’s broken that guarantee,” Newbury said. “Victorians should know they cannot trust this man, and they cannot trust this government, despite what he guarantees, despite what this government has promised.” Major business groups warned on Monday that the proposed overhaul was another layer of red tape that would result in companies deserting Victoria and expanding their businesses interstate. Business groups have not ruled out launching or joining a potential High Court challenge against the legislation if it passes. Legal experts have cast doubt over the state government’s ability to legislate a right to work from home, as most workplace laws are under the jurisdiction of the federal government. World.title: The Luxon dilemma: Should he stay or should he go?
World.content:
Analysis: Christopher Luxon's leadership is hanging by a thread as he arrives in Wellington ready to face his opponents in caucus on Wednesday morning.

In April he stared down his agitators and called a vote of confidence in himself to prove he still had a mandate as National Party leader.

He succeeded in that vote but at the same time put an extraordinary amount of pressure on himself to personally perform better and lift his polling.

There was no chance the caucus leaking and destabilisation would stop unless that happened, and on both measures Luxon has fallen short.

On the latter, the party's polling remains woefully low - last month National was down 2.1 points in the RNZ-Reid Research poll to 28.7 percent.

It was the party's fourth consecutive decline in the Reid Research series and its weakest result since Luxon became leader in November 2021.

On the former, Luxon's personal performance has had moments of reprieve from gaffes and the occasional show of strength but that was all undone last week - a week now dubbed his worst in his prime ministership.

From apologies to business leaders and defending using an NZDF plane to fly him home after a National Party fundraiser, to an 11-year unemployment high, a call to hold a referendum on MMP blindsiding his colleagues in the process, and then a political attack on Labour that derailed into three new National taxes, Luxon went from one disaster to the next.

When Luxon fronted media in April having secured a win in that confidence vote he single-handedly blamed "speculation and rumour" and a "media soap opera" for the position he'd found himself in.

There was no self-reflection that perhaps he hadn't done enough to keep his caucus happy, listened to their concerns, taken onboard their advice, or been willing to change to try lift the party's chances ahead of the November election.

Instead he sent a message direct to the destabilisation faction of the caucus that they were to blame and he had beaten them.

When the rumoured result of that confidence vote started circling in the past week it was clear the anti-Luxon faction were saddling the horses and getting ready to go.

It's now been widely reported that vote was 27-22 and when it was put to Luxon on Saturday he didn't deny it, instead saying he had the support of his caucus.

In theory Luxon doesn't know the result, only party president Sylvia Wood and junior whip Suze Redmayne who did the count know the number, but it's possible MPs dissatisfied with Luxon have been calling around their colleagues and firming up a rough idea of where the vote landed at the time.

If it's true then it would only take three MPs flipping their vote for Luxon to be goneburger.

In the past two weeks Luxon has made two captain calls without first consulting his caucus.

The first was ruling out any arrangement with Opportunity after the election if National is in a position to govern, and the second on Thursday was a commitment to hold a referendum on the MMP voting system.

Captain's calls aren't uncommon but they are usually done from a position of strength and power by a leader who enjoys wide support from their caucus.

Both Sir John Key and Dame Jacinda Ardern made them and did so successfully. Luxon is not Key or Ardern.

If Luxon can't keep his caucus on side - something he'll already know the answer to by the time he heads into that do-or-die meeting - he'll either have to step aside to make way for a new leader or be pushed by his colleagues.

Luxon and any supporters he still has will be hitting the phones late into the evening getting an indication of whether he still has a majority backing him, and if he can win a vote if he calls one.

But that's only half of the issue.

A confidence vote was won four months ago and the prime minister was adamant it had put the matter to bed and here he is again reliving the worst 24 hours of his political career to date.

Winning a confidence vote and trying to keep his caucus in line between now and November 7 could prove more difficult than facing the reality he's no longer the man for the job.

There are just six weeks until the House rises and the official six-week campaign kicks off, and at this point the National Party billboards could be emblazoned with the face of Luxon, Nicola Willis, Erica Stanford, Chris Bishop, or some other outside chance from the front bench.

When Luxon posted on social media that he had called his caucus to Wellington he said it was his "firm belief that division and disunity are a major distraction only 90 days out from the election".

World.title: Christopher Luxon refuses to speak to media as he arrives in Wellington ahead of urgent leadership meeting
World.content:
The Prime Minister Christopher Luxon refused to speak to reporters as he made his way through Wellington Airport ahead of an urgent caucus meeting on Wednesday.

His grip on National's leadership has come under scrutiny again after a series of missteps and clashes with coalition partners, including calling for an MMP referendum.

Caucus rumblings of rolling Luxon resurfaced in reporting by the New Zealand Herald on Monday evening, and by Tuesday afternoon Luxon had decided to call the urgent in-person meeting for Wednesday morning.

Political update with Craig McCulloch Morning Report Download MP3 6m

"It is my firm belief that division and disunity are a major distraction only 90 days out from the election," he wrote.

The issue needed to be resolved quickly, he said.

Stepping off the plane in Wellington on Tuesday afternoon, Luxon told reporters, "talk to you tomorrow ... take care team".

National MPs were mostly keeping quiet on the matter, and had cleared their diaries on Wednesday morning - including the party's deputy Nicola Willis and third-ranked MP Chris Bishop both cancelling interview slots scheduled with RNZ's Morning Report.

Bishop, who is often tipped as a leadership contender, had two scheduled media events on Tuesday and faced questions about Luxon at both.

National's Chris Bishop. (File photo) RNZ / Mark Papalii

He threw his full support behind his leader and warned colleagues against leaking to media.

Asked again about the leadership at the second event, Bishop told reporters there was no update.

"Mate, we were just down the road in South Auckland 90 minutes ago," he said.

He then gave a running commentary about what had happened in those 90 minutes, including getting a coffee, preparing for his next speech and calling his wife.

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown was with Bishop at the second event, standing beside him as they both took questions. Brown was asked if he wanted Bishop to be Prime Minister.

"Now there's a tricky question," Brown responded, chuckling.

Brown said Bishop was a "good bloke" but had a bit of competition for the National leadership, including from Defence Minister Chris Penk.

Penk had also been at the event, but did not stick around for the standup.

Brown said what he would really like was for the New Zealand public to choose the prime minister "instead of Winston Peters doing it."

National's James Meager told RNZ said he "absolutely" had confidence in Luxon.

"The media can interview themselves all they like about that, but its not anything we're interested in."

Meager suggested not trusting everything in the media, and referenced being quoted in the Herald in November "making claims about things about me that were entirely untrue, which have been repeated throughout the media despite the fact them not being true."

It had been reported that Meager was canvassing support for Bishop to take over as leader.

"It's false, and I denied it," Meager said.

"I'm not really interested in people's views on speculation about any of that sort of stuff, because as far as I'm concerned, it's nonsense."

He said he'd had no conversations with his fellow MPs about a change in leadership in recent days.

Senior MP Todd McClay also said he was behind Luxon.

"He's doing a good job, he's an excellent Prime Minister, he has my one hundred percent support."

Meanwhile Labour's deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni wouldn't speculate but said: "clearly they're not performing very well and there's unrest in the National party caucus - hence why they're meeting."

Sepuloni said disunity or ruptures in the National party caucus was not an issue for Labour.

World.title: Oranga Tamariki under fire for telling police to wait six months for investigation information
World.content:
The chief victims advisor has "significant concern" about revelations Oranga Tamariki told police they would have to wait almost six months for information requested as part of a investigation.

The Children's Commissioner is also "deeply concerned" by the details that have emerged.

It comes after RNZ received more than 100 pages of emails under the Official Information Act (OIA) in relation to Operation Hark.

Operation Hark began after concerns were raised in May about Detective Inspector Kevan Verry's handling of a historical sexual abuse case in Northland that had sat for a couple of years with no investigation.

That led to more than 50 child protection and sexual assault cases being re-opened.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Police are also reviewing their systems used to manage child protection and sexual assault cases and have established an External Advisory Group to provide external oversight and assurance.

The emails obtained under the OIA revealed that On 25 June, police sent an information request to Oranga Tamariki. Five days later they got a response from OT saying they would grant their request.

"As we are currently receiving more requests than anticipated, we are experiencing delays in processing these."

OT said it would supply the information by 7 December.

Internal police emails reveal the request was urgent because investigators needed information that would help identify the victim including the names and details of children placed in a person's care.

Police then emailed a staff member at OT saying they were taking another look at an older file "which we believe holds risk for both police and OT".

"It has come to our attention because of a sensitive matter which I can't elaborate on at this time.

"What I can say is that this IR relates to [redacted] so there is obvious risk and additional scrutiny attached to this."

Police asked for the request to be "escalated in the priority queue".

"The estimated response time of December 2026 by OT is going to create significant problems in addressing the risk."

It was not until 6 July, after media began asking questions, that the agency was formally told about what police had dubbed Operation Hark.

Chief victims advisor Ruth Money. NZME / Alex Burton

Chief victims advisor Ruth Money told RNZ on Tuesday she had "significant concern" that OT told police it would take almost six months to get the requested information.

"As the Chief Victims Advisor, I want to understand why this is the case.

"For example, was the initial Police request not clear, or is OT that under resourced that children at risk have to wait this long? I will be following this up because I am sure all the victims and whanau across New Zealand also wish to understand this."

She would also be seeking to understand how a file that had a victim attached to it could be closed "and then seemingly Police do not have the victims details."

"These types of issues are why the external reference group exists and these are the questions we seek to understand and more importantly ensure processes are changed so they are not repeated."

Children's Commissioner Jane Searle said in a statement to RNZ on Tuesday she was deeply concerned by the details that have emerged through Operation Hark "because at stake is the safety and wellbeing of tamariki".

"When there are concerns about the safety of a child, agencies need to be able to work together effectively and share relevant information promptly so that risks can be properly assessed and acted on.

"I understand that the cases are now being looked at with urgency. It is important that there is a thorough examination of what happened, why any delays occurred, and whether there are wider systemic issues that need to be addressed."

Searle said her team had been briefed on the approach police were taking through Operation Hark, and had been assured that police would keep them informed of any significant developments.

"Complainants and the public need to have confidence in reporting systems. Ultimately, the protection and safety of tamariki need to be at the centre of every response. We must have confidence that when concerns are raised about a child's safety, those concerns will be taken seriously and acted on promptly to protect children from harm."

DCE Tamariki and Whānau Services, Thomas Ronan, says all information requests are triaged for urgency.

Ronan said there are multiple ways police can contact Oranga Tamariki.

"These include filing a report of concern about child safety concerns, and requesting information about specific individuals at a local level through the Child Protection Protocol."

"The information request made to Oranga Tamariki in June 2026 did not go through these channels and was about an adult."

As a standard information request which was given routine priority by police it was treated as a Privacy Act Request, Ronan said.

"All requests for information are triaged for urgency, including those from police. After receiving the request, we corresponded with police to confirm the level of urgency."

"After police confirmed the request was urgent, we prioritised accordingly and the initial information release happened on 15 July 2026, 13 working days after receiving the request."

Nine reports of concern

Oranga Tamariki deputy chief executive Thomas Ronan earlier told RNZ OT had completed a review of all cases identified by police as potentially impacted and which involved children, all of whom were under 18 at the time of reporting to police.

"We did not identify any cases requiring urgent intervention to keep children safe.

"However, we continue to work with police locally to consider each case, share information, and determine any further actions required."

Asked how many of the Child Protection Protocol cases required further action by OT, Ronan said the agency had worked with police on most of the cases identified thus far to determine what further response was appropriate. This included engaging with children and families.

"Nine reports of concern have been created as a result of the police and Oranga Tamariki review of the identified cases," he said.

A report of concern is a notification to Oranga Tamariki about suspected abuse, neglect, harm, or wellbeing concerns for a child or young person.

RNZ also approached police for comment on the OIA including why the victim's name was not known and why Oranga Tamariki was not informed of the investigation before 6 July.

In response, Detective Superintendent Keith Borrell said police had made specific enquiries with OT "during an early and sensitive stage of our investigations".

"During the initial assessment phase of Operation Hark we were working to understand the scale of the situation. We have shared more fulsome information once it was appropriate to do so with OT."

World.title: Christopher Luxon calls urgent meeting to resolve 'increased speculation' about leadership
World.content:
Political update with Craig McCulloch Morning Report Download MP3 6m

The Prime Minister has called for an "urgent-in person" caucus meeting in Wellington on Wednesday morning.

It comes amid renewed pressure on Christopher Luxon's leadership.

Luxon wrote on social media on Tuesday, after postponing various prior arrangements, that it was "clear from various media reports and conversations there is increased speculation about my leadership".

"It is my firm belief that division and disunity are a major distraction only 90 days out from the election.

"I also believe this distraction is unfair to the New Zealand people, and dedicated National Party candidates, supporters and volunteers, when there is so much at stake."

For those reasons, he wrote, the issue "needs to be resolved quickly".

"I am calling an urgent in-person Caucus meeting tomorrow at 9:30am in Wellington to resolve the issue."

Moments before the social media post was published, Luxon's team abruptly postponed an RNZ podcast interview which had been scheduled for this afternoon.

Earlier today, National's Chris Bishop and Rima Nakhle threw their full support behind Christopher Luxon as his leadership comes under renewed pressure.

The Prime Minister last week endured days of mishaps and missteps and started this week inadvertently talking about three taxes the National Party may introduce if back in government.

He and his deputy, Nicola Willis, had called a press conference on Sunday to put pressure on Labour to sign up to its Budget responsibility rules, yet by his Monday morning media round Luxon was instead explaining that a fuel excise tax, bed tax, and bank tax would be on the table under a future National-led government.

Mixed responses from MPs

On Monday night the NZ Herald reported National MPs had spent the day on the phones with one confirming they had fielded "several" phone calls about a potential leadership change.

"There's going to be change in the top job. It's just a question of who is going to be it", the NZ Herald reported the MP to have said.

Bishop, who was opening a pedestrian bridge at a railway station in Auckland alongside local MP Rima Nakhle on Tuesday morning, confirmed the party caucus would hold a meeting on Zoom later in the day, as earlier reported by RNZ, but he denied Luxon's leadership would be on the agenda.

"I'm not talking to you about the internal machinations of what time the Zoom appointments are, but there is a meeting tonight."

He said it wasn't unusual to hold a meeting during a recess week.

It is not known if the Tuesday Zoom meeting will still go ahead.

"Last week the PM apologised for remarks about Rotorua, and obviously there's been a bit over the MMP call, but we back our leader, and you know he's made his position clear in relation to the MMP referendum that we'll be taking that to the election. It's not going to be the focus of the campaign, as he says in his own words."

RNZ spoke to about 10 MPs on Monday night and received a mixture of responses.

Some said they wouldn't comment, while another said they couldn't comment, and others denied there were any leadership murmurings or that they knew about them.

One MP said the direct quotes in the reporting suggested there must be some truth to it, and at least one MP said it was nonsense.

Chris Bishop dismissed the suggestion there were phone calls on Monday about the National party leadership. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Often tipped to be a leadership contender, Bishop has previously denied plotting a challenge, insisting late last year that Luxon remained the best person to be prime minister.

He dismissed the suggestion there were phone calls on Monday about the National party leadership, saying he talked to caucus members "all the time about a whole range of different things".

"Yesterday was a cabinet day, so you know clearly there were conversations between ministers and between MPs."

Bishop said it was "unhelpful" MPs were speaking to media and encouraged his colleagues not to.

"All I would say is you know people people shouldn't be talking to media like that."

Bishop said he was "getting on with the job", but then continued to answer questions from media about the leadership issue.

He said he hadn't spoken to Erica Stanford - also considered a contender - about the leadership, nor had he spoken to any of his colleagues.

Nakhle also backed Luxon saying he was "the man and the boss" and she backed him "150 percent".

Luxon says his caucus backs him

On Saturday it was put to Luxon whether the confidence vote he called on his leadership back in April had resulted in a caucus split of 27 votes to 22.

He responded, "I have the support of my caucus - I'm very confident in my leadership."

On Tuesday Bishop told RNZ it wasn't worth speculating on the leadership vote, as only "two or three" people in the country know the results for certain.

"I don't know where that reporting came from. The caucus vote is secret, and I don't know what the result was," he said.

It was speculation about whether Luxon was up to the job and had the backing of his caucus to stay on as leader that prompted him to test his support with a vote in April.

At the time Luxon said that had put the rumour to bed and he had his caucus behind him.

Just four months later MPs appear to be musing about the prospect of changing leaders again.

While some spoken to by RNZ on Monday night said they supported Luxon, it wasn't unanimous.

There has been agitating since late last year from some MPs concerned Luxon's lack of personal popularity was also dragging the party vote down, and some MPs would lose their seats in Parliament if he didn't improve.

The latest RNZ-Reid Research poll in July had National down 2.1 points to 28.7 percent, its fourth consecutive decline in the Reid Research series and its weakest result since Luxon became leader in November 2021.

While Luxon's confidence vote win looked to have given him some reprieve, his performance in recent weeks has done little to convince concerned MPs they'll be safe come November 7.

Chris Bishop said he hadn't spoken to Erica Stanford about the leadership, nor had he spoken to any of his colleagues. RNZ / Nick Monro

Last Monday Luxon apologised to leaders from the Rotorua Business Chamber after he criticised them for having a "parent-child mentality" and relying on government too much.

He also faced questions about his foreign minister Winston Peters, and why he wasn't doing anything to reprimand him after labelling his comments about another MP, "racist".

Luxon then had to justify his use of a New Zealand Defence Force plane flying him home from a National Party fundraising dinner, and on the same day unemployment hit a record 11-year high.

On Thursday he was using talkback radio to make a captain's call to hold a referendum on MMP, which blindsided his own caucus.

World.title: The hidden costs of failed building inspections
World.content:
More than 20,000 building inspections fail each year, creating tens of millions of dollars in avoidable costs, a construction industry consultant says.

Mark Kirby has just completed his research into this issue, surveying more than 100 residential construction professionals, including general managers, construction managers, site managers, project managers and subcontractors.

He found there was a systemic culture that accepted failed building inspections as part of the normal building process.

Kirby also found that this failure was becoming so routine it was often treated as part of the building process - rather than something to be prevented.

The hidden costs of failed building inspections Nine To Noon Download MP3 16m

In Auckland about 160,000 building inspections are carried out every year - about 800 every working day - and as many as 37 percent fail that first inspection.

Kirby told Nine to Noon there was a wide range of things that led to that failure of the first inspection, including plumbing and carpentry framing.

He said these results highlighted the need for a review, especially with a push towards self-certification.

"The system has let us down. My research traced it back to the mid-1980s where we had a policy change there that's really put the industry in a 'build now, fix later' type mindset, that prioritised cost and speed over quality.

"And you can see that through history with the leaky homes crisis, changes to the apprenticeship schemes, and now in the current day, it's $2.5 billion a year that it's costing us in defects and rework. So we haven't fixed that problem from back in the 1980s and I think it's getting worse."

He said the move towards self-certification was a great opportunity for the system to be reformed.

Kirby said it was not the actual defects that were slowing down productivity in the sector, it was the culture that was the issue, and that quality was the driver of productivity.

"We lack a quality culture throughout the industry and that's the primary constraint limiting our through-put."

He said there were 13,000 more homes that could be funded and built if the quality was right the first time.

"Think of the productivity gain we'd get from that, think of the boom and bust cycle that the housing policy now creates, a lot of people out of work, going to other countries, there's an opportunity there, a real opportunity that we can grasp to help improve society and productivity."

He said while some builders blamed the council for the wait to get a re-inspection, "the problem is that we should have done it right the first time".

World.title: Over half a million people owe tax. How did this happen?
World.content:
Inland Revenue needs to be asking questions about how billions of dollars in tax debt has been allowed to accumulate, one economist says.

As of March this year, more than half-a-million people had debt to Inland Revenue. Overall tax debt sat at $9.4 billion, of which Inland Revenue said 62 percent, or $5.9b, was collectable.

Total tax debt was less than $6b in 2023.

Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

Micro and small-to-medium businesses were responsible for 65 percent of outstanding tax debt, and GST and employer deductions such as PAYE were 57 percent of overall debt.

The rate of tax debt increase has slowed to 1.6 percent a year by March this year, down from 27.1 percent a year in the year to March 2024.
